THE SAINT HELENS & DISTRICT TRAMWAYS COMPANY. Incorporated by special act or Parliament, embodying sections 3 and 19 and pacts 2 and 3 of the Tramways Act, 1870, and the Companies Clauses Consohdatlon Act, and other general statutory provisions. The liabgity of sharehold« rs is limited to the amount of their sbares. Authorised share capital £70,000 in 7000 shares of £lO each. 4857 shares are now offered for subscription, to complete an issue of MO shares 1000 having been already accepted by the contractor in part payment for works, and 1143 having been subscribed for locally at par. Payments : RI per share`on application, Ll per share on allot- . . . .
ment, and the balance asthe._.-director; may determine but

(as provided in the act) by calls not exceediCag ea per share, made at intervals of not less than two months. • DIRECTORS. William Busby, Esq. (Messrs. W. and D. Busby, Liverpool). Chairman of the Wigan Tramways Company, Vice-Chair- man of the Wirral Tramways Company, and the Walla,ey Trarnways Company, Iluyton Park, Lancashire, Chairman. Mr. Alderman Harrison, Miyor of St Helens (late a Director of the St. Helens Gas Company), Market-street, Bt. Helens, Tice-Chairman, Philip Eberle, Esq., Director of the Liverpool United Tram- ways and Omnibus Company and the Chester Tramways Company, Waterloo, near Liverpool. Castle Spenceiv, Esq., Chairman of Prescot Local Board, Elm House, Knowsley. Joseph Riley, Esq., Hall-steeet, St, Helens.

BANKERS. Parr's Banking Company, Limited, St. Helens, or their Agents. Messrs. Glyn, Mills, Currie, and Co., London. ENGINEER. Charles H. Beloe, Esq., M.1.C.E., 13, Harrington-street, Liverpool, Engineer to the Southport, Wirral, Wallasey, Wigan, and Bootle Tramways. SOLICITOR.
Henry Lindon Riley, Lq , Hardshaw-street, St. Helens. BROKER.
S. De Pere Beauclerk, Esq., 2, Copthall-buildings, B.C. AUDITORS. T. W. Read, Esq., 30, Castle-street, Liverpool. Robert Slater, Esq. (Messrs. Slater and Fickton), St. Helens.
• _ SECRETARY. Mr. John Hammill, Consular Agent, be., St. Helens. Offices-23, Hardshaw-street, Bt. Helens.
PROSPECTUS.

This company was Incorporated with the object of, con- structing an efficient system of Tramways in the borough and populous neighbourhood of St. Helens, in the county of Lan- caster, within twelve miles of Liverpool. " • " • "

The. Tramways authorised by the'Act consists of a main line passing through the centre of Bt. Helens, and connecting St. Helens on the one side with the neighbouring town of Prescot, and on the other side with Haydock, with branches from the centre of St. Helens to Denton's Green on the one side and Sutton on the other. The line to Haydock will run directly through the important townships of Parr and the populous neighbourhood of Blackbrook. The future of a tramway system traversing the (principal routes of such populous district cannot, it is expected, be other- wise than highly satisfactory. The works for the line connecting Prescot with the ontskirts of St. Helens are in a very forward state, and the whole main line from Prescot to Haydock, through the centre of St. Helens, can be completed before the Ist of July in the present year. The construction of the branch lines to Denton's-green and Sut- ton will be postponed to another year, and an application is now before Parliament to obtain the necessary ex ension of time for the completion ef this part of the undertaking. St. Helens, as is well known, is the seat of important works In the chemical, copper, earthenware, glass, and iron trades, and is also the centre of an extensive coal field. The present population of the borough ',is estimated by the municipal authorities at 57,524, and there is a well populated neighbour- hood outside the actual borough boundary. The lines of the proposed tramway pass the town hall and railway station, and through many of the principal streets of St. Helens. Present is the seat of the celebrated watch movement manu- facture. It has a population of about 5,000, and is nearly four miles distant from St. Helens. The Tramway between St. Helens and Present will run past the residential district of Bt. Ann's, and the large estate known as Eccieston Park, now in course of development. It also passes one of the entrances to , Knowsley Park, and will afford accommodatim to the residents on Thatto Sheath and in the township of Whlston. The whole district on each side of the old turnpike-road, between St. Helens and Present, may be regarded as building land, and a large part is at present being rapidly developed by the erectien of residences for those engaged in the manufactures at St. Helens; and it may be anticipated that at no distant date Present and Bt. Helens will he connected by houses. A magni- ficent park at Eceleston, half way between the Iwo towns, hits been recently offered to St. Helens, and will doubtless be the cause of a large traffi3 on the Tramway. Haydock is about four miles from St. Helens. It is a con- siderable mining centre, and at the present time has a popula- tion approaching 6,000. The number of passengers at present conveyed between St. Helens and Present by the existing omnibus service is so large that there can be no doubt but that the superior accommodation provided by the tramway will produce large traffic returns. The only public conveyance at present between St. Helens and Haydock is a service of open waggonettes, some 26 of which ply for hire, and as the route is densely populated for Its entire length, a large traffic is confidently anticipated from this por- tion of thetine..

—..-- ---- - The special Act of Parliament confers powers upon the com- pany to establish a parcel service, and from this source a sub- stantial addition to the income is anticipated. A plan of the district, indicating the sites of 's. large number of its works and collieries and the route of the proposed tram- way, accompanies the prospectus. The cont, act for the main line between Prescot and St. Helens Was entered into in the month of September, 1880, and the -works from Present to the outskirts of St. Helens are being carried on under the personal superintendence of the engineer of the company, who has had very considerable experience in th& construction of tramways. The work already contracted for comps lees the laying down of fol2r miles of line and the supply of five cars, constructed on Eade's reversible pattern, and the erection of stables, car sheds, and a foreman's house, the land being found by the company, the contractor having agreed to accept payment in fully paid up shares of the com- pany to the extent of 219,000 on account of the contract price of £20,000 for this section of the line. The cost of supplying the cars and erecting the stables. sheds, Ac., as above, is estimated at £5,000, leaving £20,000, or about £5,000 per mile, as the cost of construction of the tramway itself, the section between St. Helens and Haydock can be let at a similty price, and the contract for that section will be entered into immediately after the present issue of shares has been carried out. The rails are of steel throughout, and the line is being con- structed in the most substantial manner, according to stringent specifications prepared by the engineer of the company. BRUNNER, MOND AND CO., LIMITED. . Incorporated under the Companies' Acts, 1862 to 1880. CAluxer,.—£6oo,ooo, IN 60,000 SHARES OF RIO EACH. First Isuie.—£36o.ooo, in 36,000 Shares of £lO each, on which the sum of £5 per Share will be at first called up. Directors. JOHN CROBFIELD, Chairman (Joteph Crosfield and Bons, Soap Manufacturers, Warrington) JOHN TOMLINSON BRUNNER, Managing Director (Win- nington , Northwich.) LI7DWIG MOND. Managing Director (Winnington, North- wich). CHARLES MENZIES HOLLAND (Field House, Cheater, Director of the Greenbank Alkali Works Company, Limited, St. Helens). EDWARD MILNER, J.P. (Springfield, Warrington, Salt Manufacturer, Marston, Northwl ch). Bankers. PARR'S BANKING COMPANY (Limited), Warrington and Branches. _

div.head: Solicitors.
div.p: Solicitors.
H. FORSHAW & HAWKINS, 2, Harrington-street, Liver- pool. A. & J. E. FLETCHER, Northwich, Cheshire.
Auditor. T ROMAB WILLIAM RgAD, 30, Castle-street, Liverpool.

- - Secretary. THOMAS HUNGERFORD FORGAN. Offices. WINNIN GTON, NEAR NORTFI W ICR ABRIDGED PROSPECTUS. This Company has been registered with a Capital of £600,000, divided into 60,000 Shares of £lO each. It is not intended in the first instance to issue more than 36,001 shares, of which 18,000 will be .Preference . Shares, entitling to a first charge upon the profits limited to seven pounus per centum per annum, _ _ _

The Company is formed for the purpose of carrying on the manufacture of Alkali by the Ammonia Process on a very ex- tensive] scale, and with this object to purchase and to largely extend the business of Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Co., of Win- nington and Bandbach, the only Manufacturers in the United Kingdom working this process. The pur hase will include two Alkali Works, a valuable Free- hold Estate of 140 acres, very valuable Patent Rights, and other property. The business will be taken to as a going concern as on the Ist January, 1881. The vendors will receive and pay all trade debts due to and owing by them on that day, and the profits there- after will belong to the Company, the Venders receiving in- terest at the rate of £5 per cent, per annum thence up to the completion of the purchase. The price to be paid to the Vendors for the several properties enumerated above is £200,000, from which sum will be deducted the amount of a certain mortgage affecting the property (No. 3) for £s,7oo,—the liability thereunder being taken over by the Company—and the net amount will be paid by the allotment to the Ve Mors at par of 12,000 fully, paid up £lO Ordinary Snares and the balance in cash.

Tile Company acquires these properties on very favourable terms, and obtains full value for the price paid, as will be readily seen from the following statement as to how the main items have been dealt with. The works have been put down at their cost to the Vendors, the 129 acres at Winnington have been taken at a recent valuation by Messrs. Picton, Chambers, and Bradley, of Liverpool, and the sum of £lO,OOO only has been added for Patent Eights, Trade Mark, and Goodwill. No promotion money has been or will be paid, and the Vendors will defray all the expeases up to and including the formation ' of the Company. Arrangements have been made with Messrs. Brunner and Mend under which they are to act as Managing Directors at salaries of £1,500 per annum each. The Company will take over the stocks payling for them the amount at which they stand in the books on the Ist January, 1881. The Company will also lave the benefit of advantageous forward contracts for the purchase of raw materials, and for the sale of finished products. The Vendors have during a very few years. developed their business at so rapid a rate that they rank to-day amongst the largest Alkali Manufacturers in the world ;—during 1875 their total make was only 2,500 tons, whilst last year it reached 18,800 tons. They have step by step brought their special manufacture to great perfection, and they now produce their Pure Alkali for considerably Less money than the cost of the common Soda Ash made by their competitirs. Their brand stands first in the market, and commands a higher price than any other. The Vendors have decided to convert their busiNess hat° a Limited Company, tor the reason that in their opinion the re- sults achieved and the prospects before them now warrant an enlargement, of their operations to an extent beyond the power of private means. Already a large amount of capital has been expended in preparations for extending the Winuington Works, and it is calculated that the first issue of Capital need only be partially called up to enable the Company to complete exten- sions of these Works sufficient to treble their production. The extraordinary success attained by the Vendors during a prolonged period of severe depression in trade is ample proof of the great dividend-earning power of the business acquired by the Company, and the intended increase of the make will ren- der it still more profitable in the future. The Directors have no hesitation in expressing their opinion that the Ordinary Share Capital of the Company will for years to come earn a minimum profit of Fifteen per cent, per annum, a figure which in every year of fairly good trade will be largely exceeded, and they confidently recommend the Shares as an un- usually sound and profitable investment. The Directors now offer to the public a portion of the Ordin- ary and of the Preference Shares of the Company. Application for Shares are to be made to the Bankers of the Company. Applications may be made either for Preference Shares alone, —or for Ordinary Shares and Preference Shares together,—but every application for Ordinary Shares is to be coupled with an application for at the least an equal number of Preference Shares. The sum of .21 to be paid on application; £3 on allot- ment; and £1 on the Ist of July. The Call due in July upon the Preference Shares may be paid up in advance on allot- ment. The Directors do not contemplate making any further Call during the year 1881. The only Agreement entered into by or on behalf of the Company is one dated the 25th day of February, 1881, made between John Tomlinson Brunner and Ludwig Mond of the one part and the Company of the other part, being the Agreement for Sale and Purchase of the before-mentioned Estates mid Business. A copy of this Agreement and of the Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company may be seen at the Offices of the Solicitors. Prospectuses and Forms of Appli- cation may be obtained from the Secretary, from the Bankers, or from the Solicitors.

This Company is formed to acquire that portion of the Mills and Property of Messrs. R. and G. Light°ller called the Vic- toria Mills, which were partially de•troyed by fire some time since. The Estate consists of 8,612 square yards of freehold land, at .the low rental of £lO7 13s. per annum. The Property has recently been valued in its present state by Mr. John Hoyle, the well-known mill valuer, at £11,840. A Provisional Agreement has been made between Mr. Fred. J. Light 311er on the one part, as representing Messrs. R. & G. Light°ller, and the Directors for the Company, by which the whole of this property has been agreed to be sold to the Com- pany at the low price of £7,000, including the right to use the Trade Mark and Tickers of Messrs. R. and G. Lightoller, whose Yarns have fOr the past century been well known in the Man- chester and Eastern Markets. The Mill when rebuilt will be entirely fireproof, five storeys high, with cel'ar ; will hold about 69,000 spindles, viz :-32,400 twist and 36,600 weft (with preparation), calculated to produce 51,0001b5. of Yarn per week. The Yarns which the Mill will be laid out to spin are (average) 32's Twist and 38's Weft. '- Mr. Fred. J. Lightoller has agreed; to take £lO,OOO worth of shares in the new Company, and to allow the purchase money to be paid one-third each year, so as to complete in three years; also to give his services for three years at least to the Company as Managing Director. Messrs. Platt, of Oldham, and others have given estimates for the Machinery: 36,600 weft spindles. 32,400 twist spindles, 8,272 roving spindles, 1,.792 intermediate spindles, 761 slub spindles, 10 drawing frames, 60 double cards; seutching-room machinery in proportion. Messrs. J. Clayton and Co., of Preston, have given estimates for the rebuilding of the mills, new gearing, eagines, and new bolters, Sc. After carefully going into the estimates of sundry well-known firms, including the above mentioned, the Directors conclude that a Mill of the most modern proportions, entirely fireproof, and fitted with the best machinery and engines, will be built at a cost (estimated) of 225. per spindle—a lower price than any such Mill has been put up for in Lancashire for many years. These advantngeous terms, and the excellent position of the Mill for obtaining good hands and convenience of carriage (being within 200 yards of the Lancashire and Yorkshire and London and North-Westera Railway Companies' Goods Sta- tions), will, the Directors feel sure, secure a profitable working of the concern.

As a great portion of the capital is already subscribed for, an early application for shares is desirable. For further particulars, apply to M. F. WADDELL, SOCtefAty (pro tem.), at the Mill, either personally or by letter, or to the Directors. Prospectuses may also be obtained at the Mill. Applications for shares to be made in accordance with the form accompanying the Prospectus, Messrs. OUNLIFFES BROOKS A CO., Manctester. Do. Do. Blackburn. MANCHESTER AND SALFORD BANK, Chorley. THE MINER. DOM down; down, from the light subshine, Isown-ttrie depth* of theft caverned mine; • • ' Duff, puff, puff, the engine roars, human frAght to the depths it lowers. The gay flowers bloom with surrounding fair, , The gmd birds sing, but not down there; An beauties of nature are lost to sight In the cold earth's bowels of darkest night. • lfrom early morn till set of sun He taileth hard till his work is done; t Danger's gaunt form in secret lurks. Wbere the unsuspecting miner works. • And often grim death, unseen by him. Aeconiparifes danger through caverns aim. When yeu Weak at will in the bright sunshine. When nature is charming, and glad birds chime. When you breathe the health-inspiring air, Oh, think of the miner toiling down there; When you At by your cheerful fireside bright. And faniastizt figures you shape in its light, With your wife and children, safe from harm, , Enjoying with you the firelight warm— ' Let year thonghtl descmd to earth's dark caves. . Where a thousand dangers the miner braves To gt t the coal, risking life and limb. ' Tbenfrom toy heart's depths feel pity for him; Oh, treat, him not harshly or turn prnudly aside. Ifeath his rugged exterior rests manly pride Rerisks touch for thee in the darkness dim ; Let thy laegt, in return, feel plO for him. Ft. Helens. J. G. PIokEkSGILL.

• A PLEA. FOR IRELAND. /By an Englishman.) Hibernia bleeds at limit, the gaping wounds kept rankling, festering for a thousand Years Now cry in piteous tones for quick relief. The wrongs and insults in her breast she bears Are matchless inthe misery of man, For number, magnitude, intensity. -g two wonders (having writhed beneath the heel s of her misguided sister—Britannia, Who with cold, blind, unnatural sympathy, Considered all the wrongs as kindness done, Bedeved Hibernia imbecile and weak, Contemptiblo, beneath a sister's care), That Erin's woe* now loudly finds vent? Thou stretch'st thy philanthrocic helping hand To nations in the utmost East and West, Acknowledging as brothers o en scarce men, But deaf to cries, entreaties, threats, which rose From thy twin-sister pining at thy side. Rise great world-healer! soothe thy sister's pain! Cut out he knawing cancer Min her breast! - Apply soft balm where ills needed most! And let not cries of children fraught with ira Deer thee from thy sore and thankless task. Nor cut the deeper, since she feels the pain. To feed thy prile, much thus far wrongly placed; But with humility and filial love, Heal up the wound and ems the schipg heart. And from henceforth let love, on equal terms, Cement the bands which sisters' hearts unite; Then law-abiding love will flow, where now Swift courses in her veins a deadly hate. ALPHA. Warrington, February 16th, 1881. 1.

A. LITTLE CRIPPLE. Though he was not sturdy, or strong as the others, And aged before boyhood, decrepit and small, ' Such depth hath the yearning of fathers end mothers, They loved him at home, as their treasure, their all. A cripple past hope, he was doomed to wear crutches. And life promised nought save a burden of ills; Yet his eyes had the light which softens and touches— The look of the reindeer at bay on the hills. He wistfully noted the sports and the gambols His brothers and kisters enjoyed the long day; Alas I not for him were the saces and rambles • In the meadows so near, yet so far away 1. For the sun might shine brightly, and breezes breathe mellew And earth laugh to scorn the dull thoughts of the sage; Like some sad pining bird, this poor little fellow Drank in the glad life through the bars of a cage. But days dawning sadly, and dimming so slowly, Were brightened at least through affection's truts worth; For the love that all bore him was pure and was holy, The love that can make a sweet garden of earth. And when at His beck'ning this child and this cripple • Was summoned where sorrow and death hold no place. The close of his life seemed the close of a ripple, ' So peaceful the look on the wan little face. • How vain, then, the thoughethat His mercy is narrow I How empty the doubt of the "sceptical mind I" Each day brings its crumb for the snow-frozen sparrow, And love for the helplessethe halt, and the blind Cassell's Family Magazine.

A Boston artist claims to have painted an orange peel on the sidewalk so nattually that six fat men slipped upon it -before the deception as discovered. An old author quaintly remarks :—Avoid arguments with ladies. In spinning warns among silks and satins a man •is sure to be worsted and twisted; and when a man is worsted and twisted he may consider himself wound up. Snowsteituis ars rare and strange in New Orleans, and it is said of an old Slave whk, for the first time saw the flakes falling that he called his master and said that it was rain- ing cottbn. Eugene, Oregon, has an ordinance for the punishment at any person "lying drunk across the sidewalk.' A man was recently arrested for the offence, but was discharged by the. magistrates because the testimony went to show that he was lying along the sidewalk in a longitudinal direction. They tell of a very cultured divine in Boston who, instead of saying" The collection wilt now be taken up," impres- sively remarks, "The accumulation of moneys will now en- .sue.' But a Philadelphia clergyman, a great athlete and lover of sports, forgot himself once, and said, "Here endeth the lint innings—let us pray." Was there ever a better example of the witty and concise form of expression common to the real Western American than the answer of the grim man of the Sierras, who, when asked about the character of a neighbour, sententiously re- plied, " Mister, I don't know very much about him, but my, impression is that he'd make a first-class stranger ?" During a dense fog a large river steamer had to cast anchor. A traveller, anxious to go ahead, came to the man at the wheel and asked why they stopped. "Too much fog—can't see the river." "But you can see the stars overhead!' "Yes," replied the sailor, "but until the biler busts we ain't going that way." A USE FOR RICHES.—Gen. Sheridan was recently coming over from Boston in a sleeping car, where he had a whole seetion. He was sitting on the lower berth in the morning, about to put his shoes on, when he was accosted by a kind- looking gentleman opposite, who was also putting on his shoes, with the inquiry "My friend, are you a rich man?" George looked astonished, but answered the pleasant-faced, tired-looking gentleman with a "Yes, I'm tolerably rich." A pause occurred, and then another question: "How rich are you ?" "About 700,000 dollars or 800,000. Why?" "Well," said the old man," if I were as rich as you say you are, and snored as loud as I know you do, I would hire a whole sleeping car every time I travelled." A SHARP-WITTED Boy.—An amusing story is told of the late Bishop Wilberforce's school life. The boys' study-room was a large apartment in an upper storey, quite as favour- able for sport as for study. One day they were uproarious, and shaking the whole house with their racket, when the teacher, after several fruitless warnings, rushed upstairs, cane in hand, prepared for sharp action. Young Wilberforce was nearest the door, and seemed doomed to be the first vic- tim. Bat, quick as lightning, he caught a Jewish boy by the coll4r, swung him round with his back towards the teacher, and said, with a merry twinkle in his eye, "First the Jew, sir, and then the Gentile." The joke disarmed the teacher, and both Jew and Gentile escaped. A good Paris story, now current, is that of the Abb6 Ter- raison, who had rooms on the upper floor of the house of a relative, the celebrated lawyer of the same name. When going out, he wonld corn,. down stairs fully dressed, with the exception of nis petub.e and his shoes. In the base- ment he would leave his red night-cap, and slippers of the same colour, and properly equip hims.lf fo.• the street. One day he came down stairs so much ad in reading a h e Pont volume of Homer that be forgottheneethsouflara preparationss for his walk, and going out, promenaded St. Michel in red cap and slippers. the passers- by coursee passers- by lanabed immoderately, but the/good abbe heeded. them h not. Finally an old woman called his attention to Is con- dition, and gravely thanking her, he returned a. his street toilet. As he entered the house he quietly re- marked, "I have been affording the people of Paris an en- tertainment which it cost them nothing 10 witness, and me

nothing to give." COLOSIL JONES.—A couple of old darkies met tohHe other day, day, and began talking over m ,tters and things. old Colonel Jones comb" on, what used to own you before O war? He is so ole he must he gettin' to be childish and losin' his reasoning powers." Don't know nuifin' about him. Hain't seen him since befoth last Christmas." "Why, what's de matter ?" "Ain't got no use for such old gem- mans. Last time I was dat, I fotched him a big red fish I had cotched. I tole him ef he would 'gimme a table-knife I would scrape an' clean de fish. What do &pose he Bed?" "Asked yer to come in and get a dram and chat a while about ole times on de ole plantat ion." "No, sah. He tole me ef I couldn't borry a table-knife from some of de neigh- bors, dat he would radder clean de fish himself. I s'pose he was a-feared I'd be keerless in handin' de knife back when I got done wid it" The other darkey rubbed his chin and re- marked, "I see by dat ar dat de ole man's still got de use of his reasonin' powers." " SHAKSPERE'S Boys."—" When Shakspere fled to London from the terrors of a criminal prosecution, his first expe- dient was to wait at the door of the playhouse, and hold the horses of those who had no servants, that they might be ready again after the performance. In this office be became SO conspicuous for his care and readiness, that in a short time every man as he alighted called for Will Shaks--- and scarcely any other waiter was trusted with a 1 while Will Shakspere could be had. This was the dawn of better fortune. Shakspere, finding more horse into his hand than he could hold, hired boys to wai4 his inspection, who, when Will Shakspere was summi were immediately to present themselves, lam Shales) boy, sir.' In time, Shakspere found higher employn but as long as the practice of riding to the playhouse tinned, the waiters that held the horses retained the a lation of Shakspere'b boys." lam willing to accept thi dition, for it harmonises .vith Greene's Johannes far t, I believe in life and go as the essence of young Shakstiere. He'd have wiped boots with a shoe-clout, cleaned a horse, commanded the channel fleet, the army, or the nation, or written a sermon for any Romanist or Puritan, to say no- thing of poems and Plays for young nobles and the stage.— The Royal Shakspere" for February.

SOIENTIFIC NOTES. Father Deuza, the Italian astronomer, has been making some experiments with the micro-telephone on the line of railway front Turin to Lanz°, which is about twenty miles long. The voice was distinct and clear, and so str+ong that' it was heard all over the room at Lanzo. "Conversation between A the two interlocutors was as animated as if they had been in the same place." NATURAL LIGHTNING CONDITCTORS.—In a recent number of the Journal de Geneve, M. Colladon has pointed out that a poplar or other tall tree may, if its roots strike into damp soil, servo as a lightning conductor to protect a house;, and he thinks he has verified this conjecture by examination of a number of individual cases of ljghtning-stroke. In the case, however, where the house stands between the tree and a piece of water, a pond or stream, the shortest path for the lightning from the tree to the wet conductor may be through the house! DIGESTIVE PRINCIPLE OF FIG JIIICE.—M. Bouchut,whe has been investigating the digestive principle of the papaw tree has extended his reserches to the common fig, and the result of preliminary experiments,, carried out upon .the milky juice collected from a fig ties in April last, seems to show that this juice contains a powerful ferment capable of digesting albuminoid matters. As much as 90 grammes of Moine, added -id eight successive portions, at Intervals of one or two days, to 5 grammes of the milky juice, and kept at a temperature of 50 deg. C., was for the greater part digested, leaving a small amount of a White homogenous residue, and the eolutiort having the odour of good broth. ' InsacTs IN Woor..—An entomOlogist, M. Levoiturier, of Elbeuf, lately 'communicated to the French Aeclimitatioh Society the results of an inquiry as to the coleoptera found in wools from different parts of the globe, and special to each region. It is known that ia the grease and impurities of wool there are many insects, and the author's list is quite a long one. The determination and classification of . these insects is a real service, since by a mere inspection of them the origin of a particular wool may be ascertained, and a knowledge of their origin is important with regard to the net return of wool. Thus, scouring removes a much greater weight from wool of Buenos Ayres than from that of Monte Video. Wools from the Cape and Australia leer) much leas. The table drawn up by M. Levoiturisr indicates for Australia 47 species of insects ; for the Cape of Good Hope, 52; for Buenos Ayres, 36A for Spain, 16; Russia, 6. The society of Elbeuf exhibits in its technical museum the more remarkable specimens obtained by ,M. Levoihnier, and Something of the kind might kisefully be done in other places where the wool industry is established.—Textile Manufacturer. PROPOSED ISTHMUS BETWEEN IRELAND AND GREAT linrrant.—Mr. J. C. King has published a small chart, With remarks on a plan for forming an isthmue to join Great Britain and Ireland. In a direct line north-west of London about 365 miles, ind north of Dublin 126 miles, is the nar- row passage between the two islands. The Gnlf Stream supplies the currents flowing continuously through this nar- row and shallow passage at the rate of six knots an heat; this, if stayed by a land barrier, would no longer cause the submersion of many thousands of acres of inland and coast land on both sides of the Irish Sea down to Holyhead and Dublin Bay. The water passage between the Mull of Can- tyre and Ter Point is 19 miles wide by about 474 ft. deep, at mid-current, but much shallower towards either shore. The high bluffs of Cantyre on the Scotch coast, and the still higher land comprising Mounts Cady, Estcourt, and Cam. tea on the Irish coast—from 9001 t. to 1,200 ft. high—offer facilities for gravitating the materials requisite to form the isthmus between the opposite shores. The superficial ex- tent of land required would be little more than a square mile, the average breadth and depth about 100 yards.—De- sign and Work. I PAPER CAR WnEnts.—Writing on the manufacture of paper railway wheels the Paperi World says :—The paper is straw-board of rather fine texture. It is received in the ordinary broad sheets, differing in no particular from those used for straw-board boxes or other similar work. These sheets as they come from the paper mill are square, and are first cut to a circular pattern. This is done on a table with a knife guided by a radial arm. A small disc is also cut from the centre of the sheet to admit the wheel centre. The paper has now to be converted from loose sheets into a com- pact, dense body, capable of withstanding the tremendous crushing force to which it Will be subjected in the wheels. This is accomplished aS follows: Ten sheets are pasted to- gether, one upon another, making a disc about *in. thick. Enough of these discs having been prepared to fill a power- ful hydraulic press, they are subjected to a pressure of I,Boolb. per square inch. When removed the discs are hung on poles in a steam-heated loft and left six days to dry. Thicker discs are then made, each formed by pasting to- gether two or three of those already finished. These are pressed and dried as before, and the process is repeated until a block is built 41n. thick and of about the specific, gravity of Egli= yam. After each pasting and pressing six days are allowed for drying, and when the block is completelt is left hi a drying room until thoroughly seasoned. The next - operation is that of turning the paper blocks to fit the steel tires and iron centres. This is done inlathes in the same manner as if the material worked on was tough wood. A bed or recess is worked out for the web of the tire to rest in. The block is then painted, and is ready for its place in the , wheel. THE Atmomnren.—Professor Hughes's Audiometer is an instrument, the outcome of the microphone, which is likely to become of great service to the aurist, as well as to those unfortunately afflicted with deafness. Its purpose is not to relieve that malady, but to give definite measurements of the power of hearing in an individual so that the extent of the disease may be at once gauged, and comparisons made from day to day as to progress and as to the efficiency of the remedies adopted. The Audiometer consists of a horizontal bar about fifteen inches long, furnished with a scale graduated into two hundred parts. At each end of this bar is fitted a coil of wire; that on the right hand containing about six yards of wire, and that on the lefu about one hundred yards. Another coil slides on the graduated bar, whose function it is to receive induced currents of electricity from the fixed coils at either end. A microphonic key and a battery are placed in circuit with the fixed coils and a telephone, which the patient holds to his ear, is attached to the ends of the induction coil. It stands to reason that the nearer the slid- ing coil is placed towards the larger of the fixed coils, the greater will be the induced current, and the greater the sound in the telephone, while there must be a point near the smaller coil where matters are so balanced that no sound whatever will be audible, although the operator may still be working the microphonic key. This point is the zero of the scale, and according to the perfection of the hearing faculty a patient will be able to detect sounds in the induc- tion coil as it is moved nearer or farther away from that point. Dr. B. W. Richardson constantly uses this in,tru- ment in his daily practice, and finds it of the greatest service in ascertaining the hearing powers of his patients from day to day.—Cassell's Technical Educator. THE Fox Emzerurc Lronr.—Another system of electric lighting has been introduced to public notice. This is the system of Mr. St. George Lane Fox, which comprises a peculiar method of subdividing and distributing the light and a lamp of special construction, the current being generated by a Gramme Machine. The light is an incan- descent one, and is produced by means of a loop ef carbon placed within a glass globe in vacuo. The lamp, in fact, is almost identical with those of Mr Edison, Mr. Swan, and Mr. Moxim, but the system embodies several important de- partures from and additions to their methods of distribution and regulation. Moreover, it is stated that Mr. Fox's pa- tents are of prior date to those of the gentlemen referred to. A demonstration of this system was given lately under the auspices of the British Electric Light Company in the large hall of Palace Chambers, Westminster. The hall was pleasantly lighted by a pendant ring of twelve lights, three others being placed on a table. Mr. Fox explained that the light was one of small intensity, and that each lamp could be increased or reduced in brilliancy and be turned on or off ,at will, which points he demonstrated. In fact, his system is similar in arrangement to our present gas system. He proposes to have a central producing station, from which main conductors are to be laid under the streets, and from these mains branches are to be carried to the houses. They are there to be conducted to the various apartments, and there is to be a main tap and one to each burner, just in the same way as is done with gas. There is to be a governor or regulator at the central station, which will control the elec. tro-motive force. This governor consists of an arrangement of electro-magnets, by means of which the engine driving the machine is to be controlled. When a greater demand of current is being introduced than can be consumed by reason of some of the lamps being extinguished this governor is to act in retarding the rate of production and in apportioning it to the exact requirement. By this means the current would always be available when wanted, and would be pro- duced as required. In addition to this, the current is to be stored in condensers, in order to meet any sudden or unfore- seen demand for light. Mr. Fox entered into details respect- ing the relative cost of gas and of the electric light, and, according to his figures, electricity is by far the cheaper of the two for illuminating purposes, light for light. He stated that under his system one-horse power would produce and maintain a light of 200-candle power. He further demon- strated, by boiling some water, that electricity could be used for heating as well as for lighting purposes.

A mill at Ashton belonging to the Egret Spinning and Manufacturing Company was burned down on Wednesday. The loss of property is estimated at £13,000. In Edinburgh, on Monday, Barbara Gray, alias Mclntosh, was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment for the wilful neglect and bad treatment of Children of tender age. George Harris, confidential clerk to Mr. Graves, the well imown picture:publisher, Pall Mall, has been arrested on- .

The mail steamer Caledonia'ran on to a reef of rocks near JeQey harbour on Saturday, and sank in a few minutes. The passengers and crew were saved in the steamer's boats, but the inane were lost. Heywood Local Board has received a letter from the Home Office that the charter for the incorporatioa of Hey- wood is now ready, and will be sent down to the Board forthwith.
An eccentric woman who owned property has been found dead in her house, near Farnwth. Her body was terribly emaciated, and it is evident that she died from starvation.
Fern gathering is the principal amusement at mountain resorts. Ferns generally grow in places where _pretty young ladies cannot get to without a great deal of assis- tance. •

In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tuesday, a traveller for a City firm- obtained a verdict for £2,500 against the London and North-Western Railway Company, for injuries sustained by him in an accident between Wigan and Glasgow. The Georgina, from London to Cork, with railway sleepers, was destroyed by fire, on Wednesday, off Falmouth. The crew were saved by a lifeboat. The vessel caught fire through the c tptain burning paraffin oil for a signal of distress. Henry Read, assisting in the stables el a surgeon, at Stepney, got into the brougham on Monclav night, shut the doors and windows, lighted a nandle, and fell asleep. On Tuesday he was found dead, having been suffocated from want of ventilation.

A man named Beal was called, in Sheffield police court, on Tuesday. as witness to character in a ease of assault. As he was leaving the box he was recognised as a person " wanted " for burglary on Sunday night, and a gold watch and .other stolen property was. found on .him.

Thomas Clarke-, forem.an joiner, Brighouse, who was re- cently found to have been defrauding co-operative societies by means of counterfeit tin checks, purporting to re- present certain expenditure at the " stores," has been sentenced at the Wakefield sessions to fifteen months' impri- sonment.

At Bolton on Saturday Mr. John Gorse, a cotton spinner, of Higbfield House, Haulgh, was committed for trial, and admitted to bail, on four charges of having within four months of the liquidation of his affairs by arrangement dis- posed of a quantity of cotton ttherwise than in the ordinary way of trade. The Right Hon. John Bright, as Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, has given instructions that the ancient Courts Leet of the Honour of Pontefract may be dispensed with, as investigation shows that recent legislation has deprived them of the public utility which they once possessed. At Halifax Borough Court, on Tuesday, complaints were made of attacks on the English when passing along Southowram Bank, a quarter where many Irish reside. People dare not go that way, it was said, without protec- tion, assaults being committed without any provocation. The police force in the district has been strengthened. ,Last week there were thirty-five British and foreign wrecks of which twenty,five were British—two being steamers —making a total of 393 for the present year, or an increase I of 168, as compared with the corresponding period of last year. The approximate value of property lost was 4 £5,000,000, including British £3,500,000. The Oldham Board of Guardians have resolved to drop proceedings against certain "anti-Vaccinators." This de- cision has been brought about by a communication from the Local Government Board (in reply to a request for advice) informing the Guardians that the question of repeated pro- secutions is one for the exercise of discretion,:which ought to be governed by circumstances. At Oldham, on Wednesday, John Moran, described as a big, strong-looking fellow, was committed to prison for three months for assaulting his child, 16 months old. Prisoner was stated by his wife to have beaten the child for two hours last Sunday because it "began to cry." The poor little creature still bore the marks of the violence it had suffered, and the presiding magistrate told prisoner that words could not express the magistrates' opinion of him. At Bow-street, Susan Wills Fletcher, an American "spiritualist," has been committed to take her trial on the charge of defrauding Mrs. Hart-Davies of money and jewellery. The proceedings had been adjourned to give the defence an opportunity of procuring a mandamus to compel the magistrate to allow certain questions to be put to the prosecutrix in cross-examination, but no application had been made, and the proceedings on Saturday were formal. I Bail in £1,200 was allowed. The Sandwich Election Commissioners state in their report. with respect to the contest between Sir Julian Gold- mid and Mr. Crompton Roberts in May last, that 128 per- sons were guilty of corrupt practices and bribery' in respect to the votes of other persons, and that 1,005 persons were guilty of such offences in respect to their own votes. Not less than 127 received bribes from both sides. The Com- missioners come to the conclusion that electoral corruption had long extensively prevailed in the borough. The labours of a number of miners have been successful , in filling up a large chasm caused by the river Bradford breaking through the roof of a disused mine, at Alport in Derbyshire. The stream, however, still flows through I the mass of rock and timber thrown into the opening, and finds its way to the Derwent undergrounnd. It is im- possible to divert the stream by reason ef the conforma- tion of the ground. A large number of persons have visited the spot. A dastardly outrage has been attempted at Hackenthorpe, near Sheffield. On Saturday, a gallon bottle of gunpowder was placed beneath the boiler at the works of Messrs. Thos. Staniforth and Sons, sickle manufacturers, and was fired by a train, the intention evidently being to blow up the works. Fortunately but little damage was done. Threatening letters had been sent before the outrage was attempted. The offence is ascribed to unionists. The men had been refused an advaace in wages. At a meeting of railway and carriers' servants' held at Manchester, a resolution was passed expressing "alarm and indignation" at the means which are being used by certain large employers to contract themselves out of the Employers' Liability Act, and earnestly soliciting the support of Her Majesty's Government for one or other of the bills new be- fore Parliament having for their object the prevention of employers evading the Act by private contracts. A further resolution was passed pledging the meeting to support the Railway and Carriers' Servants' Alliance. At the general meeting of the London and North-Western Railway Company on Saturday the Chairman referred to the question which had ,been in dispute between the Company and their servants in respict to the Employe's' Liability Act. The Company have need,. 46,000 persons in their employ, land the greater number of these had come to an arrange- ment for compensation in lease of death or accident. The Chairman denied that the slightest coercion had been used by the directors towards their servants in this matter. At Terme, Rhondda, on Monday, the stipendiary magis- trate sentenced a collier, named John Morgan, to a month's imprisonment for smoking in a mine. Defendant was also fined 4,05. and costs for carrying a pipe into the workings. The stipendiary said he was going to see the Home Secre- tary at once personally for the purpose of getting a clause inserted in the Mines' Act to prohibit smoking apparatus being taken into mines. At one large Rhondda colliery the men have passed a resolution expressing the utmost horror and disgust at the prevalence of carrying tobacco pipes beyond the lamp station, and agreeing to do all in their power to assist the officials in bringing offending parties before the magistrates. Mn. GLADSTONE AND THE WELSH LIBERALS.—At a meeting held at Mold a few days ago, a lecture was delivered by the Rev. Owen Jones, the well-known Welsh lecturer on the life and character of the Right Honourable William Ewart Gladstone; and at the close a vote of unabated con- fidence in Mr. Gladstone and his Government, and of sympathy with them in the great difficulties with which 'they have to contend, was carried unanimously, and sent to Mi. Gladstone, to which the following reply has been received :—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall, 21st Feb., 1881. Sir,—Mr. Gladstone desired me to thank you for your kindly-worded note, and for your courtesy in forwarding him an account of the recent meeting of Liberals at Mold. It is gratifying to him to be assured that he and his col- leagues retain the confidence of the Liberals in Wales.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, E. W. HAMILTON. THE VICISSITUDES ow FORTHRIL—A poor woman, named Talent, who has been living in Bootle in a condition of ex- treme indigence, has just become the recipient of a hand- some fortune. Mrs. Talent, who has been twice married, first of all married a man named Spark, with whom twelve or fourteen years ago she resided in Wallasey. Spark died, and the woman and her three children were left to their own resources. She subsequently married a man named Talent, and removed to Bootle, and her children were sent out to service. It has now transpired that a wealthy rela- tive of the father has died, leaving a fortune of £24,000 to the father, if alive, and in the event of his death the widow is to receive £6,000, and two of the children £4,000 each, The eldest child by a clause in the will receives nothing. It is stated that the youngest child has until recently been an inmate of the Birkenhead workhouse. Mrs. Talent's where- abouts have only been traced after extreme difficulty, and very naturally the family is highly elated with the present stroke of good fortune.

div.head: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE.
div.p: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE.

A meeting of the members of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture was held on Saturday at the Town Hall, Chester Mr. George Slater (Northwich) presiding. After Mr. Rigby (the Secretary) had read the minutes of the meeting, at which a paper was read by Major Craigie on "Local Taxation," Mr. R. O. ORTON (Tattenhall) stated• that the Taryin Board of Guardians had. recently passed. a resolution complaining of the inequality of the rating of landed property as compared with personal property; the West Broxton Highway Board had also passed a resolntion calling attention to the injustice involved in levying the cost of the maintenance and repair of disturnpilied roads upon landed property. Mr. Orton said he hoped other boards of guardians and highway boards would adopt a similar course, and thereby strengthgn the hands of the Central Chamber in its endeavour to induce the govern- ment to deal with the question of local taxation, and provide some remedy for the injustice and inequality com- plained of.
'CATTLE DISEASE IN THE COI:TETE.

• The SECIRETARY read a letter from Captain Arrowsmith, the chief constable of the county, in which it was stated that no case of pleuro-pneumonia had been reported since August last, and that swine fever existed in only two places. Foot-and-mouth disease, Captain Arrowsmith stated, ap- peared in the county on the 19th ult., and he had been able to clearly trace its introduction to a cow purehased at the Manchester market a few days befOre, which was put with other animals. It would be well, he thought, for farmers and others when purchasing fresh stock, to keep them separate from their old stock, at least for a fortnight, so as to prevent loss to themselves and their neighbours, and stop' the spread of the disease. Great care should alto he taken to keep shippons frequently whitewashed and disinfected. Up to the 12th inst. 112 animals had been attacked bythe disease; five of them had died. The progress of the disease had been much less rapid than was usual, a fact which he attributed to the operatron of the restrictions regulating the movements of animals, which were being carefully and fully carried out throughout the county. •

div.head: MILK SUPPLY ON. !ARON TOWNS.
div.p: THE MILK SUPPLY ON. !ARON TOWNS.

Dr. FRANCIS Itneort (Liveriool) read a paper on The milk supply of Liverpool and other large towns." He stated that last year the number of milch cows in the United Kingdom was one per cent:less than in 1879. Milk was, , in fact, a bye product,and the number of cattle giving milk appeared to be regulated chiefly by the price of cheese and meat. The quantity of milk sent to Liverpool every year by rail was considerably less than two million gallons, and of that quantity five times more came from Cheshire than from all the other counties combined. In Liverpool there were 452 , shippons, containing 5,235 cows, which largely augmented the milk supply of the town. The con- sumption of miJk in Liverpool was between four and form and a half million gallons per annum, about a pint for each individual in a week. Considering that one-seventh of the population was under five years of age, and that there were many who were sick, that amount was undoubtedly in- adequate. The question arose, what supply was large enough for the town ? It was not, however, easy to answer that question by giving a definite quantity. In 1868 it was found that each of the inmates of various public institutions other than hospitals consumed two-fifths of a pint per day, which might be taken as what a mixed population would consume. Three pints a week for both young and old, or less than half a pint per day, would require a yearly milk supply for Liverpool of ten million gallons Irons the country districts, or five times more than the amount at present sent. That more milk was generally needed was.proved by the increasing demand for condenefed milk, which often became stale and sour before it reached the consumer. (Hear, hear.) There was, undoubtedly, a want of confidence in the preqemt supply of milk. The families of dairy farmers were not always free from fever, which must taint the milk coming from that source ; it was therefore advisable, and indeed be held that it was the duty of everyone who bad the care of children in towns to personally inspect the source from which they obtained milk. A horrible suspicion had arisen that tubercle or " grapes," as it was often termed by farmers, could be communicated to man by the milk which he drank, and this was supported by the convergence of opinion of many eminent physicians. He (Dr. Imlach) was making experiments in that matter by feeding animals with milk obtained from cows affected by tubercle. It was often the case that milk which was not sold on the first day was kept tintil the following day, and then mixed with that day's milk. That practice was strongly to be condemned, for infantile diarrhrea was often caused by it. When milk was sent a considerable dia..' tance it ought to be poured through an efficient refrigerator. Ice waggons were frequently used for conveying fish and meat, and there was no good reason why some plan should I not be adopted for preserving milk from injury while it was being conveyed by rail. Those sending milk to large towns might by a very simple means do a good deal to preserve it from deterioration. A sack soused in water and thrown over the lid of the milk-can would, so long as evaporation continued, convert what was often a harmful into a harm- less journey. Local Government returns showed that no drug or article of diet was so frequently adulterated as milk. What was wanted to prevent this adulteration was con- tinued inspection from the moment it left the cow until it reached the consumer. Each can should be tested on its arrival at the railway station, and the distribution of its contents should be guarded by due precautions. In Liver- pool. and he believed,it was the same in all the neighbour- ing large toWns, the retail price of milk was 4d. per quart even when the poor fetched it themselves. In buying it poor people were well aware that they were getting an in- ferior article. It was out of them the greatest profit was made, though they were entitled to as good milk as the rich, seeirrg that they paid the same price. , How much of that sum did farmers get? Just about half, for the utmost the Cheshire farmers obtained was, as a rule, Od. per gallon in summer and 10d. in winter. It appeared to him that it was possible, by organisation, to diminish the price of milk, for surely distribution should not cost as much as production. He advised farmers to combine and organise a better system of distribution, and he hoped his fellow-townsmen would combine, as had been done elsewhere, with a view to secure , a larger and better supply of -good milk, if only for the benefit of little children unable to protect themselves.— (Applause.)

„ In the discussion which ensued Colonel FRANCE-HAT•• HURST (Northwich) corroborated the statement made by Dr. I Imlach as to the increasing demand for condensed milk.= Mr. Fain (Northwich) complained of the manner in which farmers were generally treated by the railway companies, I and said that the cost of the carriage of milk by rail bad I increased considerably.—Mr. J. Povint (Ince) stated that the 1 railway companies appeared to take very little care of the milk delivered to them, for they delayed it en the road and often exposed it unnecessarily to the heat of the sun. Alluding to a statement made by Dr. Imlach aft to the price obtained by-farmers for their milk, Mr. Paver said many farmers in Cheshire would be very glad to get Sd. per gallon” in summer and 10d. in winter. He knew farmers who last summer had to sell their milk for 7P. per gallon delivered at Lime-street Station. In his opinion it was advisable to form a company in that neighbourhood somewhat similar to the Aylesbury Dairy Company.—Mr. H. LINAEER (Frod- sham) asked whether the Railway Commission could not step in when farmers bad reason to complain of over- charge or delay in the carriage of milk..—The CHAIN/KAN, in reply, said he thought the Railway Commission bad no power to deal with matters of that kind.— After some observations from Mr. Walker Jones (Mollington), Mr. C. Byrd (Spnrstow), and Mr. Salisbury (Liverpool), Mr. F. Dowsss (Chester) said that when farmers were as anxious to push the sale of milk as licensed victuallers were to push their trade then the consumption of milk would greatly increase, and the cost of conveyinga by rail would soon be reduced.—Mr. Coos (Tatton) confirmed a statement made by Mr. Salisbury that the supply of milk to Liverpool was greater than the demand, and stated that milk was often adulterated after it had gone into the hands of dealers. The demand of most people in Liverpool was for something cheap. People there seemed to prefer to get an article cheap, even though it were adulterated, rather than pay a higher price for something quite free from adulteration.—Mr. T. B. Asa- TON (Kelsall) said the great difficulty farmers had to face in Liverpool was to get people to become as fond of milk as they were of Walker's beer. (Laughter). When they had managed to accomplish that feat they might hope to get a special train for their milk. On the motion of Mr. R. 0. ORTON, seconded by Mr. C. BYRD, a vote of thanks was accorded to Dr. Imlach for his paper, and he was requested to allow it to be printed for cir- culation amongst the members of the Chamber. Mr. LINASER proposed that the council of the Chamber be requested to consider what was the best course to pursue in order to bring before the railway companies the desirable- ness er securing the cheap and expeditious carriageof milk by FOYER seconded the motion, which was carried. FOOT AND MOUTH DlSEASE.—Captain Arrewsmith, chief constable of the county, reported that since the occurrence of the first case of foot-and-mouth disease in Cheshire, on the 19th ultimo, up to the 12th instant, 196 animals had been attacked, of which 5 had died, 102 had recovered, and 87 were yet under treatment.

EAST CUMBERLAND ELECTION. Mr. George James Howard (L) and Mr. James Lowther (C) were nominated, on Wednesday, as candidates for the representation of East Cumberland.
