IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MUSE OF LORDS.—Moxamt.

TIII3 WAR IN THE TRANSVAAL.—The Earl Of KIMBERLEY, replying to a question by Earl Cadogan, said it would not be for the public advantage to make known at present what oteps the Government had' taken with regard to the nego- tiations for peace between England and the, Transvaal. They had, however, moved in a way calculated to promote`a satis- factory settlement, consistently with the honour of this country. He also stated for the information of their lord- ships that President Brand would be able to preserve the neutrality at the Orange Free State, and that the difficulty would noon came to an end. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mommy.

The Speaker took the chair at 4 o'clock. Massie AND Mgmv.—ln answer to Baron de Worms, Sir C. DILE& said the Government had come to the conclusion that Russia did not intend to advance to Mery from infor- mation received from Lord Dufferin. THE NEW Amon,/ INsPEcTort.—Replyicg MI Mr. Dal- rymple, Sir WILLIAM HAncotna said the post of factory inspector was one that required, not only knowledge and ability, but tact and judgment, to prevent friction be- tween the interests of the employer and the employed, and he believed from the character he had received of Mr. J. D. Prior that that gentleman would fulfil those requirements. He had accordingly applied to the Treasury under a special Order of Council empowering the dispensing with examine- tibns in cases of special knowledge, and the Treasury had given their assent, and he was happy to say he had the concurrence of the head inspector of factories. He was glad of any opportunity to give the artisan and operative classes a share in the civil service.

THE TRANSVAAL AND PEACE NEGOTIATIONS.— Mr. GLADSTONE, in answering a question from Sir G. Campbell on the subject of the suspension of hostilities with the Boers, said that the Government had taken such steps as appeared best calculated to promote a satisfactory settlement and stay the effusion of blood, consistently with the honour of the British C-rown—(lfear, hear)—but at the present moment it would not be for the public advantage to enter into details. _

THE PROTECTION (IRELAND) BILL.—MT. GLADSTONE moved, under the new urgency rules, that all amendments to the Protection Bill not disposed of by midnight shall then be put forthwith without debate. This was carried by 415 against 63 votes, and the House then went into com- mittee on the Bill.—Mr. ERRINGTON moved to limit the Act to March, 1882, instead of September, but on a division the ,amendment was negatived by 211 to 68.—A similar amend- ment, moved by Mr. HEALY, to bring the Act to an'end on September 30, 1881, was next negatived by 162 to 48.—1 n reply to Mr. Gray, Mr. FORSTER undertook that if it be- came necessary to continue the bill it should be by a sepa- rate measure. The Committee then took up the new clauses. The first in the name of Mr. O'Shaughnessy pro- vided that every person arrested should on liberation re- ceive a certificate which would be a bar to any subsequent arrest, but the Solicitor objecting to it. it was negatived by 259 to 46. The next was Mr. Labouchere's making tem- porary provision for compeusation for Cisturbancu, but this and ten other new clauses succeeding it were ruled in- admissible bj.: the Chairman as being out of the scope of the bill or Inconsistent with clauses already sanctioned.— On the stroke of midnight the Chairman arose, his inter- 'Position being hailed with a ringing cheer.—Mr:O'Dortieuta. having replaced his eye-glass and satisfied himseit with much deliberation that it really was the Chairman who interrupted in this surprising and unexpected manner, sat down, and without preface the question was put from the Chair.—When the order went forth to clear the House for the division the Irish members remained seated, and con- sternation began to display itself in the neighbourhood of the Chair at the prospect of a repitition of a famous scene. But this was only the playfulness of the Irish members. At the very last moment they rose in a body and walked into the lobby.—A second reading was refused the clause by 392 votes against 43.—Other clauses on the amendment paper were ruled out of order, and there remained only the question that the Chairman report the bill to the House.— ' Mr. PLaypetn, in the excitement of the moment, put the question that he "report progress," but being reminded of the slip he corrected himself and the question was put in due form.At 20 minutes past 12 the committee divided on this, the last of the many "questions" submitted to it, and 20 minutes later the figures were announced—for reporting the bill 377, against 47.—1 t was thought that here, ended the tenth night in Committee on this bill of three clauses. But the Irish members, lively to the last,opposed the formal motion that the Chairman leave the chair, and Dr. LYON PLAyreut had to remain at his post till a formal vote of the Cemmittee set him free.
• • The remaining orders were disposed of. and the 'House adjourned at 25 minutes to two.
ROUSE OF LORDS.-TUESDAY.

THE OFSNING OF MUSEUMS ON SUNDAYS. Lord DUN- EAVFN brought forward a resolution which, pointing to the sucess of the opening of museums on Sundays in Dublin and elsewhere, proposed that similar arrangements should be made in London.—Lord Suerrasnraty ipoved an amend- ment to the effect that musaums in London should be opened in the evening three days a week from seven to ten. —ln the discussion which followed the amendment was sup- ported by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Earl Cairns, and the Duke of Argyll.—Lord ROSEBERY made an effective speech in favour of the resolution, which also received the support of Lord GRANVILLE.—On a division the resolution was negatived by 41 votes against 34. The amendment was then agreed to and their lordships adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COONS.-TIIESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COONS.-TIIESDAY.

MR. PARNELL'S SPILMCM AT' CLARE. The ATTORNEY- GENERAL, replying to the question by Mr. Morgan Lloyd, said Mr. Parnell's speech in Irelanl on Sunday, in the course of which he had advised tenants about to be evicted to call •their neighbours together and plough up all the ground, so as to prevent the landlord turning cattle on to graze, "had received and should receive very careful attention," This reply was received with cheers from both sides of the House. Tam IMPORTATION OP PORK. Mr. DIXON-HARTLAND wanted to know whether, in consequence of the prevalence of trichinosis, the Council were prepared to forbid the importa- tion of pork from the United States.—Mr. MIINDELLA pointed out tharthe value of pork and bscon imported from the United States was 9i millions sterling and the annual con- sumption was about 30 lb. per head of the population. It would be a very serious thing to put a stop to this enormous supply of human food, and the Council were not prepared to do so without further evidence of the necessity. The right hon. gentleman reminded the House that when a similar question had been put to the Duke of Richmond he had stated that the best means of averting danger was thoroughly to cook the food.

THE IRisH PROTECTION BILL.—The Protection of Persons and Property Bill was then "considered" as amended in Committee.—Mr. FORSTER moved a new clause which will remove a doubt as to whether the families of indigent per- sons arrested under the AO would be entitled to relief from poor-law guardians. The clause was added to the bill. Several additions and alterations proposed by Home Rule members were rejected, and Mr. FORSTER then moved, in fulfilment of his promise, that the retrospective operation of the Act should be limited to the 30th September, 1880.--I- The motion was carried, after some debate, by 164 to 41. Mr. PARNELL then moved to exclude treason-felony from the offences specified in the bill. The hon. member denied that the Land League was working with the Fenians, and expressed wonderment at the " scare " which had come over the English people. True, the Fenians had contri- buted to the League fundObat that was not because the League was working for revolutionary objects, but because it wee seeking to overthrow landlordism, the great bulwark of British misrule in Ireland. The hon. member spoke of the explosion at Salford Barracks as "probably a practical joke."—Mr. FORME retorted that the hon. member had given the House some "interesting information" as to the respective aims of the Fenians and the Land League, but he declined to accept the amendment. The right hon. gentle- man said the Government bad no fear of a Fenian rising but they desired to have power to prevent atrocious out- rages. He censured Mr. Parnell for the terms in which he had described the explosion at Salford. Referring to Mr. Parnell's confident prediction that the bill would fail, Mr. Forster said it would put down violent and unconstitutional methods of procedure, but it would not, and was not in- tended to, prevent an agitation within the limits of the Con- stitution.—Mr. HEALS playfully remarked, in his own manner, that the Salford outrage might be a mere explosion of gas, and as to Fenianism, he said the only evidence of its existence was supplied by informers, and was, therefore, worth very little.—Sir W. HARCotiRT said there was un- doubted evidence that a " feul " Fenian conspiracy existed, and he quoted the recent writings of O'Donovan Rossa in proof of his statement. In a paper published bv Bosse, the assassination of Her Majesty's Ministers was openly recom- mended. The right hon. gentleman read extracts from the writinss of a Mr. Devoy, recommending most "detestable villanies." It appeared that Devoy was soliciting sub- scriptions for the "skirmishing fund," bat Mr. Healy in- formed the House that that fund ceased to exist Some time ago.—At midnight the first reminder that public business I had been solemnly declared "urgent" was supplied from the Chair.—An amendment being pressed, the SERA= de- claredwithhe calledthe that " the Noes" had it. His decision being chal- lenged,nuepwo n rulethe tohbajts cet oelsh to e toren d rleq p question on accor- dance without a division if the minority do not exceed twenty. The Speaker, counting ascertain a ed that the mal- contents were over twenty, discovery hailed by the Par cheers. - abre. nellites with mocking ee rns. hTheer at division4sth,e nowen same rendered d necessary, fixed the pre process showing that in various parts of the building 244 members were awaiting the Conclusioaann of the weary business.—The House adjourned at 2-15

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEowEsDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEowEsDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. IRISE AGRARIAN CRIME.-.-.Mr. FORSTER, replying to Mr. Sexton, said he did not think it was necessary to give fort- nightly returns of agrarian crime in Ireland. As regarded the detailed return for December, be had done all in his power to hasten it, and ho hoped that it would be in the bands of members in the course of a few days. In reply to Mr. T. P. O'Connor, the right hon. gentleman further said that he would certainly not defer the third reading of the Coercion Bill until that return was issued. PROTECTION OF PERSON AND PROPERTY (IitELLND BILL.—The further consideration of the report on this bill 55 amended was proceeded with. The debate itself offered no point of interest. The speaking was almost entirely with the Irish members, who raised questions with reference mainly to the treatmeat of such persons as may be arrested

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 26, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 26, 1881.

under the Act, one member being anxious that they should be treated as first-class misdemeanants, another that they should be 'placed in dry, well-lighted, and suitably heated rooms, and a third that they should have proper associates and as much exercise daily as they might desire. The speakers repeated speeches made on earlier stages of the debate, and the SPEAKER several times interposed with the object of bring- ing members to the point.—Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN being thus warned immediately resumed his seat.—Mr. HEALY pro- ceeding in the same strain was, after a considerable exercise of patience, ruled by the SPEAKER to be guilty of the new (statutable) Parliamentary offence of repeating his argu- ments in tedious fashion, and was called upon to resume his seat, which he did, Mr. LEAKY taking up the thread of his argument.—Mr. METGE, warned a little later of a similar tendency, was wise irt time. No opportunity of taking a division was missed, and when at a quarter to six the de- bate was interrupted by the operation of the Standing Order there yet remained a page of amendments. The remaining orders were run through and the House adjourned.

ROUSE OF LORDS.-THURSDAT. ARMY ORGANISATION.-LORD STRATH/gAIRIQ moved for the production of the report of the Committee on Army Organisation' over which Lord Airey presided. It was ex- plained on the part of the Government that the report would be published on Tuesday, and the motion was ulti- mately withdrawn. During the debate which took place, the Duke of Cambridge urged that the question of army organisation ought not to be discussed in a party spirit, and the Duke of Richmond and Gordon declared that without doubt some change must be made in the existing system, as at the present moment the military authorities were obliged to fill up the ranks of battalions with men who had not been dismised drill.

k HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TAT. MINISTERIAL STATEMENT.—Lord IleumwaYog, on behalf of Mr. Gladstone, announced that the statement respecting the future progress of public business would be postponed until Monday, when he trusted that the Prime Minister would be able to make it. The noble lord added that the necessity for proceeding with the business of supply had be- come so indispensable that the House would be asked to go into Committee of Supply on Monday, when the War Minister would move the Army Estimates.—Sir S. Nolan- COTS, after a graceful expression of sympathy for the Prime Minister, asked how supply could be taken in presence of an order giving precedence to the Coercion Bill, and also referred to a notice which appeared on the paper in Mr. ' Gladstone's name, proposing a limition of the right of mem- I hers to raise debates on the motion for going into Com- mittee of Supply, to question relating to the Estimates proposed to be taken. Lord Hamm:Prow explained, with reference to the latter point, that a mistake had arisen and that the notice was given by his noble relitiye the Secretary to the Treasury. He thought under the circumstances, it would be more con- venient that it should not be made until to-day. The noble lord added that he hoped to be able to see the Premier to-day, and be would then make a further statement. THE Connmobr Mts.—Lord HARTINGTON brought for- ward Mr. Gladstone's motion for a farther application of the cl6ture. The'resoletien provided that any amendments to the report on the Coercion Bill remaining on the paper at seven o'clock should be put without debate. The motion was carried by 371 votes to 53 When seven o'clock arrived an amendment to Mr. Forster's motion adding a provision for the periodical re-consideration by the Lord-Lieutenant of the case of any person under arrest, was still being debated. Divisions upon this and other amendments followed in rapid succession, the votes of the minority varying from 24 to 41. Several proposals were ruled by the Speaker to be out of order.—Mr. Fonernst afterwards rose amidst loud Ministerial cheers to most the third reading of the bill. The right bon. gentleman con- fined his speech, which was very brief, to a justificntion- of the;unusaal course taken', by the Government in asking the House to proceed at once with the last stage of the measure.—Mr. Jtmnst MTARTHY Moved that the bill be read a third time that day six months.—The debate was continued by Colonel Colthurst, Mr. O'Sullivan, Mr. Moore, Mr. Dawson, Mr. Finigan, the Home Secretary, and other members. The debate was adjourned.

Alderman COOK said he understood Mr. Taylor was about I Ito lay his land out in villas, and very likely of such a char- acter that wealthy families with horses and carriages would inhabit them. And of course those would have to drive through the, park. All the loads of coal would 6robably be taken that way, and the same with produce. He thought it was a very objectionable clause, because that drive through the park was a carriage drive, And was not made sufficiently strong for heavy carts. There was also a quarry, and the stone would probably be carted through the park when building commenced. Alderman JOHNSON was very Much surprised to hear the remarks expressed by those gentlemen who went with him to Mr. Taylor, as they all came away very favourably im- pressed with what passed. Mr. Taylor showed a disposition to meet the objection of the committee. With regard to what Alderman Cook had said he entirely agreed that it was objectionable, but then Mr. Henry Taylor had stated he would personally induce Mr. Taylor to forego that. With respect to the objection raised by Councillor Twyford, he (Alderman Johnson) would say that if they could obtain a piece of ground somewhere near Carr Mill, by all means do it. Let Dr. Twyford, as a representative of Parr, try to obtain a park on similar conditions to the present offer, and he for one would be glad to support it. They could not establish parks in the centre of the town, and there was no better position generally than the one at Bccleston, and he would venture to say that there was no portion of the town where such large numbers of people went as Prescot-road. As to the probability of there being a drought, he asked UV water engineer how many times they were visited with one, and he replied there had been one during the last 16 years, so that if they were not likely to have a drought more than once in 18 years they were not likely to be troubled with that reservation. It was scarcely fair for Councillor W. W. Pilkington to attribute such conduct as hp had described to Mr. Taylor. Mr. W. W. PILICINGTON: Past experience. Alderman JOHNSON said that Mr. Taylor had contended for hie rights in the law cases they had had, and when that question was raised before the Commissioners there was only a majority of one in favour of testing their rights. He fought the question, and obtained a verdict against the Cor- poration, and it was not fair that that should be thrown at him when he was making them an offer of a park. Let them treat the offer properly, and not attribute motives of that kind. The place was a beautiful one, and, as no town In Lancashire needed a park more than St. Helens, Id. in the l was not a great deal for its maintenance. Mr. W. W. PILIONGTON : Mr. Taylor acted up to his rights before, and be will simply act up to his rights again. He has a right to turn that water one way or the other, and if Mr. Taylor acts up to his rights in one case be will in another. Mr. Swirr said there wee two objections which had been mentioned, the reservations about the water and the cart road, and the discussion had proceeded as if those two were the only objections. There was an old proverb about look- ing a gift horse in the rtiouth, but was it a gift or an offer of a gift? Ho affirmed tbere was no single element of a gift about it from beginning to end. (Hear, bear.) Mr. Taylor had offered to buy from them something which he wanted very much, and offered them nothing comparatively in re- turn. Talk about that as a park; they had. one better already than that. It was a cemetery truly,—(l aughter)— but it was equally a park, and they had 20 acres of land at Windleshaw, equally as well laid out, where people could. walk as much as they liked within reaeonable hours. There was the old Windleshaw Abbey and that splenotid park with a beautiful road to-day, from the gates of old Windleshaw to that road near te Crank, and those, who wanted the Park- like exercise could go there. What was it Mr. Taylor offered them? Simply the privilege of walking along his old car- riage drive, and on the banks of thoss dams. And what did he expect them to do for that? He offered them a carriage drive, bounded on two sides by a narrow strip of land, as narrow as it was possible to make it. There did net appear to be more than a few feet from the carriage drive to the boundary, and in return for the privilege of allowing the people of St. Helens to walk up that drive, and go a little in that direction and a little bit in tbi% asked them to convert the place," which is at present in a rough, wild, and neglected condition," into a little paradise in order that his surrounding land might be enhanced in value, and expected them to maintain for the benefit of his estate that margin to his property. He really offered them nothing at all worthy of their acceptance. All through his life he had been celebrated fer making good bargains, and his last offer was an endeavour to make about the best bargain ever made personally in his life. Instead of being a place fit for human beings to walk in, it was hardly one to bury them in. When the Burial Board of that district wanted a cemetery they went aid bought 20 acres, and here was a park for living men—less than 17 acres—and they were asked to keep it in order at great expense. No, let him build upon it; but liii dared say it would not answer very well for building, and therefore he wanted to make it attractive, so that people might briny], round it. If be gave them the quarry they might make it into a grotto—(laughter)—but the thing was bald and meagre as it was, and was not spontaneously and generously given, but as a bait, at which they were expected to bite and swallow, in order that Mr. Taylor, his heirs, and successors might be largely benefited. Nobody ever heard of Mr. Taylor doing a noble and a generous thing, and the ruling passion, apparently, was strong in death, and he was showing the same greediness now that he had manifested in life— Mr. BAXTER: I think we are not here to try Mr. Tay- lor's character. Mr. SWIFT: I ans speaking on the offer, and— Mr. BLIT= : I must rel -- Mr. Swirr said that ape from the ' general objection, looking at its inadequacy, it was paltry to call it a park. It was land consisting mostly of roads to ba converted into cart roads, which they had never been before. It was not worthy the acceptance of the Council in any sense what- ever, and he did not think the &ouncil would be justified in putting the ratepayers to the present and prospective ex- pense for the purpose of securing it. Mr. ALLEN looking at the question broadly thought that the place under the circumstances was not suitable for their accent- ance. He would like to see places for the use of the poor •children who were cooped up in their 'narrow streets and alleys. That park would also be a great nuisance to the inhabitants of that district, and would injure the property very much. Mr. Barr= moved that if the Town Clerk can make satisfactory terms in regard to the reseriations the Conncil accept the offer. , Mr. FORSTER seconded the motion. , , , Mr. BROOK suggested that the Town Clerk draw up a rough legal draft to be signed by Idr. Taylor. Alderman GAMBLE said that if they accepted the offer, it would be like buying a pig in a poke. There were a great r many footpaths and fields to walk through, and be hoped by the legislation of the future the noxious gases would be reduced to a minimum. Mr. BAXTER did not think Mr. Taylor would enter into further negotiations. A vote was then taken, 15 being recorded against the amendment of Mr. Baxter; the park therefore being refused. Mr. R. PimmroTcas said ,that one regretted that certain remarks had been made. No doubt Mr. Taylor thought be bad made a good offer and they (the committee) had been received with every courtesy. He would therefore move "that while we regret the conditions as attached to the offer are such as prevent us accepting the offer, we desire to ex- press our thanks Ito Mr. Tayior for his offer." He would suggest that the reporters be requested to submit their re- poets to the Mayor so that he may expunge any expre.sions he thought desirable. Alderman JOHNSON said he thought that would do more Injury than if it were allowed to go before the public. The public would be more curious to know what bad been said. Mr. BAKTER could not help thinking there had been a good deal of unnecessiry feeling thrown into the matter. The MAYOR thought it would be met by expunging the objectionable remarks. Mr. B&CER said he had never seen Mr. Taylor, but he thought he had net been treated in the manner he ought to have been. He believed he had been of great benefit to that district, and had allowed his estate to be used for stowing water. Mr. SiviET: For rent. (Laughter.) The motion of Mr. R. Pilkington was carried, and the Council adjourned.
SPECIAL AND IMPORTANT MEETING.,

A special meeting of the St. Helens Town Council was held at the Town Hall, St. Helens, on Wednesday "to con- sider the expediency of opposing a bill now pending in Par- liament intitulcd bill to extend the time for the com- pletion of certain of the tramways authorised by the St. Helens and District Tramways Act, 1879,' and if thought necessary to pass a resolution or resolutions to oppose the said hi;! in Parliament, and also to sanction the payment of the costs, charges, and exp-nses incurred, and to be in- curred in opposing the same, Out of the borough fund and borough iate, or out of other funds or rates applicable for such purpose." The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were also present, Alderman Gamble, Councillors Swift, J. C. Gamble, Twyford, T. Cook, McKechnie, Walker, ' Hanson, Brook, Belsher, Massey, Wilcock, R. Pilkington, Allen, Messrs. T. Brewis (town clerk), and J. H. Craik (deputy town clerk.) THE TRAMWAY COMPANY'S RILL TO BE OPPOSED. GRATE ALLEGATIONS AGAINST THE COMPANT. The Tows CLERK: In pursuance of the resolution passed at the last meeting of the Council I found it necessary to comply with the staining orders of the House of Com. moos, to present a petition against the Bill to obtain a locus standi. The meeting of the Council took place on Wed- nesday. I did not know then the position of the Bill before the House of Commons, and I immediately communicated with London, and found that a petition must be presented by the Tuesday following. There was therefore no time to convene another Council meeting to take instructions, and I therefore acted upon the instructions given at the last meeting to take all necessary steps to oppose the Bill. I therefore prepared a petition and laid it before the Tram- ways Committee and the Mayor, and presented it in due course. I propose to have the Bill and petition read to you. The Deputy Town Clerk then read the Bill applying for an extension of time to lay the tramways; and also the petition presented against it. The TOWN CLERK said the company had given notice of their objection to the locus standi of the Council. Councillor COOK : Has there been any communication with the cemriany as to what will meet our requirements in reference to this postponement ? The TOWN CLERK: I have no communication whatever. Councillor Coos. theught the resolution was that they , should oppose the bill unless some promise was made. The Tows CLERK: That was so. I don't think the com- mittee have taken any steps to come to an widerstanding.

The feeling was that the Tramways Company should ap- proach the committee rather than the committee should appaoach the company. Councillor COOK : That was the object of my enquiry; whether we had any communication from the Tramways Company. The MAYOR asked the Town Clerk to read the Council the resolution of the committee, so that they could see whether I it was for the company to approach the committee or for the committee to approach the Tramways Company. , 'Tice Tows; CLERK read the resolution as follows :—That the minutes be not confirmed, and that the Council oppose the Bill in Parliament unless the committee make such terms with the company as may meet with the approval of the Council, and that the Town Clerk take all necessary steps to oppose the Bill. Alderman GAMBLE moved the following resolution : " That the meeting having considered the clauses and pro- visions of the bill intituled a bill to extend the time for the completion of certain of the tramways authorised by the St. Helens and District Tramways Act, 1879,' it is resolved that this Council do oppose the said bill in Parliament, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to take all necessary steps by petition or otherwise as may be deemed ex- pedient for the due protection of the rights and interests of the borough of St. Helens as represented by this Council. That the costs, charges, and expenses incurred and to be incurred in such opposition be paid out of the borough fund and borough rates, and out of the funds or rate applicable to the purpose." He was serry the chairman of the committee was not there to take the initiative in the matter, for he (the speaker) did not pretend to be fully informed as to the exact position of the Corpo- ration. But he believed there were two companies who applied to them for permission to lay tramways from St. Helens to Havdock, and that the Council thought whatever company obtained their consent should be bound to com- plete a system of tramways the Council thought the borough should have. The present company agreed to complete the tramways not only from Prescot to Havdock, but also to Denton's Green and Marshall's Cross. He believed the branch from St. Helens to Marshall's Cross was their own suggestion from the first, but the branch from St. Helens to Denton's Green was forced upon them by the conditions of the Council. The company, when they had laid the tramways most of the distance from Prescot to St. Helens, applied to the Corporation for leave to enter thc borough, break up the roads, and lay the rails. Ile should have said the Corporation for the purpose of ensuring the arrange- ments they made with the company that the tramways system should be completed in the borough by laying trams to Denton's Green and Marshall's Cross, got the company to insert a clause in their Bill providing that before they opened the roads in St. Helens, the whole of their capital should be subscribed and one half of it paid up. When the company applied to them for permission to lay the rails they asked the company whether they had complied with this clause. They sent them in reply to that request a document which wa'Sdistinctly intended to inform the Council thatabe whole of the capital was subscribed and one half of it paid up. Now it appeared the company had applied for this extension of time. He dared say the company would say the reason they wanted this extension of time was that the Corporation had stopped them from going on with their work as they had a right to do under that clause. But at any rate they had applied for an extension of time, and it gave the Council an opportunity of doing anything they might think necessary to secure the interests of the town. The company had advertised in the daily papers of the past week the prospectus of the company stating that above 1;100 shares had been subscribed .for, and 4,000 had not been subscribed for, being distinctly contrary to the meaning of the reply they gave to the Corporation when asked if the whole of the capital was subscribed. The fact Of the matter was that a week ago there was only one third of the capital subscribed, and in that respect the company had cheated or attempted to cheat them. And now there was circulated that morning with the prospectus that had been advertised for some days a map showing the tramway from Prescot through St. Helens to Haydock. Denton's Green was shown on it, but no tramway was shown on the plan, and Marshall's Cross was not en'the map. It was the evident intention—in fact, they had heard from the direc- tors of the company it was their distinct intention—to abandon the tramways to Denton's Green and Marshall's Cross; and he thought all the Council had to consider was whether they would allow the company to go on with their application without havina some clause put into the Bill which should oblige them to make those tramways. The feeling of the borough seemed to lie in the direction that there should be a complete system of tramways in the hands of one company, and they had provided for it as well as they knew how by the insertion of the clause requiring to be subscribed all the capital that was necessary for making these trams before they began breaking the roads. But it seemed now doubtful whether that clause was sufficient. The agreement was that the company should make these lines, and now they certainly did intend to abandon them. The objection was that the ground would be occupied by the tramways and:no other company could come in, or if the Council chose to make them themselves the company could so work their line that none of the branches would fit. In fact, they could so act as to work so badly With the branch ttams that they could do nothing except sell them to the main company on such terms as the company chose to make with therm. He thought the Tramways Company had not acted fairly, and he might say in addition to the charges he had against them for not acting fairly with the Corporation they never told the Council anything about this Bill that they intended to oppose, and even when the Law Clerk, in obedience to the resolutions of the last meet- ing, asked the solicitor of the company the position of the Bill he was not able to get the information from him, and he had to telegraph to London to know what the Tramways Company were doing. They bad not consulted the Coun- cil, they had acted in defiance of them, and the question was whether it was not necessary they should spend the money of the ratepayers in opposing the Bill unless there was some prospect of getting some advantage from them. He supposed what the Council meant to do was to follow the determination of the Tramways Committee to endeavour to get the whole system of tramways completed, but whether the expense of doing that would be more than the Council ought to incur for the purpose he did not know. Mr. Mama said he would like to know what authority Alderman Gamble had for making the statement that the company intended to abandon the tramways to Denton's Green and Marshall's Cross. He had never heard of it before, and nothing was said in the application to Parlia- ment in reference to it. Alderman GAMBLE remarked that nothing was said about it, but he had it from a party whose name he did not choose to mention, that the company had discussed it, and it was their intention to abandon them. The plan he had already mentioned did not show the branches, but merely the main line from Prescot through St. Helens to Haydock. The prospectus of the company said they were able to make the main tramways before the time specified in the original Act, 24th July, 1881, but they wanted further time to complete the others. He believed that was merely a deceit as most of the com- pany's transactions with the Corporation had been. He knew distinctly they wished to abandon the branches. He was afraid there was nothing in the old Act which obliged the company to complete the tramways beyond the deposit money which they bad paid £2,100. If the company were to abandon the branches they would lose a proportion of the deposit, perhaps £5OO. That was the only security the Corporation had, and whether Parliament would give them further security he was unable to say. Councillor COOK said the aspect which Alderman Gamble had put upon the matter rather altered it to his mind. They were there not as the opponents of the Tramways Com- pany, but as the conservators of the public interests—the interests of the ratepayers; and when the Council consented to these trams being carried out it was on condition that the whole of the trams should be completed. If it was as Alderman Gamble stated that the company were going to abandon a portion of the trams which would be for the public convenience, from Marshall's Cross and Denion's Green, he thought they ought in all fairness and faithfulness to the interests of the ratepayers whom they represented, to oppose the passing of the Bill. If the Tramways Company had ap- proached the Council and asked them on what grounds they were willing to support them, the probability was that an arrangeinent might have been come to. But as nothing,had been settled by the company in that way they were bound to take such steps as would protect the interests of the rate- payers. There was no question that the tramways to Den- ton's Green, and Marshall's Cross, would be a public con- venience, and he-was sure the ratepayers of Sutton and that district would cry oat very loudly against their representa- tives if they did not protect the interests of that portion of the borough. He thought, looking at the whole question, they, as representatives of the ratepayers, were bound to oppose this application for an extension of time. He seconded the resolution. Councillor MASSEY said the Town Clerk intimated a short time ago he had received notice of an objection there was to the locus stand iof the Council. He should llike to know on what ground that objection was taken. The TOWN CLERK: Generally, that the rights of the borough are not being interfered with. It is a formal sort of notice. Alderman GAMBLE said it was the first ster a company took when opposition was made against thon. They ob- jected to the locus standi of the person opposing. In all cases the cost was less in subsequent alreceedings, and they began straightway with opposition. Of course, the objection might posssibly succeed, and when they wanted to crush opposition they took every step to do so. Councillor BROOK did not know as yet on what ground the Council could oppose the extension of time. They all knew it was impossible to complete the whole of the scheme before the 24th July, and as the company said in their notice the lines connecting Prescot with the outskirts of St. Helens were in a very forward state, and the whole of the main line from Prescot to St. Helens-would be completed before the first July, they evidently intended to finish that line, and there could be no objection to an extension of time for the laying of the branch lines to Marshall's Cross and Denton's Green. The company did intend to complete the whole scheme as far as he had been informed—and that wis this week; and as long as they could not be completed in the time he could not see on what ground the Council could oppose the Bill. He saw the Bill had been read a second time, and however they opposed it would be of no use. The Examiner had sanctioned the preamble as to the extension of time. It would be no use, only throwing the ratepayers' money away, and it would put the Tramways Company to unneces- sary expense. He could not see any earthly use for an opposition to an extension of time to complete the branch lines. The town had nothing to lose but everything to gain by the Tramways Company being allowed to go on. It was nothing but a lot of factious opposition.

Counciilor AICKECIINIE said it appeared the Council had not power now to compel the company to carry out the whole scheme, and if they opposed the Bid they might get further powers which would compel them to do so. Councillor PrbarcerroN did not see what other course the Council could take than to oppose. It was the ordinary course taken to Match the interests of the Corporation on any Bill that was before Parliament, unless certain undertakings were given in writing in the first instance, which would pre- vent that. 'What Alderman Gamble had said about the subscribed capital was quite true. It was an undoubted fact that the worst of the company had been that they had not had capital sufficient to fulfil the necessary requirements of the Corporation, and had they really had sufficient to attend to the whole of the matter there would have been no trouble whatever. With regard to theabandoning of thelines,andthe line from Prescot through the town to Haydock—that line was already, to a certain extent, accommodated by a rail- way, but they had no railway whateyer in the direction of Denton's Green. Those traiimays would be one of the greatest bOons to the publiC of St. Helens, and he thought it was a great pity they did not consult the interests of the town sooner and secure themselves on that point. Mr. Brook asked what was th • use of opposing the Bill when the preamble was passed. He hoped the company would get the Bill as he hoped they woald get the Bill they first applied for, but if the Council had not then watched the company in Parliament they would not have got the provisions they had got. It was the usual course to watch the interests of the Corporation - and it was absolntely necessary that the Council as the appointed guardians of all public highways should see that no liberties were taken with them.. If the preamble had not been passed they would have lost the Bill to commence with, and he did not see that the Corporation had any other coursai—ualess, as Alderman Gamble said, the Tramways' Company approached them and made such provisions and terms i they knew would be to the interests of the Corporation than to oppose the Bill, in order to get the public interests of the town protected. That was all they wanted. The TOWN CLERK, in reply to Councillor Massey, said the objection would be read, but he did not think it desirable to discuss the question of locus stank there that day. It was a matter to be discussed before the referee in the House of Commons.

The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK then read the objection, which alleged that the Corporation had no ground which, accord- ing to the rules of Parliainent, entitled thera to be heard against the Bill. Mr. MAssnv thought they should have this question of position—not having complied with the standing orders— thrashed out now. He believed the objection was to the notice of opposition not having complied with the stand- ing orders. The petition did not allege, nor was it a fact that the interests of the town were in any wayaffected. He referred the Town Clerk to the standing orders of the House of Commons, of which No. 134 stated —"It: shall be com- petent to the referees on private bills to admit the peti- tioners, being the municipal or other authority having the local management of the metropolis, or of any town, or the inhabitants of any town or district alleged to be injuriously affected by a Bill, to be heard against such Bill if they shall think.fit." The allegation that the interests of the town were injuriously affected by the Bill was a sine pta non. The TOWN CLERK : As I said before, it is not at all desirable that any discussion upon the subject should take place here, __

Councillor liatasox hid as far 'as the principle of the Bill was being affected they should oppose, but as to the question of an extension of time he should not oppose. It seemed to him the company were going to abandon the branches from Denton's Green and Marshall's Cross, and therefore it affected the original question. On that ground he should support the resolution. The Manna: Do they intend to abandon the branch lines permanently or only for a year? Councillor HANSON : lam only taking what Alder- man Gamble says—that he knows from a private source that they are going to abandon ahem. Alderman GAMBLE : Permanently. • ,Councillor FILICINQTON : Why don't they appmach the Council and give some undertaking? _ _
Councillor MASSEY said Councillor Cook had properly reminded the representatives of East Sutton and,. that pot- .. .

tion of the town which lay towards Denton's Green that they in particular had duties in this matter more than the other councillors, because of a mere suspicion—and of course there was no attempted proof whatever given to the Council—that the Tramways Company intended to abandon their lines from St. Helens to Denton's Green, and from Sr. Helens to Marshall's Cross. The opposition that day seemed to be based upon two `grounds. The first was this ground of suspicion, and it was a question whether the Council could consider that at all. If any one came there, and in the face of an undertaking sanctioned by Parliament, in black and white— incontrovertible, and a pledge in the shape of a deposit of .£2,600 having been given to carry it out, and said there was an intention to abandon the two lines which he had named, be thought he should be asked to give his authority. One authority was as good as another. He had been told only that day, by a gentlemen interested in the Tramways Com- pany that there was not the slightest intention of abandon- ing any portion of the lines, but that they meant to carry out their undertaking to its full extent. That was from an authority which he would certainly give to the Council if they desired it. The company were compelled to do the work by thoir Act, fun.'. in the event of their failing to carry it out the deposit money_would be forfeited.

Alderman bannaLE : •No, no; a pottion of it. Councillor MASSEY (continuing) asked was it likely that the company would refuse to carry out the scheme. He granted that the two lines, and particularly the one to Den- ton's Green, might not be so profitable as the other lines, but the line to Marshall's Cross would, he was sure, be profitable, perhaps one of the most profitable lines in the whole undertaking. Sutton was a very large district, and he thought the directors of the company would almost be lunatics if for one moment they considered the question of giving up the line to Marshall's Cross. It was there the company would naturally expect to make the largest profits, and as a representative of East Sutton he fully believed that the Tramways Company would carry out faithfully their undertaking, and extend their line towards Marshall's Cross. This bogey—a ground of suspicion was in his opinion entirely disposed of. He questioned very much the propriety or advisability of bringing before the Council statements of this character—suspicions for which no authority was given—and he was rather surprised that gentlemen sitting at that table should be influenced for one moment by a mere ground of suspicion like this. He asked again what would they gain even in point of time. Sup- posing the Council opposed the Tramways Company in Parliament successftilly, and the company was at an end. What m7as the Council's poeition? A new company would be formed Which it would probably take twelve months to form, dad it woUld probably take them another twelve months to make their lines, so that thg Council would really not be gainers. This company only asked for an extension of time for two years, but they expected in that time to have com- pleted the whole of the scheme. In their prospectus they , said at the end of July the principal lines in the borough would be completed, and the Council had a guarantee to that effect, by the fact that there was at the present time a sufficient called-up capital to meet the requirements of the Corporation and to pay the cost of making those lines. Then he asked them to look at the enormous expense of any opposition to the extension of time. As to the Corporation not having complied with the standing orders he said that according to the Town Clerk, sufficiently showed to them very great ground indeed, to see whether the Council had complied with the requirements of the House of Commons. He did not think the Council had complied with them. He He did not blame the Town Clerk for it, but rather the Tramways -Committee for not having brought this matter before the Town Cleft so that steps might have been taken at the proper time. In addition to the opposition to the compliance of the standing orders, the Corporation had to oppose the Bill itself. He supposed they all could form an accurate idea of what the cost- of anaopposition to a Bill in Parliament was. Then it became a question whether it was worth their while to oppose the Bill, whether they were really acting in the interests of the Corporation in opposing the Bill, and what would be gained by opposing it. He did not see himself that any benefit could possibly be gained, but that the money of the ratepayers would be fruitlessly spent in litigation with the company and no useful end gained by it. His opinion was that the Corporation had clogged the company br a lot of useless and silly conditions, conditions which would have the effect of preventing them carrying out their under. taking. He certainly considered it was the ditty of the committee, in pursuance of the resolution passed by the Council at their last meeting, to approach the company. The resolution read in that way, and it was perfectly evident that it was the feeling of the Council that the committee should approach the company, and he had no doubt what- ever if that had been done it would have been possible for the committee to have got such conditions from the Tram- ways' Company as would have prevented the Council going on with their opposition. He hoped it was not too late to do that yet, that the good feeling which had existed between the Tramways' Committee and the company would continue, and that the company would not do anything that was nn- reasonable or unbnsiness-like, or that would prejudice the interest* of the Corporation in the slightest particular. eUpon ben these submitted. grounds he should oppose the resolution that had Councillor BEISHER felt it his duty to correct Councillor Massey's statement that if the Corporation lost their locus stands the fault would not rest with the Town Clerk, but owfiththatthehe eempbert Committee. committee Tramways' a notice from Cie Town Clerk to do so, and he thought the committee would have done as they always attended unlesseessa He had had a great deal to do with the, Tramways Com- mittee, done when they neCvoenrun were required to attend to business. and his experience had been that they had always endeavoured fairly and honestly to meet the company, and had afforded the latter every facility they possibly could. lie could not see what advantage they could gain by opposing the company. They could not compel the corn- Ipany to lay the main lines or the branches. The company had only to allow the time to elapse, and the matter was at an end. If by opposition to the present application the Cor- poration could get such terms as would force the company to lay the whole of the system which the company told them they intended to lay at the outset, then the Council would be perfectly justified in opposing the application. Unless they could do that, he did not see the slightest use in opposing the company, and, so far as the discussion had gone, he did not feel justified in supporting the resolution: Alderman GAMBLE, in reply, said he had no doubt the ai trbihoa enn dd if ietnehgi et trnhCeeonubenyr ohhde oe amount i was e da o ot oti shcceotnehtei ni company u,pelainiktyo: Town Clerk had taken care that he had ground to go upon regardhl eo eoepbP;t wwWioituthhl would
MMAI I=ll

£700; but be was not certain that Parliament always in. . listed upon the forfeiture of the money when an application was made for an extensien of time. As to the statement he had made, the information was given to him by a pets= who knew all that was done by the Tramways Company, and was bound by his position to know. He had no doubt the allegation he had made that the company intended to abandon those two lines would have been contradicted by a director of the company who was present if it could have been honestly contradicted; so that he thought they might take it as a fact that the company in- tended to abandon the branch x 4. The opposition, if it suc- ceeded, would he to ensure that the branches would be laid. That the Tramways Committee and the Council considered should be done, and, as he had said before, these lines could never be laid if they were not laid by the present company. He hoped the committee, in carrying out the resolution, would adopt such a course as this—that they would ask the solicitor of the company to give them a letter undertaking that a clause should be inserted in the new Act providing that until the company completed the whole of the tramways authorised by the original Act they would pay no dividends. Such a clause as that would do the company no harm whatever, and the company could give them that undertaking, Which could be presented to the Committee of the House of Commons, and would stop the Bill with very little expense to the Corporation. If the company intended to make the lines they would consent to give such an under- taking, and it would de away with their "oppiosition, and would not cost the company a farthing if they really meant to complete the scheme. But if they would not give such a letter it would show they did not intend to complete the work, and that opposition was absolutely necessary in the interests of the town.

The MAYOR aired if there was any stipulation binding the companyA derman GAMBLE said there was nothing except the deposit money, of which they would lose £7OO if they did to complete any portion of their line. not complete the branches. That was the only compulsion, but they had agreed with the Corporation to make the tram- *R:va. The Corporation would not have consented to the Passing of the Act at all if it had not been for that agree- ment. It was only on that distinct undertaking that the Council consented to the original Act, which the company DOW wanted to get rid of. Councillor SWIFT' asked if the suggestion of Alderman Gamble could not be incorporated with the resolution. The TOWN CLERK said the proper course would be to pass the resolution, and then to pass a subsequent resolution. Councillor Swirl,: Suppose we pass a resolution that it is desirable the Bill should contain a clause such as he sug- gests, which appears to me to be a proper suggestion, we could pass a general resolution afterwards. The Town CLERK: I want a separate resolution to go to the ratepayers' meeting, and afterwards to Parliament. The resolution was then unanimously passed, on condi- tion that another resolution was submitted. Alderman GAMBLE then moved : "That if the Tramways Company will give the Corporation an undertaking in writing to insert in this Bill before Parliament a clause or clauses to the satisfaction of the Town'Clerk, providing that the company shall pay no dividend in these schemes until the whole of the tramways, sanctioned by the Act of 1879 be completed and opened, then that th e Tramways Committee of this Council be and are hereby. authorised to withdraw this Council's opposition of the Bill." Councillor Puxulovon seconded, and this resolution was also unanimously carried. The meeting then terminated. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. /A meeting of the above committee was held at the Town Hall. St. Helens, on Wednesday, when Councillor Allen presided, and there were also present Councillors Cook and Swift; and Mr. J. 11. Craik (deputy town clerk.)

THE OFFICERS' REPORT. Mr. BAMFORD reported as follows :—I beg to submit to you the following report for the past month. Since the date of your last meeting the names of 1,052 absent and irregular scholars have been reported by the various teachers in my district. I have found a great many of the children absent through the parents being out of work and not able to pay the school fees ; and in many eases not having sufficient food and clothing to send their children to school. During the month 30 notices have been served upon the parents of 49 of the most irregular of the above- named scholars to appear before your Investigation Com- mittee to state the reason for such irregularity. Ten parents not being able to give satisfactory reasons for their children's absence from school, and having been previously warned by the committee, and nearly all of them having been fined by the magistrates before, were ordered to be sum- moned again, and were with the following results :-9 were fined 6d. and costs, and one attendance order granted with a a view of sending the boy to the Liverpool Truant School, and three boys were recommended by the Committee to be sent to Industrial Schools. Mr. Durrox stated :-Since the 26th, ult., the date of your last meeting, the names of 994 absent and irregular scholars had been sent in by the teachers of the schools in my dis- trict. .44 parents, representing 94 of the most irregular of them, were served with notices to appear before your Investi- gation Committee on the 10th instant, and 13.n0t being able to give a reasonable excuse for their children's absence or irrigularity, were then ordered to be sommoned, which has been done with the following resnlt-12 were fined in the usual penalty of 58. including costs, and one school atten-- dance order granted. I have signed 141. childrens' school. books during the month. The ch;ef cause of absence from school has been poverty, owing to the parents being out of work and not having sufficient food and clothes to send them in.. Herewith I submit the names and particulars of previous proceedings against the parents of three boys as suitable cases for industrial or truant schools. Thomas Conway, 10 years; John Sephton, 11; John Doran. 11; Thomas Fitzpatrick, Patrick Shed, and Emmanuel Spash were ordered to be sent to an industrial school, and William Potter to a truant school.

PAOPOTED CATHOLiC BAzAen AT Sr. HELENS. —lt has•already been announced that a bazaar is to be held early in May for the purpose of raising funds to repair and complete Holy Cross Church, and the event is being looked forward to with pleasure. Offers of help have already been received from several quarters. In order to put the work .into proper order, the congregations of Lowe House and Holy .Cross Churches were invited to meet together on Tues- day evening last, and accordingly a number of ladies and gentlemen gathered in the Girls' School, Duke-street, when the subject was explained. Alderman Johnson was voted to the chair, and, after a few prefatory remarks, he called upon the Rev. Father Cardwell, who informed the meeting that the beautiful stained glass windows of the church, which had been placed in it.at such a'great expense, were in danger of being lost by their decaying or falling oat unless immediate steps were taken to efficiently guard against that. He had been informed that the beat thing they could do was to put in the windows a thin kind of plate glass so as to prevent the 'stained windows being injured in the future. It was his wish to have the principal entrance to the church improved by erecting a flight of ittps leading np tO it, its present condition rendering it both unsightly and dangerous. He proposed to have the chmth properly railed round, and these additions and improve- ments would cost a considerable sum of money, but he was quite sure that those who had erected such a magnificent structure as Holy Cross Church would not allow it to deteriorate, and he felt quite safe in leaving the matter in their hands. (Applause.) The reverend father read letters from •everal gentlemen regretting their inability to attend the meeting, and fully approving its objects and promising their assistance. He also announced that of the seven stalls required for the purposes of the bazaar, four had already been promised, three by generous benefactors and one by the a Children'of Mary" of Holy Cross—(applause)—so that only three more remained to be provided, and he would say to them give him the materials and he would undertake to find the purchasers Resolutions were carried that three additional stalls be provided, one to be called the "Lowe House Stall," another the "Holy Cross Stall," and the third , the "Irish Stall." the promoters of which are to be respec- tively the Rev. Fathers Turner, Dignam, and Cardwell, who will each form a committee of ladies to carry out the work.

Sr. HErstss COUNTY COURT.—Before Mr. Collier, judge.—George Gerrard was sued by Matilda Makin, pro- vision dealer, for about £(3, for goods sold and delivered. The defendant, who was a " s:nker," was ordered to pay 4s a month.—Mr. Dobie, draper, sued a man named Clary fo. the price of a shawl supplied to defendant's wife. Defen- dant denied giving the order, and when the shawl arrived he ordered his wife to take it back. Defendant's wife was called, who said she ordered the shawl, and sold it in order that she might be able to pay the rent. This was in August last, and, as her husband was out of work, she had no money i for Ike rent. Defendant said he was no; n such a position as tehe unable to pay the rent, and he rather thought that his wife sold the shawl for some other purpose. His Honour said if the wile sold the shawl to pay the rent, defendant, as an honourable man, ought to pay for the shawl. Defendant: Yes, if it is the case; but it is not. His Honour: Well, I think, as a matter of law, defendant is not liable, and there- fore plaintiff will be nonsuited. Plaintiff offered to take half of the debt, but gonoarral Hayes, goods eoes, collier, was sued by Samuel. itLimnmcoounrdt.f—orTgma odd idganeindendtelivweraeds co . Mr. Swift appeared for plaintiff, and Mr. Riley defended. De- fondant admitted owing £lO. Mr. Riley said the circum- stances were about as distressing as they coild be. De- fendant was a collier, but had been out of work six weeks. He had seven children none of whom were working, one of them being a cripple 31 years of age, They had had several funerals lately, and plaintiff's wife, who now asked with such emphasis for an immediate order, offered to take the money at 3s:a week. Plaintiff's wife said defendant was a very steady man and did not touch beer and therefore ought to Pay his debts. Mr. Swift showed by the books that de- fendant had paid large sums of money at short intervals to the plaintiff, thereby showing that if be chose to work he was quite able to pay the present debt. Mr. Riley submitted. that the present circumstances of the man should be looked at, and also the fact that BO many deaths had taken place in his family quite recently. An order for 4s. a month was made.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL. THE PARK REJECTED.
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL. THE PARK REJECTED.

An adjourned meeting of the council was held on Satur- day morning there being present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aldermen Gamble, Cook, and Johnson; Council- lors .1. C. Gample, Allen, Twyford, R. Pilkington, Baxter. Massey, Foster, McKecknie, Walker, Harrison, Belsher, Swift, Wilcock, Brook, and W. W. Pilkington. The MAYOR said he had to report that a committee waited upon Mr. Henry Taylor, solicitor, Manchester, and submitted the resolution and requirements of the Council. Mr. Taylor had met the committee in a very fair spirit and offered every facility that lay in his power to meet the Corporation, especially on the water question. He also promised to arrange as far as possible to keap the big dam full, but could not entertain the proposal to negotiate for the purchase of the freehold, as that was outside the question of the offer —cline Man- chester sawly c at rhtai nt gi t wtharso uo bg hi ec ttihoen apb of the park entirely. With regard to the other conditions park—but 111 rm. Tr a Ty al oyrl, oor sMe na l e , laid great stress on it. But afterwards he said he might waive that altogether. They had the ,advice of the water engineer in regard to the lowering of the water, but he could not guarantee to keep that dam full. The following letter was read:—" 8, John Dalton- Street, Manchester, 17th February,—Park,—Dear Sir,—On the other side I send copy of memorandum of the terms arranged this morning as to the great dam. lam writing by this post to Mr. Taylor asking his consent to watvettlie reservations of the right to send carts through the park, and unless you hear frOm me to the contrary by eleven o'clock on Saturday next, you may assume that this reservation will be waived.—l am yours. faithfully, HENRY TAYLOR.".--" Memorandum of provision as to great dam to apply on expiration of lease of London and North-Western railway company. If at any. time Mr. Taylor or his heirs, Arc., permit the level of the water in the great dam to remain for six weeks consecutively more than two feet below the level of the existing waste weir, then the obligation of the Corporation to maintain the dam and its embankments has to cease, and the Corporation thenceforth is publicly at liberty to use the dam for other park purposes, this provision net to apply if the lowering of the water level is caused by dronght or by the drain becoming not water-tight, the six weeks to run from receipt of notice in ' writing." The following telegram received at half-past ten that morning was read :—From Henry Taylor, 8 John Dalton,. street, to Town Clerk. Park. Just received letter from Mr. Taylor. He refuses to waive reservation as to carts, but I personally will endeavour to induce him to meet wishes of Corporation. For purposes of meeting to-day you must state Taylor refuses to waive right. Definite answer must be given by Corporation rumtt Monday." Mr. R. Pirairmroli said they received every courtesy and attention from Mr. Hy. Taylor. With reference to the water, the deputation pointed out that if they could get sufficient water so long 'as he would guarantee to keep it fall, they should certainly use it as an ornamental lake t but they did want to have that right. Ile did not think the amendment would at all put the Corporation safe Mr. Taylor admitted that the water which supplies the large dam could be cut off at any time and sent into Eccles- ton weir, and they could cut it off within a few yards from where it enters the clam. That condition would enable Mr. Taylor to keep the dam short of water; and as to there being a drought what would be considered a drought in a lawsuit? If a month Mr. Taylor would doubtless come off the victor. There were the elements of a lawsuit, and if they could not get the park free from obligations they would not be safe. It would be far more beneficial to Mr. Taylor for the Corpora- tion to accept the park than for Mr. Taylor to have it himself. They would be making a great mistake If the Car- porationaccepted the offer under the circumstances, He would therefore move "That the Corporation are not justi- fied in accepting the Offer with the present reservations and conditions." Alderman GAMBLE seconded the motion, remarking that be was not prepared to accept the park with any conditions whatever that could not be got rid of by something they could do within the next few ram:ohs. Mr. BAXTER was very sorry to qiffer from their esteemed alderman, for he believed there was nothing whatever in the water question. It was more valuable to the Corporation with that condition than without it, for the simple reason that if they wanted a sheet of water there they could not have one without Mr. Taylor's assistance. They could not possibly ask him to give them that water in perpetuity. If he had offered it without that condition the park would be accepted, but the park was made more valuable through that. Dr. TWYFORD supported the resolution of Councillor Pilkington, and he fully endorsed all that he had said. What advantage would the park be to those in Parr who were three miles away? Mr. W. W. PILKINGTON said be was very much astonished at what Mr. Baxter had to say after what he had said the other day. But his own words condemned him. He said without Mr. Taylor's assistance they could not have this orna- mental sheet of water. That was to say they might have it or not, exactly as Mr. Taylor pleased. The drought, as his brother had said, would probably lead to a law transaction, and that would simply be a repetition of what they had already had with Mr. Taylor. There was a water course going right across to St. Helens dam, and there was a pecu- liar mud arrangement. That water sometimes went into the mere and Sometimes went to St. Helens, but there was actually ' a way underneath which carried. The water from the higher part went down into the mere until the mere was 'till, and when it was full a clough was put down. Of course Mr. Taylor would ex- amine these when it suitedlis purpose and wrtrk the water as be wanted it. If they looked upon their past experience with Mr. Taylor in regard to the water question, they would not be ready in accepting the present offer with such con- ditions attached. If the Corporation accepted the offer it would be a great advantage to Mr. Taylor, as it would enhance the value of his property in that locality consider- ably. Mr. McKxcarriz said they had spent a great deal of time, they had gone thoroughly into the question, and they could not blame any of them for speaking out their minds. He had thought that for the people of St. Helens the park would be a great boon. He still thought it would be one, though some of the reservations seemed rather dangerous. There was a difference in the town as in the Town Council as to the wisdom of accepting the offer, but the distance the pro- posed park was from the town was no argument at all, for . where else could they get a park nearer St. Helens?

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 26, 1881.

TUE Protection of Person and Property (Ireland) Bill, after being subjected to the most minute and litter criticism in &bates which have monopolised the whole time of the House for several weeks, is now on the point of being sent up from the House of Com- mons to the House of Lords, and presents very much the shape in which it will become law. The Peers may be trusted to pass the Bill with expedition, not- withstanding that it is the measure of a Liberal Government, and with probably trifling, if any, amendments. That the House of Lords can be de- pended upon to pass a Bill relating to Ireland simply because it is a penal measure, whilst if it was a BiE to enlarge the rights and liberties of the mass of the Irish people the dauger of its rejection by that chamber would be regarded as considerable, is not a circumstance that reflects much credit upon the Upper House as a branch of the British Legislature. But it is a fact we are compelled to take account of; and it is one of the few remaining legitimate grounds' of grudge by Irishmen against the Imperial Parliament by which they are rded, and which some of them are striving hard to aupercede by an Irish Parliament, that one House of the British Parliament is .always ready to repress thera, but is seldom willing to assist In redressing their wrongs or remedying the Ills from which they suffer. English Liberals are unable to blame the Irish people for their antipathy for a governing body of Lords which seems to exist only to defeat any 'substnntial reform of the laws for their relief, or else to insert such alterations in measures of that kind as will enable the landlord class to neutralise their effect when passed. But we, do not see why Irishmen should hold the Liberal party and Government accountable for the consequences of the perverse opposition to Irish reforms displayed by a House of Lords in which the Tory element is so largely preponderant. But looking at this'Protection Bill, which is now as good as pass, we have-to say that it is one which, indeed, a Liberal Government has framed, and a Liberal House of Commons sup- ported, but whish,Liberals can' contemplate the sue- - tess of with ,no pleasure whatever. When grand measures for reconciliation and restitution triumph over opposition iaParliament and pass into laws, a , jubilant shout of exultation rises <from the militant I host of the party of freedom, justice, and pre,gress. But an enactment that will curtail .popular liberties, necessary as it may be demonstrated to .be. for the ,euppression of cria inal offences, is received by that party with, at beat, cold acquiescence and ill-con- cealed dislike. The electors who returned the present Government to power, backed by a powerful majority in the House of Commons, have loyally stood by that Government in its ',hour of serious difficulty, and have sustained their representatives in voting for the powers which Ministers with the fullest know- ledge of the realities of the position in Ireland Lave regarded as indispeutable to the preservation of crder in that country. In no spirit of enmity to Irishmen, •even of the most extreme political section, have they done this; but only in obediene to a stern dictate of conscience as their imperative duty to the State of which they are citizesc. The sole objects of tkeir reprehension are the perpetrators of those outrages and acts of gross illegality who have obi:lgen.' the Executive to resort to these exeoptional means to stop their zeieffeeds and to secure the criminals. ;If the, Irish Land League and its recognised leaders have had nothing to do with the icstigation of these mmliciocs and revengeful deeds—as they profess .notto have— then neither the . sharp condemnation of English public opinion nor the penalties and ,pains of the Proteetion Act, when paesed, will extend go them. , Punishments are prepared for the guilty, not for the iumecent ; and no Irishman who knows himself to be entirely free from any ocmplicity with the authors .of flagrant breaches of the law or of sanguinary erime,, need alarm himself ,about the effects of the Bill which the House of Commons has so decisively sanctioned. Neither do we understand only-so many conspicuous Irish politicians, who declare their abhor- rence of the outrages, should be at so much pains to prevent effectual measures being taken by I:lea:sem- five for the arrest of the actual transgressors. Mr. ,Parnell and his friends, taking them at their own valuation as strictly. Lawful agitators, should he as anxious as all Englishmen are that the offences .of personal violence and the attacks upon property which have certainly taken place, and hare been committed in nearly every instance with impunity, should .belput clown. Their movement may thug, and thus alone, be cleared from the reproach which :eats upon it, .so long as law-breakers, pretending to be agents of the Land League, outrage the persons and domiciles of their neighbours, prohibit their trade, mutilate their cattle, and get off soot-free. The language of the ant clause of the Protection Nil, in which the gist of , the special power it gives to the authorities is con- tamed, defines the nature of the offences to be parti- cularly dealt with. The persons who may be arrested under the Lord-Lieutecant's warrant and detained in custody are those who are "reasonably sresPected of having been guilty of felony, or treasonable practices," or of crimes punish- able bylaw, including "acts "high treason, treason- of violence or intimida- tion," or incitements to such acts. Treasonable practices may be roughly for eohsre attemptitre destruction the vt iooi . nt. t e others ofrebl eas e kot of stated to comprehend any proevobeliertl-kaac; trepfrdirseozhenoenslrlsip,oknorac; "acts aorfrites or other public buildings. The term vio- lence, or intimidation," relates more to the class of attacks upon private citizens which have recently been ripe in Ireland. It would be easy to insist dull the expression" reasonably suspected," as furnishing the ground of the arrest, is sufficiently indefinite to leave a wide discretionary power to the Executive. We do not dispute that. It could not well be different, for in the absence of the usual process of indictment any- thing like established proof of felony before detention is out of the question. An arbitrary Lord-Lieutenant might abuse this power to almost any extent, we grant. ,But the Irish Executive is amenable to the
