div.p: THE T.IXAMINER4. SATtItRA_Y, VEBRITARY N, 1881.

public sentiment of the count:y ns to the manner in which these powers are used. Its members would be quickly called to account in t'ne House of Commons if they were to act with undue harshness even to known offenders or bad charact'ers, still more if it could be I shown that orderly subjects had been incarcerated on false suspicion. The thing is not to be sdone in the dark; for it is provided that " a list of all persons for the time being detained in prison under this Act, with a statement opposite such person's ns.rne of the prison in which he is detained for the time being, and of the ground stated for his arrest in the warrant under which he is detained," shall be laid before Parliament monthly, when it is in session, and at other times shall be published in the _Dublin. Gazette. Also any relative of the arrested person or his solicitor is entitled to have a certified copy of the warrant. i People in England do not expect that many arrests will be made under this enactment. , They hope that,its value will be much more as a de- terrent from crime than as a means of inflioting sum- mary pemolties for crime. Even Mr. Parnell thinks I that the victims will be few, and that, as he puts it, ' the measure will operate rather in the shape of "intimidation than coercion." The more it intimi- dates men who may harbour thoughts of crime from their committal, the better for them and for the whole community. He further anticipates there will not be many more unjust evictions now, and we heartily trust he may be right. The cruelties of certain un- principled landlords and agents which preceded and provoked the outrages of some of the more desperate of the tenant class, are not forgotten by the people in England ; who only regret that the excesses on the other side have recently forced them to divide the in- dignation stirred by inhuman conduct which pre- viously descended upon rapacious landlords alone. We abide in the confident expectation that as the measure now passing through will protect the land- lord and his allies, in person and property, the Go- vernment's Land Bill which is to follow will, when passed, as thoroughly protect and maintain the honest and respectable tenant farmers of Ireland in their holdings, in the fairness of their rentals, and in the recovery of a full money equivalent to their investment of capital, labour, and science in the improvement of the land, on the eventual surrender of their holdings. Happily, whilst the Protection Act will not remain in force more than eighteen months at the longest, the Land Act, once passed, will be permanent in its action, subject to future amendments of its clauses or beneficial amplifica- tion of its main principles. Irishmen should take courage from that. The restraint will soon cease.; the enfranchisement, that cannot be delayed, will be for all time to come.

A Parliamentary paper just issued will prove highly interesting to Mr. Bradlaugh, and all who wish him well in the movement he is making against perpetual pensions. The paper we refer to is a re- turn "showing hirer many, and which of the per- petual pensions, are actually paid to other than the persons named as the recipients in the financial ac- counts, and in each such case to whom the said several pensions arenow really paid." From this return we learn that an annuity of £4,000 was granted to the Duke of Schomberg in the days of William 111. Of this sum £2,616 was commuted, and the rest is paid in annual sums to half a dozen persons who are as remotely connected with the original recipient as Private O'Flaherity, of the Ist Connaught Rangers, has with the Field Marshal commanding-in-chief. A pension of £3OOO a year, subject to deductions, was granted by His Majesty King Charles /1., to John Granville, Earl of Bath. One moiety of this pension was bought up by the Treasury in 1826, the other moiety was transferred to the Consolidated Fund in 1856. The amouet now due £1,200, ic paid to F. ' C. Maitland, and F. J. Blake as .trustees for ' the heirs of Captain F. Garth. Amorig the other anomalies of this „pension list which may be mentioned is a sum of £4,000 granted by King George Thl. to William Penn in consideration of his services in. America, and this sum is ncosrpaid to Colonel Stuart, a descendant of the great ;historical Pennsylvanian. A duty of is. per childron on coal exported from the Tyne and consumed in •England, was granted under Letters Patent, on the 18th December, 1676, to the Duke of Richmond. This pension was commuted into an annuity of 41900 per annum for a -sum of £490,833 lie. 61, which sum was.invested in the purchase of £633,333 .6s. ,Pd. consols. By the Act .39 and 40 George HI., c.. 103, a.portion, £485,434 4s. 7d., of this stock was sold and invested in land, and by the 1 Vict., c.. 54, power was given to sell the balance of stock remaining and to invest in land. The remaining stock has been .sold and invested in land, with the ex- caption of a sum of £B6 Os. 9d.., representing a balance of .ales of enfranchisementa,lr.c., subsequent to the purchase .of the property and which is retained 'to keep the trust account open. The lands purchased under the above :mentioned Acts will revert _to the Crown, in &Adult of male issue of the.boly of the first Duke of .Richmond. Surely it is high time that the anomalies shOWLI in this list were wept away.

At the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians this week, the report of the committee appointed to investigate the charges against the master and mistress of the house, I was presented. The document may be briefly summarised as follows :—lt was found that the potatoes had been given to the pony without the knowledge of the master and mistress, who were cautioned to exercise more care in the future. The eatables provided for a certain guardian, when he had his tea at the house were provided out of the pri- vate funds of the matron. It was acknowledged that when the members of the Assessment Committee met on a Board day, they had at the end of their special business gone to• the master's room and had refreshment at his table. The committee recommended that such refreshments_: be not allowed in future. On the reading of the report, a lively and personal discussion took place, in the course of which Mr. Challoner very coolly said that they were not to mind what the law said, after he had been distinctly, told by the Cleark. that it was Illegal for the Guardians to have dinner at the House under any circumstances. The Local Government Board have had immense experience of the scandals which have arisen in various parts of the country through guardians being entertained at workhouses, and other such matters, and have prohibited such private dinners. If gentlemen covet the honour of being Poor Law Guardians, they must be prepared to take the office with a few attendant inconveniences be- longing to it, remembering that there is a law of compensa- tion in all things. Though the committee recommended that the refreshment provided for the Assessment Commit- tee at the master's table should be discontinued, it watt agreed, with only two dissentients, that this recommenda- tion should be eliminated from the report. No doubt it is very awkward to have to stay at the work- house for a considerable number •of hours without being enabled to supply the wants tf the inner man at a good table, but when the gentlemen who grumble took office, they knew that this was one of the disadvantages. This, however, does not prevent their being full of fervour at an election time. Example is greater than precept, and they who have so much to do with administering the Poor Law, ought to be'particularly careful that their public acts are free from the appearance of evil. It would be a comparative easy matter to devise a plan whereby the hungry members of the Board could have their little bodily wants supplied with- oat giving cause for complaint.

BRUNNER, MOND, AIM OD. (Larrran).—Under this title a company has been registered, with a capital of £600,000, in shares of £lO each, to acquire and extend the business of Messrs.Bruhner,Mond,and Co., of Winnington and Sandbach, the only manufacturers of alkali by the Ammonia process in the kingdom. It will be seen from the ptospectus in our advertising columns that the company take over the pro- perties on favourable terms, and save arranged to retain Messrs. Brunner and Mond, as managing directors.

FUNERAL SERMON OPT= LATE MR& PETERS, OF Widnes.—On Sunday afternoon the Congregational Chapel, Simm's Cross, was .filled by a large congregation, which I had assembled to-do honour to the memory of Mrs. Peters, 1 the deceased wife and their esteemed pastor the Rev. T. Peters. The service was conducted hy the Rev. John Yens, ; of Wycliffe Church; Warrington, who preached from Epbesiana, 3rd -chapter, part of the 15th verse.:" Ihe whole family in heaven and earth." Mr. Yonge said that he had not felt at liberty to preach a sermon of any per- sonal descsiptien, inasmuch of his knowledge of Mrs. Peters was too slight to enable him to tlo so. But he was there principally to give expression for himself and all who knew Mr. Peters-to the deep sympathy left for him and his family in this sad and sadden bereavement. From what he had heard trom,varions sources of the late Mrs. Peters he be- lieved she.had lived an earnest Christian life, a life of use- fulness in the house and Church, a life which would be missal and mourned by very many. She had served her I generation according to the will of God, and now had fallen asleep. He hoped Mr. Peters and his family would be lovingly upheld by many friends, and by God, who is the giver o/ peace and comfort.

WRECK .OF A SCHOONER TRADING BETWEILN tcwcoze AND ELEAST.—The schooner Tasso, trading between Atun- corn and JBelfast, was sunk on Monday evening, and the master, Captaia Drysdale, drowned. The vessel, which is about 190 tone burderil left Runcorn On Saturday night with a cargo of salt consigned by Messrs. Verdict Brothers. On Monday night, when off Red Bay, County Antrim, the schooner collided with the steamer Telegrafobic, .outward bound .from Londonderry. The schooner sank soon after the collision. Those onboard the steamer succeeded in saving four of the crew of the 'lasso, who were landed in Liverpool, on Tuesday. Captain Drysdale has traded to Ituncorn for manylrears, and is well known in the port as -late master of the Catwcronian, one of the old vessels belongingto thafirm of McElroy and Pollock, of Belfast.

BALLAD CONCERT -AT RuNconer.—A concert 1946 given in the Reline Hall, on Thursday, which possessed a-strong local interest, it being advertised as Mr. Bantoektrierpoinl's first concert, as many of our readers are aware. Mr. Pier- point is -a Runcornian, at present studying at -the .Royal Academyof Music, having chosen music as his future pro- fession. He was assisted by Miss Falkner, a pupil of Mrs. Sims Reeves; Miss Lloyd; of the Royal Academy.; and Mr. Bywaterof Wolverhampton. The members of the.Runcorn Madrigal, Club, under the baton of Mr. W. S. Argent,-sang Iseverakchoice glees with their accustomed ability, making up, as mill be at once seen, a thoroughly varied and attractive programme. The audience was a large and appreciative one, eomprising the-dite and beauty of the neighbourhood, seri the attendance must have been very encouraging to Mr. Pierpoiuteand lisoperty. We feel somewhat .nrclined to conclude the notice by saying that all the ,pieces were ex- ce.edingiy well performed, leaving little to be desired either in musical expression or artistic rendering. However, severalof the selectione were evidently so much.eympathised with by the audience, that we feel bound to single them out by .a .brief notice. These remarks are especially true of the pieces forming the second part.' Mr. Pierpohat sang "The Raft" (Piasuti).and the "Village Blacksmith" (Weiss) with fine declamation and sympa- thetic expression. . Mica Falkner, too, showed herzpower an a ballad singer in her rendering of "The Kerry Dance" (Motley), and her appreciation of clear articulation, and intenationdo Randers Aria from Theodora's "Angels ever bright and lair." Mies Lloyd fairly brought down the house by the irresistible manner of her singing "d'unchi-, nello" (Moltoy), and in response to the call of the audience sang in eplendid style -Sullivan's "Lost Chord." Mr., By. water sang with magnificent verve and declamatory power' the martial racena . Draw the sword, Scotland" (Rodwel). During the evening there were numerous -encores, which were gracefullyncknowlelged. The success of the.concert was considerably indebted to the excellent accompanying of Mr. LiveerCarroll, (E.A.M.), who during the evening performed two 'solos on the pianoforte; and the ,judicious manipulation of theharnienium by Mr. Bywater, giving at 'times the effect of a full, orchestra, so appropriate.to the descriptive verses in , the songs "The Raft" and -"The ;Village Blacksmith." Wertrust this will not be the last of similar musical beats, and hope that each future one mill receive the same .er greater measure of appreciation and eypport. COCICHEDOR 31.188,102 e SUNDAY SCNOOL, WASZNINOTON. —The annual treat to. the ,children attending this echo.) was given in the schoolroom, Brick-street, on Monday and Tuweay evenings. Xhose,engaged in the work of the miseion are much encouraged, ly the success of the Sunday schoo), which has almost doubled its numbers during the last two years. Monday evening was set apart (Or the delectation of the infanta, numbering about 280, who were entertained by pictures shown through the magic lantern by Mr. Smith, representing -scenes in the life of Joseph, and entitled "...Joseph and his .brethren." A number of comic pictures were also exhibited muclarto the amusement of the little folks,, and they sang several hymns from the screen. Songs and recitations were given, and at the conclusion of the proceedings the children enjoyed themselves with an hour's romp about the school, each receiving an orange on departieg. On Tuesday evening the .distribution of prizes to those scholars who had been most regular in their atten- dance during the year took place. Mr.2iba Armitage, who each year provides the prizes, which consisted of hooks, occupied the chair, and there were about3Qo scholars present.. Mrs. Armitage, the Rev. J. Yonge, Mr. A. Smith (the mis- sionary), and Mr. it. Farrar occupied seats on the platform. The Chairman preeented the prizes to the successful scholars, of whom there were 60, speaking a few kind words to each recipient. Seaga, recitations.airc., were given by the scholars during the eveoing, Mr. P. Travis preeiding at the harmonium. Mr. Smith, in proposing a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, remarked on the good behaviour of the children, and spoke wilt regret of the loss of Mr. Rigby, who had taken a deep interest in the school, bat he was glad that they had one of the firm still with then; in the person of Mr. Armitage. The motion was seconded by Mr. Farrar, and supported by the Rev. Yonge. The room wa.- then cleared, and the scholars engiged in various game. until ten o'clock, each receiving an orange, as on the pre- vious evening.

WOILEWELL'S MENAGERIE AT WARRINGTON.— The Fair Ground was occupied on Tuesday and Wednesday last by Mrs. Edmond's (late Wombwell's) menagerie, which con- tained some excellent Zoological specimens. The menagerie was visited by a large number of persons, who were much interested in the exhibition, several recent additions, inclu- ding the vlacke vark, which was captured in Zululand, coming in for a large share of attention. . .

ELECTION OF AUDITORS FOR Wtonamaxos.—The nomi- nation of gentlemen to serve as auditors for the ensuing year took place on Saturday last, when papers were delivered to Mr. W. H. Brook, the' town clerk, nominating Mr. Richard Dowd, Mr. John Harrison, and Mr. John Main- Waring. There were only two vacancies, and as three can- didates had been nominated a contest seemed probable,but en Monday afternoon, when the Mayor attended at the Town Hall to receive objections, Mr. Dowd retired. This left the same number of candidates as there were vacancies, and Messrs. Harrison and Main Waring were therefore declared duly elected.

_ C. Yates, coroner, held an inquest at the Bridge Inn, Latchford, on Friday morning, touching the death of Maud Mary Ashton, the infant daughter of Mr. Joseph Ashton, the landlord. It appeared that the deceased was taken to bed on Monday night, when she appeared to be perfectly well. At one o'clock next morning the mother awoke, and the deceased seemed all right, but when Mrs. Ashton arose at six o'clock she found the child dead. The deceased was discoloured about the face, and had every appearance of having been suffocated. The jury returned a verdict of "Died from suffocation."

WESLEYLN HOME MISSIONS : WIDNES %Lamm— The annual sett-nons in aid of the Widnes branch of the Wesleyan Methodist Home Missionary Society were ,preached, on Sunday, in the Victoria-road Chapel, by the 41te
nr. John Newell, of Runcorn.. On Monday, the annual

meeting was field in the same piece. Mr- Thomas Sadler presidedpand there were also present the Revs. C..Bingant. J. Tesseymatt, and J. S. Pawlyn, of London, ,who attended as the deputation), Messrs. Benjamin Brown, T. Robinson, ,and T. S. Swale.'The Rev. C. Ilingant made a few remarks expressive of his regret at the inability of the Rev. T. Peters to be present, and the sad bereavement which had pre- vented his attendance.—The Chairman spoke of his deep sympathy with home mission work, and said that when•they considered the great amount of practical heathenism which there was in so-called Christian England, it as high time all of them tried to do more to bring the influence of Chtis- tianity to bear upon the masses of the people. There were thousands in the kingdom who never attended God's house. —The Rev. C. Bingant read the report, which showed that the local branch had contributed asdollows during the year: 'Yearly collection, £9 145.; congregational collections in the whole circait, £l2 15s. Pd.; and public meeting, £4 Is. 6d. —The Rev.-Z. S. Pawlyn delivered a long address on home ,mission work, dealing especially with Londonovhich he did , mot think was, all things considered, worse than Liverpool, Manchester, and, perhaps' Widnes. Taking a radius of -seven miles from Charing Cross. theoQueen-there possessed ,more subject's than the Kings of Denmark, Sweden, and ,Greece. He argued, at considerable length, in a brilliant speech, in favour of the necessity of home mission work.' Re next dwelt upon his belief that the hybrid nations were gradually dying out. Under these,circumstancee, the con- version of members of the Anglo-Saxon race became a matter of the most vital importance.—The usual voteg of thenks werepassed, and after the collection, whicli realised .£2 Zs. 71d., the proceedings terminated.

,FROPERTY SALES AT WARRIXGTON. On Wednesday afternoon, Mr. Thomas Sutton, auctioneer, offered for sale, at the Lion 'Hotel, several lots of freehold and leasehold property situate in Warrington. There was a very good attendance of , property owners and others. Mr. Sutton first offered in one lot the building occypied ascefices adjoining Parr 's Bank, in.Winwick-street ; and also the public-house, calledthe Theatre Tavern at the .corner of Scotland-road and Winwick-street, with the dwelling-house in Scotland- road, adjoining, and the premises extending up to and beyond, bat not. iacluding the theatre, to the shop °cooked by Mr. Matthew Chorley, with a right of way under. the stage of the theatre. The bidding commenced at £l,OOO, and rose .very slowly to £3,500, at which sum the lot stood for some time and was then withdrawn. Mr. J. R. Buckton offered t£5,000, but the offer was declined. Mr. Buckton, however, eventually purchased the property by private treaty for £6,000. Mr. Sutton then brought under the hammer several other lots of property. Lot I consisted of that leasehold dwelling-house, No. 8, Bewsey-road, War- . rinOon. The lot, which was subject to the apportioned ground rent of £7 Ile, per annum, and held with other property for the residue of a term of 999 years from 1840, was knocked down for £605 to Mr. F. Massey for Mr. Parsonage. Lot 2 was the leasehold dwelling-house, No. 12, Bewsey-road, and was sold subject to the apportioned ground rent of f;:d per annum to Mr. Thos. Davies for £420: Lot three, that leasehold dwelling-house, adjoining the last- named, subject to the apportioned ground rent of £3 per annum, was purchased for £417 10s. by Mr. Edwin Richard- son. The fourth let, a leasehold dwelling-house in the occupation of Mr. Samuel Jcuies, was knocked down to Mr. F. Massey for £420. This lot was also sold subject to the apportioned ground rent of £3 per annum. The fifth lot, that freehold field or close of land, on the east side of Lovely-lane, containing la. Ir. 14p. or thereBb3utB, was withdrawn, the highest bid being £260. The last lot com- prised two leasehold dwelling-honnes, yes. 77 and 79, Church-street, Warrington, with the outbuildings and rope walk behind. This lot is held for the remainder of a term expiring at Michaelmas, 1917, and was sold, subject to a ground rent of £2 3s. per annum, to Mr. John Buckley for £l6O.

- The House assembled at the Co-operative Hall on Mon- day evening, and the Speaker (Dr. Hugon-More) occupied the chair. There was a much better attendance than on the previous week, although the Treasury benches still pre- sented a very deserted appearance. The "strangers gallery " contained a goodly number of occupants, and a noticeable feature was the number of ladies who were present, and who had probably assembled to hear the debate on the bill for the abolition of actions for breaches of promise to marry, but if this was the case they were disappointed, as the ad- journed debate on vivisection occupied the whole of the sitting.

The right hon. member for NORWICH gave an explana- tion, which was considered a satisfactory answer to the question. The HOME SEcnrrAny, replying to the member for Leo- minster, said it was a fact that a Mr. Stannard had been brought before the court for not preaching doctrines in accordance with the trust deeds of his chapel, and he had been obliged to withdraw from ministering at the Ramsden- street Chapel, Huddersfield, of which he was minister. THE VIVISECTION DEBATE. The COLONIAL SEcitieraux rose to point of explanation and complained that the mover of the Bill and himself had been grossly insulted by the charges made against them that they were ignorant of the subject under discussien. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER objected to the Bill because it was not restrictive. He maintained that know- ledge to be exact must be founded upon the direct examina- tion of living organism. He commented upon the language used by the mover of the Bill, and took exception to the term " hideous art." To apply such a term to the science of physiology which was not a humbug, he said was—not nice. (Laughter.) He asked were the results of vivisection the work of devils? He said rather they were the discoveries of angels, administering to the alleviation of human suffering. (Hear, hear, and applause.)" The science of life was neces- ary for the benefit of humanity. That science could not be studied without the practise of vivi- section; therefore the practise of vivisec- tion was necessrry s for the _ welfare of mankind. Speaking with respect to the charges of cruelty, he stated that vivisectionists were as sensitive to pain, and objected to the practice of wanton cruelty as much as anyone. lie re- ferred to cruelties which were perpetrate' every clay, and instanced the oyster, whose bivalve was opened with a knife not too sharp, and then instead of oil and wine being ap- plied it was vinegar and cayenne pepper. (Loud laughter.) if the objectors to vivisection were vegetarians he could umierstand them, because they objected to the slaughtering of cattle and heasts, he supposed, under any circumstances. If they were not, he maintained their position was an 'illogical one. They should leave the matter in the hands of the medical profession and physiologists, and if they could show them that the results of vivisection had been beneficial to the welfare of humanity then in all fairness they must object to the Bill. (Applause.) The member for YARMOUTH objected to the bill before. the House, because he believed that painful vivisection had been, yea, and would continue to be beneficial to mankind, and that it might be the means of discovering facts that would enable them to prevent,far more pain than they in- flicted. ,

The member for WARRINGTON spoke against, and the right hon. member for NORWICH supported the bill. The HOME SECRETARY would certainly not go in for the total abolition of vivisection, though he thought it ought to be practised under more stringent conditions, and that all cruelty should, as far as possible, be prevented. The LEADER a the OPPOSITION remarked that the gist of the whole subject lay in this—that hon. gentlemen who took what he sh,,uld call the ultra-humanitatian view, as- sumed that life as mere life had value. Now the whole teaching of nature showed that life as mere life had no value whatever. It was by the moral qualities that life became of value. What was it that excited their admira- tion in the nurse who might carry away with her the dis- ease of the patient, the doctor who went about with his life in his hands, and in the soldier? It was their bravery and self-sacrifice. (Hear, hear.) If they were to hesitate from destroying life as mere life, they would not only stop at the interesting insects of which the right hon. member for Montrose drew such a pathetic picture, but would not even drink a drop of water, if they once saw that drop through a microscope. (Hear, hear.) He would have supported the right hon. member for Kendal if he had brought in a bill to modify the conditions under which vivisection was to be practised, but when he told the House the results were almost nil when experience assured them that the results were admirable in every way, and the results to be hoped for were still greater, he could not but echo back the warn- ing which had already been eloquently given to the House, they might save some lives of animals, but it would be at the expense of the lives of thousands of men. (Ap- plause.). . . - _

„ The , righthon. member for DROGHEDA thought none of them would object to the men who ranked highest in their profession being allowed within certain limits to perform, purely for the benefit of tneuical science, such experiments as they deemed necessary and desirable to carry out that object. (Hear, hear.) He could not support the Bill be- cause the mover of it had not disabused their minds of the fact that great progress had been made in medical science for the benefit of the human family by vivisection. The right hon. member for Lambeth then took the chair, and

The member for BUCKINGHAM remarked that really they were there to discuss the resolution before the House, but it needed very little from him to show that the right hon. member for Kendal had not quite considered what he was putting before the House, for he asked the House to pass a bill for the total abolition of vivisection and prohibiting vivisection for experimental purposes, the only purpose for which it was of any earthly use. To show to others that certain facts were so the right hon. gentleman left quite open and permissible, but to search out whether a thing was true or not was to be prohibited. That should be quite sufficient to cause the right hon, gentleman to withdraw the Bill. It was the ignorance of medical men that made vivisection necessary. If they were not ignorant they would not want knowledge. Medical men only professed to know a little more tlaan the general public, and they wanted to know a great deal more—for whose benefit? For the benefit of the whole race. He granted that doctors were a necessary evil, but so long as they were necessary it was desirable they should obtain the greatest good from that evil—(hear, hear)—and in order that that evil should be most efficient, and give the public the full benefit, let them have all the means possible for doing it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He granted that the blunder- ing of the faculty was appalling, but he would ask them to throw out that Bill and every other Bill to make that blundering less appalling. (Applause.) meTnthse orfigthhtehvoanriomuesmspbeearkfeorrs,KrindnethLe Bill was puthtetoargthue- House and rejected without a division. The House then adjourned.

Miss Marian Williams and Mr. Tharley Beale have been engaged as vocalists, and from the programme contained in our public notices column a capital concert may be expected.

LATCHFORD BETHEL BAPTIST SUNHAT SCHOOL. The annual tea meeting in connection with the above school was held on Thursday, when a goodly number of scholars, teachers, and friends partook of an excellent repast. After tea suitable sous, anthems, and recitations, were rendered in a very praisworthy manner. The recitations were a special feature and the interest manifested in the proceedings showed that the school is rightly regarded as an important and flourishing institution. The singing reflected great credit on all who took part therein.

ACCIDENT TO MR. GLADSTONE.

----- --- An inconvenient but not very serious accident has hap- pened to Mr. Gladstone. After dining with the Prince of Wales, on Wednesday night, the Prime Minister drove I. Downing-street. While hurrying from his carriage into the house, the right hon. gentleman slipped in the melting snow, and fell backwards rather heavily. He was not in any degree stunned; but it was found that he had cut the back of his head on the garden step. Such a mishap to a man of Mr. Gladstone's years might easily have bees attended with the most serious consequences, and when it became knollen on Thursday there was a brief renewal of the intense public anxiety and excitement which prevailed almost without cessation during the Premier's ,recent ill- ness. At a recent Widnes Petty Sessions, a new Poorla Rate of 2s. 4d. in the,.£ was sanctioned. I believe I was. right in stating that the rate,. which includes the +School Beard one, is estimated to realise ...£11,750. The estimate, includes £5,000 arrears,..£3ooo.anticipated, School, Board ....£2,750, and county £l,OOO. The School Board rate is for the.ensuing twelve months, but as that body will require all .the money to be paid in before September, it is quite ,probable .that the amount mentioned will be found inadequate. The trial of the three boatmen at Knutsford SeSBioll.3 this week for an alleged gross assault on the keeper. et the Mariners' Arms, ,Percival-lane, Runcorn. was marked by mere than a solitaryjneident worthy of a'line. It appears that, first of all,the intellectual and brilliant jury .who had to decide upon the merits of the case, at one part of. the proceedings, told the chairman they had agreed that twe of the prisoners were guilty, and then, after haviog bad time for the facts to penetrate a little further Leo their somewhat thick skulls, they.eame inta court with a verdict of "Not guilty" in the case of. each of the prisoners! It really.is enough to make one tremble to think that by some unlucky train of circumstances the writer should souse day ,find hiM- self in the hande of .twilve of his ceuntrymen,.who might happen to be as clear headed as this wonderful jury. Trial by pry is said to be one of the grand points of Magna Charta, but I should prefer to risk my fate in the hands ot one of Her Majesty's judges rather than have .it, in the hands of a jury ,compoced of no better materiaLs than this linutsford one. During the progress of the.case it came out that two a the men conoerned in it had ,done con- siderable in the way of barter. In one instance they had "swopped" homes, and on the man who had given 30s. for his bargain going to look at the poor beast which.he had bought, he found it kal ceased to live! In the other, com- mercial transaction, they ,had "swapped" what they, for the sake of politeness, call their wives, in a Runcorn public- house, and the bargain bad been duly rendered valid by jumping over a broom! The ether .day, a Runcorn dentist found himself in a,bit of a fix which did not tend .to render him very pleiteanti tempered for a short time afterwards. customer eiatered! his establishment and expressed his great anxiety to have one of his teeth instantly removed. The dentist set to work,: and very speedily had the molar, or whatever other deserip-! Lion of tooth it was, in his hand. As he Ives inspecting it, his customer said he would have to trust him for that, as he had no money! The dentist gave an anxious look at the somewhat large cavity which he had made iathe man's jaw, as if he was anxious to replace the tooth, but as his astonish- mental the large amount of pay he had received for his work had subsided, he came to the conclusion that his best plan was to take the matter philosophically, and not show his chagrin, so he said, "Very well," and Mr. Innocent, departed. It is stated that at a meeting of the River Weaver Trustees on Wednesday, it was resolved to recommend that if the proposed scheme of the Mersey Salt and Zane Co. comes into operation, the trustees should at once allow all salt carried down the river to Weston Point, and transhipped into seagoing vessels, to pass .own the navigation free of toll.

Within the last fev,' days a Runcorn merchant received five shillings in stamps, with the following note :—" Dear Sir,—Entdosed is fire shillings worth of stamps. It is the amount of property that I once unjustly deprived you of. toping that this may find you in good health and spirits." uly it may be said that ."conscience makes cowards cf ns all."

LONDON CORRESPONDENCE The Broness Burdett-Coutts, who is staying with her bus- band at Inoledon, near Ashford, has been seriously indis- posed during the last few days. Her ladyship has been attended by Dr. Wilkes, physician to the Duchess of Edin- burgh, and is now somewhat better. The authorities at Windsor are still kept on the alert by fresh indications of the ex,i.stence of the plot to blow up the I Castle. I understand they discountenance the belief in the existence of serious intention on the part of marauders. I Nevertheless very strict watch is preserved, and the sen- tries, more particularly at night, challenge all corners as if I in time of war. What the authorities pay least attention to are those statements made every day about the appearance and disappearance of mysterious strangers, leaving behind them the smell of brimstone and some grains of gunpowder. If there is any real danger, it is known that it will not take this melodramic aspect. The Princess Louise is really going back to Canada in May. Her stay an England has greatly improve 4 her health, a little stricken by her upset from the sleigh, and something undermined by the dull monotony of the Cana- dian Court. Her Royal Highness is happily of a quiet, do- me4ticated nature that does not demand too much in the shape of excitement. But Ottawa, as any who know the place, or rather the people, will understand, does not supply the IRV needed. Great efforts are being made, on the return of the Princess, to get up whoa Mr. Mark Tapley would call a general appearance of jollity. There is to be in particular a prolonged picnic in the shape ef a fishing excursion. I understand that one abuse among the many which have made law costs insufferably burdensome is about to be chal- lenged. The Incorporated Law Society will consider the question whether fees paid to barristers are not quite heavy enough, and whether the unfortunate litigant ought also to pay fees to the barristers' clerks. When two counsel meet to discuss a point of law at the senior's chambers, the latter's clerk gets 7s. Bd., and the jonior's2s. 6d. When the simplest guinea brief comes before a barrister his clerk takes an ad- ditional half-crown, and at every stage of the proceeding the clerk has his legal claim. The services he renders to the client are of the slightest conceivable nature, scarcely more important than those which a doctor's butler renders to a patient: and yet the claim is legalised. The post is in truth ridiculously over-paid, and the Law-Society are quite right in dealing with the question. In the course of the inquiry as to the resources that may be available for improving and increasing the accommoda- tion of members of the House of Commons outside the area devoted to the deliberative business, it has become known that in the various rooms for the use and convenience of the legislators the Peers haye 13,000 square feet more ac- commodation than is given to the Commons. Of course the latter are much more numerous, and are in the habit of giving a much larger share of personal attendance. Some of the daring spirits who are making a determined effort to procure at least some improvement in the matter of the Commons smoke-room, have ventured to look covetously on comparatively unused spaces sacred to the peers. But they have been warned that there is nothing to hope for in the shape of concession from Lord Redesdale, the chief authority in the matter of the accommodation appertaining to the members of the tipper House. Some important amendments in the law relating to patfonag,e, simony, and exchange of beneficesin the Church of England are proposed by the bill for which Mr. Stanhope, Mr. Albert Grey, Mr. Stanley Leighton, and Mr. Stuart Wortley are sponsors. Power is given to a bishop to refuse, if be think fit, to issue a presentee if he be under 25 or over 70 years of age, or if he does not produce a testimony under the hands of three beneficed clergymen of his former good life and behaviour. The diocesan is also empowered to issue a commission of irquiry into the eligibility of any pre- sentee for the duties of the benefice, and on receiving an unfavourable report to refuse to institute or col'ate. Among the other provisions is one abolishing donatives, and con- stituting them presentive benefices, and another requiring the approval of the bishop in the matter of exchanges and resignations from pecuniary considerations. The sale of presentation apart from the whole advowson is forbidden, and finally, "diocesan patronage boards" are created, con- sisting of the bishop and four other persons, two cleygymen, and two laymen.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

RtrNcorav v. Noimrwms.—This mate la was played on the ground of the latter in Winnington Park, and ended in a win for the visitors. Scores :—Runcorn : 2 goals, 2 tries, 1 poster. 4 touchdowns to nil. Runcorn kicked off against a slight breeze, and up to half time 1 goal and 2 tries were scored, the tries being obtained by Hankinson, Bate, and Joule; the latter by a splendid run obtained his try. After half time the forwards on both sides worked hard, but the superiority of the Runcorn team soon showed itself as the ball was taken in close proximity to the Northwich goal, and from a line out Wright obtained a try. The ball was again put in motion, and from a loose scrimmage J. Pownall dribbled the ball over the line but slipped directly he got over. Gatly, however, was close at band and obtained the try, which Bate converted into a goal, which was the last point scored. For Runcorn, Wright, Hughes, Lightfoot, Beesley, and Andrews played best, as did Burgess, Capper, Forster, and Johnson for Northwicia. RuNcome (21na) v. WEMOTT. —This match was played on the ground of the former, at Irwell-lane. Weston, win ning the toss, decided to play with the wind. Runcorn kicked off, and ran the ball close ta the Weston goal line, and here the first scrimmage was formed, but nothing re- sulted. Johnson now returned the ball close to the Runcorn goal line, but Brimelow again returned it. Riley followed up the ball, and was thus able to score the first try for Run- corn, which Sherlock converted into a goal, the ball being brought out half way. Weston kicked off Roach, then ran a few yard,,, but he was well tackled by Roberts. Runcorn then ran the ball to the other end of the field, when Pownall ran in and scored the first try for Runcorn, which Sherlock again converted into a goal. Weston then played more toget'-er, and with a little more spirit ; but Riley, after a good run, obtained another try, but it was not improved upon. Soon after this Weston was able to score a touch- down. Half time being called and ends changed, the ball was again put in motion and several scrimmages occurred, Weston trying hard to score, but without avail. Dunbavand then obtained another try for Runcorn, when Sherlock was again successful at the kick at goal. Weston, nothing daunted at their defeat, played well. but Cox again scored another try for Runzorn. Sherlock missed the kick at goal, but Pownall was on the alert. and with some smart play he again scored another try for Runcorn, which was improved upon. Try after try was then registered for Rnncorn by Riley, Walky, Marlow, and Roach,the latter's playing being very much admired. Roberts was on the point of scoring, when Walky tackled him very well. Johnson got the ball, and was running away very nicely with it, when Pownall stopped his further advance, nothing only minor points being scored when no side was called. Score : --Runcorn : 4 goals, 5 tries, 3 touchdowns, and 2 dead balls; to Weston 1 touchdown and 2 de ,d balls. Riley, Roach, Walky, Sherlock, Cox, Jones, and Pownall played well for Runcorn; and Mason, Wainwright, Johnson, and Marlow played well for Weston.

div.head: WIDNES WORKMAN. PUBLIC-
div.p: THE WIDNES WORKMAN. PUBLIC-
HOUSE COMPANY.

The annual meeting of this company was held on Tues- day. Amongst those present were the following directors: —Messrs. R H. Davies (chairman), F. H. Gossage, E. K. Muspratt, Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Tharsis Copper Works), John Matthews, and John Betney. The report stated that the directors regretted that they bad for a third time to submit a report showing a loss on the year's work log. In accordance with the decision of the last annua meeting, the Anne-street premises were altered into two shops. Both of these were tenanted in a short time, but one was now unoccupied. In consequence of this there was still a serious loss on this portion of the company's pre- Daises. As to the Hutchinson-street rooms, there had been a falling off in the returns during the year, and a small loss bad resulted on the working account. It would be for the shareholders to consider whether they were willing that the company should be carried on. in the hope of ultimate suc- cess, or the advisability of winding it up in accordance with the articles of association. From the extent of the business done, the directors were sure that the house was meeting a want much felt by a portion of the working. population of the town, and decidedly beneticist to the neighbourhood.— Mr. Davis made a few remarks expressive of his regret that the outlook was so gloomy. He also said that he nail bad conversations with several managers of similar houses in Liverpool, and they were of opinion that, considering the fact that there was a tarn of over £5OO per annufn at the Hutchinson-street building, it ought to pay. He proposed the adoption of the report, which was passed.—After a few observations from Mr. Eustace Carey, it was agreed to call another meeting to decide what action should be taken in respect to the state of the company's affairs.

The Post-office telegraphs account shows daring the past year a profit of £354,030, equal to 336 per cent. on the capital raised. At Tunbridge Wells, on Tuesday, the Rev. Hue Edward Blakeley Allen' a clergyman of the Church of England, was committed for trial on a charge of obtaining board, dm., at the Bull Hotel by fraudulently representing that he was a friend of the vicar and that he expected the sum of £1,300 to be paid into a local bank, on which he gave a cheque for £lO. The cheque was dishonoured, and on inquiries being made he decamped, leaving a bill of £l3 unpaid'. Prisoner bad just undergone four months' imprisonment in Reading (Inca on a similar charge.

ScOCESS OF A LAITC.ASHIBE STUDENT AT CAKEOUDGE.— The Craven University scholarship has !seen adjudged to T. G. Tucker, of St. John's College, a former pupil of the Royal Grammar School, Lancaster, under Rev. W. E. Pryke, M. A. The Craven is the highest classical distinc- tion which Cambridge can bestow, higher even than the position of senior classic itself, inasmuch as the competition is open to students of all three years of residence. This is the second occasion on which a Lancaster boy has been elected, Mr. Whitelaw having been Craven fc'mlar in 1864. Among former holders of the Craven have been Porson (1781), Bishop Bloomfield (1806), Bishop Thirlwall (1815), Lord Macauley (1821), Bishop Prince Lee (1827), Bishop Wordsworth (1829), Dean Vaughan (1836), Lord Lyttleton (1837), Professor Munro (1641), Canon 11. M. Birch (1341), Professor Jebb (1860). The scholarship is of thexannual value of £BO, and is tenable for seven years.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual meeting of this Board of Guardians was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. John Ashton, vice-chairman. There were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Weir, Mclntyre, J. Mid- weod, Hazlehurst, Norman, Challoner, Darbyshire, Briscoe, J. Smith, sen., J. Knowles, J. Darbyshire, Williams, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk). TETI EITHENDITCICE OF THE RATES. Mr. Mchrrerts gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board he should call attention to the expenditure of 'the rates levied in the Union, and to the fact that during the past year the Trustees of the River Weaver Navigation have not made any payment to the county treasurer, and that he would move for the appointment of a committee to enquire into the subjects and report to the Board. I THE ALLEGED EXTRATAGANCE.—REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE. The ASSISTANT CLERK read the report of the committee appointed to investigate the charges against the master and matron of the workhouse respecting the management thereof, which was as follows: The co:nmittee met at the Workhouse on Tuesday, February 22nd, 1881; present, the Chairman, Vice-Chairman, Messrs. Weir, Darbyshire, Smith, Andrews, and Henry Lowe. It appeared that some potatoes were given by one of the servants to the horse without the cogni- zance of the master and matron. The master and matron were cautioned to take more care in the future. It appeared that the impression conveyed to the Board that certain Guardians were in the habit of calling at the workhouse for their tea, was erroneous, the only instance thereof being that on one particular Board day Mrs. Jones asked a Guardian to tea, the eatables for which had been purchased by her out of her own funds. The statement of Mr. Wil- kinson that he had seen bottles of wine on the table in the master's room is explained by the fact that 4oz. bottles of gin, brandy, and port wine, containing .samples, were sent every half year by tradesmen tendering to suPPIY the house. With reference to the charge that the master was in the habit of entertaining large parties, the master acknowledged that he had a party o istmas f personal friends to tea and stand-up supper at Chr, , the materials for which he had purchased out of his own resources, and produced the tradesmen's bills. This statement was confirmed by our reference to the provisions receipt and consumption book. With respect to the charge that a favoured few of the Guardians were in the habit of dining at the house every Board day it was upon enquiry found to be mistaken, the only ground for the charge being that when the Assessment Committee have met at 10 a.m. certain mem- bers on the Board day have, at the expiration of the Assess- ment Committee meeting, whilst waiting for the general Board meeting, gone to the master's room and had some refreshment at his table. Recommended that such refresh- ment be not allowed for the future. , Mr. Cnettorrian said having heard the report read, and haying heard the discussion and the language used in that 'room previously, for his own part he was thoroughly dis- gusted with the report in one way, and in another he was thoroughly satisfied. When guardians came forward in that room and made such statements—they were all aware what I the statements were—and when the committee had investi- gated them and not a single one was preyed in any way, these men (he was sorry to see they were not present) ought to be thoroughly ashamed of themselves. (Hear, hear.) They were ashamed of themselves, and that was the reason they were not present that day. (Hear, hear.) The servant gave the horse two and a half potatoes and that had gone through the length and breadth of the country. What were they worth ? Why a score of them were worth a farthing 1 or scarcely that. For a man to bring charges—be was going to say untruths—that he could not prove, for the sake of half a farthing, was really scandalous. Then it was stated that Mr. Jones had three or four parties in the length of the winter at which 18 or 20 persons were , present at a time, and that the Guardians found the pro- I visions. The Master acknowledged that he had had one , party. and that he bought the provisions himself. If he I were the master and could bring an action against him, he I would do and very soon tr, ste.',lear, hear)—and if the master found he could not pay the expense be would put a sovereign down. In reference to the eating-house he wondered how much they had had to eat. He had heard them asked whether they would act on the committees, but they would not act on one. They started from home about one o'clock and stayed at the meeting half an hour. He had left home at half-past nine in the morning during the time he had been a Guardian-9 months—and had got back about four or five o'clock. He did not think a man would go there and starve himself, and it was unreasonable to ex- pect it. Both Mr. Lowe and Mr. Wilkinson ouc,,ht to be ashamed of themselves. Mr. Norman told Mr. Wilkinson as a secret that he had had his tea there, or Mr. Wilkinson would not have known. Mr. Lowe said Mr. Norman went there for the purpose of getting his tea, but he did not believe that. [Mr. Norman : I never did it in my life.] The auditor had gone through the books, and that work- house was conducted at a less expenditure by hundreds of pounds a year compared with other workhouses. (Hear, hear.) Yet Mr. Lowe said the workhouse was extravagantly conducted. More than that, he said there were many com- plaints against the Master. The complaints were only made by such men as Mr. Lowe and Mr. Wilkinson. No man who possessed common sense would make them. As to , the bottles of wine they were samples, and yet those gentle- men told them the 'Board bought wine for the Guardians. It was nothing but animosity from beginning to end. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Tanner and Mr. Norman were two old Guar- dians who had attended regularly for a long time. Mr. Norman was admitted to be the best Guardian who came to that Board—(hear, hear)—and he had read years ago he was the best Guardian, and for them to be tantalised by men like Mr. Wilkinson, was a shame. He should call upon those members to apologise to Mr. Norman, Mr. Tanner, and Mr. and Mrs. Jones; and if they would not do so let them leave the room and not enter again until they did. He was sorry to see that townships would elect such men as those as Guardians. The report of the Committee recommended that no dinner or refreshment should be provided. He had nothing to say against that except that the members of the committee could take his place on the other committees, as he was quite willing to stay at home and leave later for the Board meeting. Then they could eat their lunch behind the door as he had seen the (31erk do. It was really shameful that the Chairman must bring his lunch in his pocket and eat it before the Board. It was a shame for any Board of Guar- dians to allow it—(hear, hear) ; and when this subject had been thoroughly discussed he should move in the matter. The CHAIRMAN: Will you move that the report be adopted? Mr. CITALLONER took exception to the last recommenda-

tion. Mr. DAIIIVESTIIRE explained that the recommendation was made in order to comply with the law. Mr. CHALLONER said they mot not go exactly by the law. He had heard lawyers say there never was an Act passed but what they could pass a carriage and horses through it. They must go by common sense. Mr. KNOWLES thought Mr. Lowe was perfectly right in naming the matter. From what little he saw in the papers he did not agree with the way Mr. Tanner and Mr. Norman treated him. He did not think the language used by Mr. Challoner was much better than that Mr. Lowe and the rest of them used. The CHAIRMAN : To put ourselves in order would you propose that the report be read and adopted, altering what- ever yeu choose? Mr. CHALLONER moved that the report be adopted, with the exception of the last sentence. Mr. HAZLEHURST seconded the motion. , I Mr. MclrryrtE said after hearing the reput it would ap- pear that the mountain bad brought forth, and behold it had been a mouse. (Laughter.) He did not deny the right of any gentleman who sat there to investigate to the very foundation anything that he thought be had just cause for investigating, and if he thought any abuse existed it was his bounden duty to make an investigation, but still he thought it behoved every Guardian to see that he bad just ground for it. (Hear, hear.) He thought he ought to have more ground than they evidently had according to the re- port which had been presented. They ought to have a better and more sure foundation to stand upon before they sent forth to the world statements which they had sent forth. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the law he would like to ask for a little information in regard to the point under discus- sion. He had been a Guardian a good many years now, and. on going home he had been obliged to beg—(laughter)—for a crust of something to eat; and he thought it was very hard if those Guardians who came there to feed the poor could not get a crumb for themselves. [A Voice: It is a shame.] They had high authority for the command that they were not to muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn—(hear, hear)—and if the Guardians, administering relief to the poor, were going to be starved, it was a bard law. But he did not believe it was the law. It was not the spirit of the law at any rate, he was certain, if it was the law; and it would have been far more effective to his mind if the gentle- men who had found fault with the Guardians having a crust after they had been, to use a Cheshire phrase, " clemmed "—it would have been far better if they had attended more to the work. (Hear, hear.) If they did a little more of the work, probably they would be able to get home earlier. He did not think there was a Guardian sitting round that table hut who knew it was con- trary to nature to go so long without food. Nature's wants must be supplied, and he himself had gone to beg a crust in that house. He had brought bread and meat with him from home and carried it back again, but after what he had beard that day be would bring no tore. He often had to leave home at nine o'clock in the morning, and it'was five or six o'clock before be got back, but he was not going to do with- out a lunch. The Board would not begrudge the Guardians bread and cheese, and .a glass of beer-(hear, hear); and be did not think the ratepayers would begrudge it. As to Mr. Jones, were they going to deny him the common rights of an individual, and was Mrs. Jones not to be allowed to invite a friend? He read the report that a Guardian had had tea with them, but he did not know whether that Guardian had tea as a member of that Board or as a friend of Mr. and Mrs. Jones. He supposed he went as an invited friend; but did the law prohibit Mr. and Mrs. Jones inviting a friend to have a cup of tea? He thought if such was the case it was .t very hard one, and he would not like to be the master of that house. He did not think the Board could deny them the common rights of humanity to invite a friend. (A voice: Certainly not.) As a matter of course, the Board would draw a wide distinction between 'that invitation and the "large parties," of which, from the report that had been presented, nothing had come to light. (Hear hear.) Mr. Nonaraw said he was very much astonished at the result of the investigations, and yet he was not astonished.

If the complaints had come from a man or some member of that Board who had attended to his duty, and had done what the ratepayers who sent him there expected him to do, he (Mr. Norman) would not have said so much about the matter. Mr. Lowe was not surprised at whatever he said— (laughter)—although he would be surprised if Mr. Tanner said it; but he was very much surprised that Mr. Lowe should come there, and be one of the first men to find fault, and that his friend Mr. Andrews should second the proposi- tiont hee would w to find fault, and also Mr. Wilkinson—three men whom tellthe w they themfind at when y would e tßhoear Board e perhaps get h pse oosr five e meet- ings—let someone give notice of motion to raise some man's salary, and they would soon have them there. They did memtibmeress. at H not attend to the business of that Board. He was free to confess he did not think Mr. Lowe knew how the paupers were treated in his township. He did not believe Mr. Lowe knew that very moment whether there was some man or a family in his township receiving 3s. 61. a week where 2s. would suffice, or that there was some poor widow and her family who were only receiving 2s. a week who ought to have 3s. 6d. If be understood the duty of a guardian rightly, it was to administer relief and to see that it was properly administered. But here men like Mr. Lowe left home at half-past twelve, and got to the Board at one o'clock, and he had seen him leave his seat at half-past two I o'clock Or a quartet to three. He was sure they would bear him out that Mr. Lowe was very seldom seen at that Board, and then he came and found fault with men who bore the burden of the business of the Board. If they took away five or six men from that Board, how was the business going to be conducted? Then Mr. Lowe said Mr. Norman and Mr. Tanner wanted to have their own way. Away with such bosh! Let Mr. Lowe take up the work, as he freely confessed he was very willing to give it up. But someone must do the work. He came fortnight after fortnight, and, when the Assessment Cern- , mittee was sitting week, after week, and he came at ten o'clock in the morning on the days the Guardians met. He thought the reflections that had been cast upon the Master and Matroa of that house were unfounded. He was con- fident of it, and the report proved they were unfounded; and he thought men like Mr. Andrews, Mr. Lowe, and Mr. Wilkinson, who scarcely ever attended to the duties of the people who sent them there, ought make a public with- drawal of what they had said. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Knowles said he thought Mr. Tanner and he—(the speaker)—were too hard upon Mr. Lowe. He should like to know how Mr. Knowles got hold of that information. When Mrs. Jones was summoned into that room he remembered very well she denied that there were any potatoes—there was nothing except potato peelitigs. Then when the man was called he said there were 21 petatoes and the cook said the same. He was sorry to say that at the time Mr. Jones was not in a state of health to look after these things and his e,ife had to do so. But they never said they disbelieved Mr. I owe. They said after the investigation they quite exonerated Mrs. Jones from blame. He thought it was the case. [Mr. Derbyshire: That was so.] What could the Guardians do otherwise? Could they say they believed Mr. Low b thaGa cullender of hot potatoes had been put into the horse's corn when three persons said it was not so? Why did not Mr. Lowe let the thing drop, or bring the potatoes and place them on the table to prove his case? He never did prove his case. If he wanted to do Mr. and Mrs. Jones a serious injury he would have asked for the cullender and would have brought it before the Guardians, and asked them to examine it. Then there would have been proof. But he had never heard such a case brought forward in his life, and he would go so far as to say that he believed any other guardian, if he had seen a thing of that kind and did not like it, would have gone to Mrs. Jones and said "there are potatoes being given to your horse, and if such a thing takes place againl shall report it." (Hear, hear.) He was not afraid of investigation, and as to the wine he never saw a bottle in the House except the sample bottles and the bottles in the cellar that contained gin, brandy, and wine. He was a teetotaller and would not touch it. (Hear, hear.) When people sent to the world statements that had no right to he sent without there was great cause he thought it was a great shame, and also thought with Mr. Challoner they ought to withdraw every word they had said. (Hear, hear.) Mr. HAZLEIIIMST : I should like to ask the clerk a ques- tion. Is it really illegal for the Guardians to have dinner here under any circumstances? The CLERK: Certainly. Mr. BARBYSHIRE : That question was asked by the com- mittee, and lAs a member of the committee should have objected to the clause in the report, but we did it to fall in with the law. Mr. HAZLEMIAST thought it was a matter of subscription amorgst the Guardians. The CLERK said it was perfectly open for that t be done. Mr. NORMAN had forgotten to mention that. He really thought when a man left his home at 9 o'clock in the morn- ing to go to that House there ought to be a " whip "round the table for dinner, and that every Guardian ought to pay his quota. If members could not attend to the business of the Board and to their daties as representatives of certain townships, he thought they ought not to object to pay is. each towards providing dinner for those Guardians who attended. Mr. KrrowLEs : Better have a special rate for it, Mr. Norman. Mr. NORMAN thought that would be a rate. Mr. HAELEHERSL I understood a remark was made that at same Unions guardians have their dinners. The CLERK : At certain Unions they have what is called an interest fend, but that is being done away with now. They are surcharged right and left about it. You have never done anything of the kind. Mr. BARBYSIIIRE said he should just like to say that that morning as hen he left home he left with the feeling he had to investigate the case fairly, leaning neither to one I side nor the other. But he was very sorry to find the corn- ' mittee had gone into a matter which none of the charges touched at all. However, he was very pleased that it could go to the public that Mr. and Mrs. Jones had come off " honest." (Hear, hear.) He explained that the feeling of the committee was against the insertion of the last sen- tence in the report, but the question was asked "can this be done legally ?" and the reply was a negative. There was a charge that a favoured few were in the haoit of dining at the house, and it was with a view to including all the mem- bers of the Board that the recommendation was added. Mr. Hannurnsr observed that if the Guardians could not legally dine at the house there was no necessity for the recommendation. The report, which was seconded, was then adopted, with the exception of the last sentence. Mr. CHALLONER : I think we, as members of the Board, ought to call upon these Guardians to retract or apologise for tvhat they had said to Mr. Tanner, Mr. Norman, and Mr. and Mrs. Jones. The CHAIRMAN: Have we any power? Mr. MCINTYRE : I think you had better leave it to their honour. Mr. CHALLONER : Honour! Where is their honour? (Laughter.) Mr. MCINTYRE would leave it to them, believing that they did it labouring under a mistake. He would put the most charitable construction upon their motives. Mr. CIIALLONER : We ought to call upon them to do some- thing. The CHAIRMAN : Suppose they refuse? Mr. CHALLONER : They could refuse, according to their honour. I think we ought to propose a resolution to go into the papers that these gentlemen ought to be ashamed of themselves. Mr. HAMEHERST : Suppose we pass a unanimous vote of confidence in the master? Mr. NORMAN: Yes, that will be the thing. Mr. HAZLEHURST : I propose that. Mr. CHALLONER : I move a vote of censure on the two guardians. (Laughter.) I will add that to the motion, with' your permission, Mr. Hazlehurst—a vote of censure for bringing unfounded charges. Mr. HAMEHURST declined to make the suggested addition to Ids motion, and Mr. Mei/gamin remarked that they all said things in the heat of debate which they regretted afterwards, when they cooled down. Mr. HAZLEIMRST included the name of Mrs. Jones, and Mr. BRISCOE having seconded, the vote of confidence in Mr. aml Mrs. Jones was unanimously carried. Mr. Warn felt proud that they had finished with the matter. He had been one of the committee who had gone into the matter as well as they could, but as the last item in the report did not meet with the Board's approbation he might say he was sure the committee did it for the best. He was very glad the Clerk had explained the provisions book. He asked whether Mr. Jones could spend £4 or £5 for these parties without being detected; but the Clerk soon told them nothing of the sort could be done. Everything had to be accounted for in the books—(hear, hear,)—and he was sure when that was done nothing in the way of fraud could be committed in that house. (Hear, hear.) Mr. CHALLONER said he was sorry the Chairman of the Board was not present as he had intended to move that the , chairman should read the funeral service, as Mr. Wilkinson had dug the grave, and Mr. Lowe had rung the bell. EXPLOSION ON BOARD A WARRINGTON STEAMER.—AS the steamer Pioneer, belonging to Messrs. Pairclough and Sons, of Mersey Mills, was steaming up the river from Liverpoo on Thursday afternoon the boiler exploded, causing some consternation in the immediate neighbourhood. Fortunately no one was injr red. HEALTH or WARRINGTON.—The Medical Officer of IHealth (Mr. Gornall) reports for the week ending, 12th of February, that 46 births and 19 deaths, including 3 at the workhouse, 2at the fever hospital, and 1 at the infirmary, have been registered. On the estimated population, includ- ing Latchford, of 40,000, the birth rate was equal to 59.8 in the 1,000, and the death rate 241, against 436 in the cor- responding week of 1880 and 351 in 1879. The deaths of persons under 5 years of age were 2, and under 1 3, 40 9, and 60 and upwards 5. The total of 19 deaths includes 1 from malignant smallpox, 1 from enteric fever, 4 from tubercular disease, 3 from lung diseases, and 10 from all other causes. The prsportionate mortality from preventible diseases was 131 per cent. There has been no case of infectious disease reported during the week.

Mr. PIERCE next said he understood that a certain amount of money was appropriated to the improvement of Victoria- road, and he wos instructed that the sum had not been all spent upon the road, though the total amount had been expended. £lO,OOO was appropriated for the Victoria-road, and only £6,000 had been spent upon it. The LAW CLERK thought Mr. Pierce must be labouring under some misapprehension. The Board were granted a lump sum of £ll,OOO for certain specified improvements, but. they were not compelled to spend a specific amount upon any Particular road, although in the estimates prepared such sum that might be mentioned. Mr. PIERCE felt bound to say that the Board had not exercised a wise descretion in improving the town, as they appeared to have carried out their improvements at the out- skitts. The LAW CLERK said this was a matter of opinion. He, Personally, thought that the work had been well and sub- stantially done. Assertions had been made to the effect that money borrowed for street improvements had been im- properly spent, and he should like the clients of Mr. Pierce to give an instance of that kind. Mr. PIERCE: Well, of course, I take your statement. My instructions are that you had a specific sum borrowed for the purpose of improving Victoria-road. The LAW CLERK: No ; not a separate amount for Vic- toria-road, but a lump sum granted for various improve- ments, one of which was that road. Can you say where any portion of that money has been spent improperly, as we are anxious to learn? Mr. PIERCE said his clients were of opinion that the Board ought to have first expended more money upon the roads in the town before dealing with those in the out districts. The LAW CLERK : But it is only an assumption to say that we havebeen expending capital improperly, in repairing roads. Mr. DARLINGTON: All that the deputation care about is to see that these sums are appropriated to the particular purpose for which they were sanctioned. Mr. PIERCE: No doubt. The LAW CLERK: It has not been stated that a single penny has been spent irregularly. Mr. PIERCE: There is another matter, viz., the expenses at the election and the annual inspection of the district. I do not know what powers ,the Local Board have as to spending money in refreshments, wine, and all that sort of thing. (Laughter.) Mr. DARLINGTON : Well, the provisions of the Public Health Act are a little elastic as regards that. (Lauhter.) The Act says "such refreshments as may be allowed"; but if there is any objection as to any ,particular item, I shall be glad to cansider it. Mr. KNIGHT (a member of the Board): Perhaps Mr. Pierce will state what he objects to of that character, and when it was supplied. Mr. PIERCE: There are dinners, teas, suppers, &c., £2O; and there is also another item of £29 for refreshments. One of the assistants to Mr. Darlington said that these items were not in this year's account. Mr. PIERCE: As to the annual inspection of the district, there is a charge of £29 15s. 6d. by Mrs. VVainwright, con- fectioner. Mr. DARLINGTON: Is that in this year's accounts? Mr. PIERCE: I believe that it is in the wateraccounts. r. Mr. DARLINGTON: Well, I will make a note o _ Mr. PIERCE: And the election expenses,—£2o Mr. DARLINOTON: Yes, I have those. The LAW CLERK : Those are items whicharenottax aLle by the Returning Officer, unless they are unreasonable.
