The MATRON reported that on Friday night three preg- nant women, for whom there were no beds' were sent by her to three empty beds in the hospital, but Miss Leatham re- fused to admit them. The mistress sent a note to Miss Leattiam asking her to find room for them, but she again refused. Subsequently the mistress went to the hospital and told the women to get into their beds, when Miss. Lintham behaved' in a very insolent manner, and about two hours afterwards went to one of the women and, dragged the clothes off her, and made her get up and go into another bed. The matron, nurse, and other officers having appeared before the Board and given their statements, it was decided to ask the nurse to resign. _ _

IN WANT OF A LAUNDRESS. 1 It was decided to advertise for a laundress, Mr. Meadows , entering his protest against it, as he was of opinion that thee work could be done by some of the women in the House, under the supervision of the matron. THE comEcruna OF TER UNION'S MONEY. Mr. FIDLER brought before the notice of the Board 'a statement that he had come across accidentally, that a family of brothers at St. Helens, in good circumstances, •were in debt to the Guardians to the extent of over £l4, and be wanted to know how this amount hail been allowed to run on. • The Rev. T. ORAMBERS reminded the Guardians of the motion he intended bringing forward at a future date to make the offices of pay clerk and collector into one. Mr. SEDDON, the collector, was called in, and he, stated that notices had been sent to the parties, and he had spoken to the relieving officers, but they did not like to prosecute seeing the circumstances the men were in. It would be much better if the collector were empowered to,prosecatet Mr. FIDLER said he knew that it was a fact the debtors , were in a good business. (To Mr. Seddon.) . How much money have you out, £1,000? Mr.Snnnox intimatpd that was about the figure. Mr. non= : This trade these men are empleyed In is about the most profitable. Resolved that the collector supply the Board with a fort-, nightly statement.

div.head: STRIKE AT THE WORKHOUSE:.
div.p: STRIKE AT THE WORKHOUSE:.

At a meeting of the Employment Committee, the Clerk reported that the able-bodied men employed by the Guar- dians, refused to 'work until Ave o'clock last Saturday, and in the absence of the Guardians he had permitted them to work upon the original terms in force before the special meeting of the GnAlians. The action of the clerk :VW justified. A deputation of men waited upon the Committee that morning to ask that they be allowed to drop work at five o'clock on Saturdays, that soup be substituted for cheese, and that the 3d per day knecked off the married men's dllowance be given. The Committee declined to grant those terms.

div.head: LATE BAND MA,STEE.
div.p: THE LATE BAND MA,STEE.

Mr. Joseph Corns again asked by letter that a quarter's salary be paid him, as he considered himself entitled to it having been sent away without notice. The Guardians having previously refused to grant the request, the letter was allowed to lie on the table.

div.head: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. H. A. Bright and R. Piikington. Tan Row ay Smow.—John Quinn, a young man (resi- ding at Sutton), with his head bandaged, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday, the 12th inst., and also with assaulting P.S. Banks.—P.S. Banks said that on , the night in question, shortly before twelve o'clock, the prisoner' along with 21 others, were singing, shouting, curs- ing, add swearing on Worsley-brow, Sutton. He requested them one by one to go away, but they refuted. He then I went away and returned with P.O. Dansen, whom he ordered to apprehend Byrom, and while he (the sergeant) was fastening the handcuffs on the prisoner Byrom the prisoner Quinn threw a piece of slag, which caught him on the head. He fell insensible on the grouud.—P.C. Denson corroborated the statement, and on being qtiestioned by Mr. Swift, who defended, he admitted that the sergeant knocked the prisoner down with , his staff.—Henry Whalley gave evidence, and in answer to Mr. Swift he said he saw the policeman strike one or two, and he did not see Quinn do anything to hurt the constable.—Superintendent Johnston intimated that he would not call any more witnesses.—Mr. Swift said this showed the white feather and the weakness of his case in declining to call any more witnesses. They had been sent out of the room, and now when he saw that the last witness went against him he would not call any more.—Superintendent Johnston asked that the Bench would not hear the railing against him, but that Mr. Swift should conduct his 'own case.—Mr. Swift said that was an imper- tinent ihterruption' which ought not to be made. —Mr. Bright Oh, never mind.—Superintendent Johnston then asked that the last witnem might be recalled and questioned as to his receiving a threatening letter.—Mr. Swift objected, as that had nothing to do with the case, as it was not alleged that the defendant was the author of the letter, and he protested against such a question being asked.—Mr. Bright said he', would put the question, but Mr. Swift again objected, on the ground of its irrelevancy.—Mr. Spencely then had an in- audible conversation with the Bench,—Mr. Swift said the . Bench had no right to hear anything that a jury might not hear.—Mr. Bright: You moot really be quiet.--Mr. Swift said he knew very well that Mr. Bright had no right to ask the witness whether he had received a threatening letter.— Mr. Bright: I urn just consulting with Mr. Spencely, if I have a right to do it; and if I have a right I shall do it, and if I find I have not I shall mot.—Mr. Swift: Will you let us hear this conversation? This is a public -court.—Mr. I.;right : Oh, not at all.—Mr. Swift: I protest against it. There is no claim for the existence of any such right, What- ever passes between the Bench and a third party it ought to be beard in the presence of the defendant and his advocate., —Mr. Bright: Very well; 1 shall decide that myself.— I After a short time Mr. Bright said he would not put the .question.—Mr. Swift then said the case was extremely , doubtful and suspicious, and as witnesses had 'been sent out of the room he would call them and risk it.—. James Lucas, stationmaster at Sutton Oak, Emma Whit- taker, of the Queen's Arms, Sutton .Oak, and Wm. Brown, spoke to seeing the row, but all of them stated they did not see the defendant strike the sergeant.—For the defence Michael Quinn, brother to the defendant, said defendant was not in the row.—Defendant was fined £5 and costs, or two months' iroprisdnment, and the charge of drunkenness was withdrawn. ILLEGALLY REMOVING Goons.— Frederick Whittle, of Eccleston, was charged with illegally and clandestinely re- moving goods in order to avoid a distraint —Ma. John Wil- cox, Peter-street, said he was agent for the owner of the house of which the defendant was tenant, and on Monday the 31st January he went as usual to collect the rent, but found the door locked. He went again the same night and found the door locked. He went again on the Tuesday fol- lowing and found that some of the things bad been sold to Mr. Bennett, broker. The amount of rent demanded was £2 Os., and the value of the goods in the house was XS.— The Bench said there was no legal evidence that the goods were removed clandestinely, and therefore they were not in a position to make any wider. A TRAMWAY CONTRACTOR FlNED.—Joseph Speight, who was represented by one of his employes, was summoned for obstructing the street by laying down rails.—Mr. Swift ap- peared to prosecute, and said the case was adjourned at the previous Monday's sitting at the request of Mr. Speight, who desired td have legal assistance, but it appeared he had not availed himself of the interval—Mr. Swift went on to say that Mr. Speight had not been allowed to commence operations within the town, as it had not been proved to the satisfaction of the Corporation that £20,000 of the capital had been accepted, and that half cf that sum had been paid up. Mr. Speight bad allowed rails to be laid along the street, although Mr. Hart, the borough engineer, had said to him that if he did lay them he would have to take the respon- sibility. He had been called upon to remove them, but he had not yet dons so, and he (Mr. Swift) asked that a fine might be inflicted.—Mr. Hart having given evidence, Mr. Speight's representative said that defendant was unwell last week, and he had been authorised to engage Mr. Riley for that day, but Mr. Riley being solicitor for the company re- fused to conduct the case.—Defendant was fined 20s. and costs. MESSRS. LYON'S APPRENTICES.—Patrick Linton, Allen Tankard, Edwarn Pickavance, and James Kelley were charged with unlawfully absenting themselves from the em- ployment of Messrs. Lyon, glass bottle manufacturers.— Mr. Swift prosecuted, and called James Middlehurat, the foreman who detailed the facts.—Linton was fined 9s. and costs, and the others, who said they were grumbled and cursed at because they could not "knock" the glass off, were ordered to go to work. PoAcniNG.—Williarn Radlev was fined 20s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for trespassing in pursuit of game, and for using a "grin" or gin for the purpose of taking game, on land in the occupation of James Warburton, Bold, on the 2nd inst. STEALING A HAM. Michael Norton was charged with stealing a ham and a hook, value 9s. lid, the property of William Howard, provision dealer, Bridg-street. He was further charged with assaulting P.C.impson.—lt appeared that the officer saw the prisoner Walking along Bridge- street with a ham under his coat, and he followed him into Water-street, when the strike him on the face with officer gave chase and overtook been suspended. The officer Init oaoirciherootkoookn t o which his the nests.ha int Thehat to ptiroisgohniesr,hwahodo to ottheims attempted to ward off the blow received severe wound.—The prisoner was sent to prison for two months' with hard labour.

LonD DERBY AND THE armada, PARTY.—It is stated that the Earl of Derby has consented to becorne the President of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Associa- tion, and that his Lordship has also sent a contribution of £lOO to the funds of the South-East Lancashire Liberal Association.

THE SOUTHPORT AND WEST LANCASHIRE BANK.—The Directors of this bank and the committee of shareholders held a meeting on Wednesday to consider the reconstruction scheme. It is stated that in the course of a few days the scheme may probably be ready for presentation to the share- holders for their sanction before being submitted to the Mais:cir ' of the Rolls. PLOUGHING MATCHES' AT ST. HELENS AND RAINFORD.

/ The annual match . known as the Ecclestan and .Windle ploughing match took place on Monday, in a field belong- ing to Mr. William 13irchall, near the Griffin Inn, Eccleston. For some years past the competition has been confined to Eccleston, but last year it was thought desirablp to embrace ' a wider area, and'Windle was at the fast match privileged to send its knights of the plough to try their skill against the Eccleston men. The competition was then considerably keener than it had ever been. before, and would no doubt have been even more so this year had not the committee, through financial "reasons, been compelled to curtail the is.gth of the programme and offer prizes in one class only: n„moly, to men who are farmers or who are employed in the township of Eccleston and Windle, and who have held their farms or been so employed from the Ist day of January last. The weather was very cold, but notwithstanding this a good number of farmers and friends turned out to see the match, which was well contested. The following was the judges' awards: Ist prize, £6, C. Sephton, ploughman to R. Sephton. Windle • 2nd prize, £5, John Ratcliffe, ploughman to Richard Appleton, Eccleston ; 3rd prize; £4, John Cromp- tbn, owner and ploughman, Eccieston ; 4th prize, £3, Edwin Banks, ploughman to Jane Banks, Ecclestan ; sth prize, £2, Thomas Parr, owner and ploughman, Eecleston ; ab prize, I AI, Michael kfulme, ploughman to James Hayes, Eccleston ; ' 7th prize, 10s., Thomas Moran, ploughman to William Swift, Winile. For the' neatest and cleanest turnouts, the first prize, £l, was awarded to Isaac Plunkett, plosghman to ' William Bitchall, Eccleston ; the second prize being given to John Howard, ploughman to Mrs. Howard, of Eccleston ; third prize, 55., to John Crompton, owner and ploughman, Eccleston. In the evening, the committee oui competitors- partook of dinner at the Griffin Inn, and amide justice was done to it. Mr. and Mrs. Sefton catered in goon style, and showed every attention to the guests. Toasts were given during the evening, and several songs enlivened the pro- , ceedings.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 26, 1881.

div.head: RAINFORD PLOUGHING MATCH.
div.p: RAINFORD PLOUGHING MATCH.

The annual Rainford ploughing. match, established in 1834, took place, on Wednesday, in a field near Bainford junction, in the occupation of Messrs. Grace and Bothwell The weather was extremely favourable for the occasitn, the slight unpleasantness of the raw wind being counteracted by the genial rays of the sun, which shone brightly in the middle of the day. The time allowed for ploughing was at the rate of 14 hours to the statute acre; and the dimensions of the furrows were to be six inches deep and eight inches broad, the last four furrows to be trench ploughed. For the ploughing Mears. Henry Banks, of Burnscough ;.W. Harry, of Ilaydock; and John Halsall, ofHalebank were the judges, and for the turnout,; Mr. John Barnes of Liverpool, acted as judge. The arrangements of the, match were carried by a committee composed of the following/ gentlemen :—Messrs. R. J. Birchall, Joseph Robinson, James Agnew, sem, J. R. bottom, Thomas Boardman, 'Edward Birchall, John Birch- all, Mill House Farm; R. Winstanley, John Whalley, John Fazackerley, James Dean, H. Webster, W. Stockley, John Smith, and W. Moss; treasurer, Mr.Josepli Clare; secretary, Mr. Joseph Peachey. The ploughing on the whole was considered to be executed in excellent style, and the judges made their awards as follow :—First class ploughmen, open to all England. A silver cup value £5 to Boter Berry, Lathom ; 2nd, Thomas Cold well, Buttonwood; 3rd, Thomas Woods, Bickerstaffe ; 4th, Robert Rosbothain iScarisbrick ; sth, Thomas Blackburii, Skelmersdale. Second olass plough- men (for men who have not, won a prize of the value of £4, since January, 1878.) let, prize £5 Richard Blamer, Biekerstaffe ; second, £3 • 108, John Dean, Rain- ford; third, £2, Thomas Owen, Hainford ;, fourth, £l, Edward Scarisbrick, Bickerstaffe; fifth, 155., Edmund Berry, Skel- meradare ; sixth, EX, William Forshaw„, Skelmersdale. Third-class ploughmen, being men who reside and who have never l got a first prize in the third-class, or any prize Many other class :—First prize, £2, Henry Webster, Rainford; Ekcond, £l, Thomas VVebater, Rah:lord ; third, 10k., James Laithwaite, Rainford. A prize of £1 was awarded to Isaac Plunkett, Ecciestom ploughman for Mr. William Birchall, for having the cleanest and neatest turnout,, as regards the person, horse and harness, the harness not being new; Geo. Moss, of Bickerstaffe, receiving the second prize. A prize of 108. was awarded to Isaac Plunkett, Eccleston, for having the beat pair of horses in the ploughing match, being the property of Mr. W. Birchall. At five olclock the competi- tors and committee sat down to a substantial dinner pro- vided at the house of Mr. James Middlehurst, Junction Hotel, near to the field. Mr. Richard Tilkington, of Bain- ford Hall, presided, and toasts and songs followed the removal of the cloth. •

div.head: ST. HELENS PARLLAZENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: ST. HELENS PARLLAZENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.
The usual meeting of this sooiety was held on Frida7 evening, Dr. MeNicoll (the speaker) presiding. . .

The member for DEVONSHIRE continued the debate on the Ministerial statement, and congratulated the Conservative Ministry on their very liberal ,policy. That being his maiden speech he would try in his very humble woy to criticise the statement. As to reoommending Greece to accept "any reasonable offer " from the Turks, the sooner 'Turkey was swept away from the face of the earth the better for this country. Ele also.condemned that paragraph elating to the energetic military measures in the 'trans- vaal, and which expressed the hope that British authority would be coon established there. Lie defended the Boers and their action in the present 'struggle, and said there was not a greater land robber under the sun than England. Who stole Scotland? The .English. (Laughter.) Who stole Ireland? The English. (More laughter.) Who stole Wales? The English. (Renewed laughter.) And who wanted two millions of money in respect to Candahar, and who was going to pay it.? <The member for WINDSOR, on the Conservative benches: The English.) (Laughter.) That was very.ques- tionable when they had gentlemen like Gladstone,. Bright and Charles Dilke at the helm of affairs. He wished success to the Boer Republic, and a fig for British tyranny and despotism. English Jingoism could be better explained in a parody of the well-known Jingo song—
We don't want to fight, but by Jingo if we do, We'd ratherafight the Nachman, for we then put on the screw, --• • - •

The member for WOODSTOCE, in dealing with the argu- ments of the previous speaker, remarked that the Aborigines had as much right in the Transvaal as had the Dutch settlers, and if the English Government could govern the place better, then they had a perfect right to do so. If the natives were ground down by the Boers, as he contended they were, it was time for the British to interfere. The second member for CANTERBURY !oohed upon the Ministerial statement with a mixed feeling of astonishment and pleasure. Its most important paragraphs were essen- tially Radical. When Len. gentlemen were in Opposition nothing was too harsh with regard to Ireland; but now a change had come over them, and they had a warm anprecia- tion of Radical teaching—(" No ")—and their most impor- tant paragraph was kindred to the one they condemned when in Opposition, only they travelled far beyond what they then described as Communistic in tendency, and in- volving principles which no business man in fairness and justice could adopt. He received with unqualified pleasure Ike intimation that fraud, force, and folly were now changed to fixity of tenure, free sale, and fair rents. That was what he called turning ths political coat. As to advising Greece to accept any reasonable offer, would Turkey do that? (Member for South Devon : She has.) Well, did she ever intend to fulfil it? (Laughter.) He had no doubt the hon. member thought so honestly, but be (the speaker) could only stand in wonder at the childlike simplicity of his mind. (Laughter.) He thought the policy showed a base desertion of a noble country struggling to recover some of its ancient glory, and was a blot and stain upon the Con- servative Ministry. The hon. member for PORTSIDMITM next addressed the House, and was proceeding to criticise the conduct of Mr. Gladstone when it was ruled by the Speaker on a point of order raised by the late Solicitor-General that be was travel- ling away from the subject. He then went on to say that the Imperial Government, with Mr. Gladstone at its head, were engaged in three little wars, but this provoked cries of " Left by the Tories." The hon. member for BODMIN said in reading over the Ministerial statement be bad come to the conclusion that all the Conservatism had settled down to the bottom, the last paragraph expressing the intention of the Government to maintain the union between Church and State, and to keep intact the British Constitution. (Laughter.) He really could not understand what modern Conservatism meant. For example, they had, a proposed measure for legalising marriage with a deceased wife's sister, although all the bishops voted strongly against it a while ago. In reference to the paragraph about the Cor- rupt Practices Bill, which they were going to introduce, he read an extract showing that one of the Conservative can- didates at the general election began the contest with the intention of procuring votes corrupt, and a magistrate, a town councillor,Vand he regretted to say a churchwarden, put forth the sum of £1,500, which was distributed amongst the electors. _ After criticising the Irish parSgraph, he went on to say that the war in the Transvaal was the result of the immoral policy of the late Government—the policy of centralisation as opposed to Radical ideas. The bon. member for CHRISTCHURCH (Conservative) did sot see what the Conservatives had to do with a Bench of Bishops, and why they should be frightened of the bishops in bringing in a bill to legalise marriage with a deceased wife's sister, as he believed the majority ef them were Liberals. Notices of questions were then given, and the House adjourned.

THE LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY COM- PANI.-At the half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of this company, on Wednesday, it was stated that the com- pensation to passengers for perscnal injuries amounted to the sum of £23,000, an increase of £16,000, principally due to the accident at Burscough Junction, but the chairman said it might be considered that the liabilities connected with that accident were all settled. A considerable increase was announced in the receipts from both passengers and merchandise traffic. The report was adopted.

8-- MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES.

On Wednesday the annual home and foreign missionary meeting was held in the Free Methodist Church, Oakland- street, Widnes. Mr. C. Jones presided, and there were also present the Revs. H. J. Weatherhead, St. Helens,- and J. Billington. The CRAIRMAN said the object of the meeting was to discuss mission work at home and abroad. There was a great work to4sbe done, and they all knew that without means that work could not be carried on. There were hundreds in our own land who never entered a place of worship, and some even who never heard the word of God used except in oaths. Missionaries who were toiling for the Master in distant lands had to be sustained, and others were still needed.', They could not all be missionaries, but they might all contribute their mite towards helping the

cause. Mr. GANDY, of Runcorn, read the report, which he said ; was certainly gratifying. Notwithstanding all the bad trade, they had been enabled to send to the missions the , wain of £l5 during the year. There were many difficulties in the way of the foreign missionary, and he did not hesi- tate to say that one ef them was bad legislation. In Africa the white man had to face the facts of the mean actions done by some of our fathers, and although he preached that our religion was one of love and peace, there were many demonstrations to the contrary. But were they to fall back because of the difficulties which beset them? He trusted not, but hoped that by the grace of God they would level the mountain to a plain. The Rev. J. BILLINGTON said they might depend upon it that the man who kept his religion to himself would not experience the same joy as one who tried to spread it. He wished them all to believe that they were brethren, and that it was the duty of every Christian to help his brother. The brave men who went out with their lives in their hands to preach to the heathen, often came home again wasted and worn out, through toiling in unhealthy climates, and such deserved the sympathy and prayers of all and as much of their cash as they could spare. The Rev. H. J. WEATHERHEAD said they had met together to advance, as far as they could, the work of home and foreign missions. Even as a matter of pure selfishness it was a wise thing to engage in the missionary work. Some people asked him whether anything had been accom- plished by religious work. If they looked around them, they would find evidences of much good done in every country of the globe. In conclusion, he hoped that they would all do their utmost to spread the blessed tidings of the Gospel. The proceedings terminated after the usual collection had seen made.

FRODSHA.M. FRODSHAM CHURCH TEMPERANCE MEETING.—A public meeting of the Frodsham branch of the Church Temperance Society was held in the Girls' School on Wednesday, when the vicar presided, and addresses were delivered by the Rev. W. Cogswell, vicar of St. Thomas's, Chester, and the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, senior curate of Frodsham. A number of recitations and temperance melodies were given by the members of the Band of Hope. HARE AND Horrms " meet " of the Frodsham Hare and Hounds Club took place in Overton, on Saturday afternoon, the hares being Messrs. Daniel Ashton and Albert Harrison. There was a poor muster of members, but a good run was made, the " track " leading them through Beacon Hill, the Forest, Ashton, Manley, Dunham, and thence to Frodsham, the hares arriving about 20 minutes in advance of the pursuers. TAR " CAMERONIANS AT KINGSLEY.—A miscellaneouS concert and charade was given in the Kingsley school on Tuesday, by the Frodsham " Cameronians," in aid of the school fund, which it was explained by the vicar—Rev. Samuel Hague—was required to purchase desks, &c., for the girls' school. The first part of the programme consisted of glees, soon &c. Miss K. S. Rigby nicely rendered the song "Joy," and Messrs. George Rigby, John Rigby, and B. Rigby gave respectively "The Anchor's Weighed," "The Bay of Biscay," and "I fear no foe," which were all very successful. It was the first appearance of Mr. B. Rigby, who has a good baritone voice, and gives promise of being an acquisition to the local talent. Mr. W. Cameron received enthusiastic encores for the comic songs "He's got 'em on," and "When I gets to be a M.P., the latter song containing a hustings speech, which was capitally acted. Mr. Quayle received an encore for "Uncle Jack," and Mr. W. Digninn recited the pathetic piece called "The Beauti- ful Snow. The second part of the programme consisted of a charade in three parts, the solution being the word "night- mare," and showed that the " Cameronians " were "well up" in the histrionic art. Mr. George Rigby made a good Sir Jeremiah Griggs, and Robinson his clerk (Mr. B. Rigby). Snaggs the constable (Mr. J. Rigby), Farmer Danhead (Mr. W. Cameron), Mrs. Larkins (Miss B. Rigby), and the house- maid (Miss K. Rigby) were well impersonat d. The other characters in the piece were also taken by the same persons, the change of costume being quickly effected. Mr. W. Dignum gave a stump speech in character, which was much enjoyed. An appropriate epilogue was recited by Mr G. Rigby. The R2Y. S. Hague proposed a vote of thanks to the " Cameronians," and remarked that their services were entirely gratuitous. The motion was seconded by Mr. Robert Ashton, and carried by acclamation. The amount received at the door was £l4 9s.

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. ROBBERIES ABOUT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON-LE- WILLOWS.—On Saturday morning last, two sheep belonging to Mr. T. Stone were stolen, after being killed and skinned ha the field. Several fortes were visited, and quantities of potatoes taken away; some hen roosts were patronized and large numbers of valuable fowls stolen. A lot of the fowls' heads, wings, &c., were found afterwards on Newton Com- mon. Marty trees, hedges, &c., have also been cut down for firewood about Earlestown. MEETING OF COLLIERS AT NEWTON COMMON. The meeting fixed for Monday last on Newton Common turned out a complete failure, as only about 200 or 250 were pre- sent, the greater proportion of the number being from the Leigh district. Many present did not appear in the best of humour, seeming bent on mischief, but their numbers were too small to succeed in any demonstration of that kind, par- ticularly as every precaution haul been taken by stationing a sufficient force of police at a convenient distance. Many colliers under Messrs. Evans and Co. resumed work, on Monday, and others followed during the succeeding days. During the strike the colliers in this district and their families have suffered terribly, notwithstanding a fair amount of liberality shown to them by the inhabitants. FORMATION OF A STARR-BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY me EARLESTOWN.—A lecture was delivered on Monday, in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, by the founder of the Starr-Bowkett Building Societies, Mr. R. B. Starr, who is becoming well known in Lancashire, and was attended by a crowded audience. The lecture being the first step towards establishing one of these societies in Earlestown, great interest was exhibited. The chair was occupied by Mr. James Fairclough, one of the trustees, who was supported by Messrs. E. T. Evans, E. Ice, H. L. Riley (solicitor to the society), J. Roberts, J. Barr, W. Blair, W. Mills, J. Talbot, J. Taylor, and 0. A. Griffin (secretary to the society and to the Ist and 2nd St. Helens societies) and others. The lecturer' after being briefly introduced by the chairman, said he had to perform a very pleasing duty to lecture upon the interesting questions "Why pay rent, and how can I become my own landlord by the payment of a small weekly subscription ?" They had not come up to that perfection " Don't pay rent," and had not come to "Boycott" them, but to " Bowkett " them. Thrift was the theme of the day—every one was talking and writing about thrift, and he was sorry that the things they had then were not introduced years ago. It was a grand thing for workingmen to be able to save something after working hard. Yet how many work- ing men were there who never Bayed a penny? Instead of living for 20 years in a house and not a brick of it being theirs, by the exercise of a little forethought every brick of the house might become their own. He had not come there in hostility to existing societies for they could not do the work his societies did. As a rule in a permanent society to borrow £3OO, a person would have to find property worth .i 350 and when he had borrowed would have interest to pay —in other words an advance of £3OO would cost £450. lie had known working-men long enough to say that there were very few who were able to borrow under such circum- stances. In explaining the working of the societies Mr. Starr referred to the very small amount of the weekly subscription-6d. per share—which was fixed low so as not to shut out the working classes. On each share a member would be entitled to £lOO free of interest, and after every member had received an advance the subscriptions thetas - selves would be returned, less Is. 3d. per year per share for working expenses. The first subscription night of that society was fixed for the 28th of March, and five weeks after that date the first appropriation would be made. A member could use his ballot in three ways (Ist) he could buy pro- perty, the full value of which would be advanced to him; (2nd) he could return it to the society until he wanted it; -or (3rd) he could sell it and make a handsome profit. The last appropriation had been calculated to take place in 18 years. The societies had several sources of profit, viz., pre- miums were charged to those members who sold their appro- priations ; the society could buy and re-sell, giving the pur- chaser opportunity of repaying the purchase money along with his repayments ; then there was bank interest arid fines, but the latter could be avoided by members if they chose to pay as much advance as in arrears. After more fully explaining the general working details of the society, Mr. Starr spoke in an earnest, eloquent manner of the moral and social effect of such societies, urged upon parents the duty of making provision for their children, and of all pro- viding against the workhouse and old age. After the lecture Mr. Starr threw the meeting open for questions, but no ques- tions were asked. Directors and auditors wee then appointed, Is many as 200 shares being then taken up.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

On Thursday the monthly meeting was held, and pre- ceded by an extraordinary meeting—held a quarter of an hour earlier—for the purpose of electing a member to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. W. H. Price. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis presided, and there were also present the Rev. George Holloway, and Messrs. Bradshaw, Brock, O'Keeffejaylor, Shaw, and Danby (clerk). Mr. Bitans-new moved that Mr. Richard Holden Davis, of 166, Upper Parliament-street, Liverpool, be elected. Mr. Bnocit seconded the motion, which was carried unani- mously, and after the Chairman had declared Mr. Davis elected, the proceedings of the extraordinary meeting ter- minated, and the ordinary business was proceeded with. THE OFFICERS OF THE BOARD AND THEIR DUTIES. Mr. DEACON read the report of the District Education Committee, which stated that during the month of January the number of cases summoned before the committee was 210, of which 138 were applications for payment of fees, and 72 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 128 cases, five applications were refused, and five adjourned for further enquiries. The com- mittee recommended that permission be given to the atten- dance officers to act as enumerators, and assist the sub- registrars with information in taking the census in April next. Mr. Deacon proposed the adoption of the report. The CHAIRMAN seconded the proposition. Mr. MARTIN TAYLOR took distinct objection to the re- commendation about enumerators, and said the other day the Clerk had shown him a letter from one of the Board's head teachers, asking a similar favour. He thought they I ought not to encourage servants of the Board in making such applications, when they knew very well that there were many men who knew the district quite as well as their attendance officers who were out of employment, and had not the means of keeping their families. He hoped that the decision which would be given by the Board on that occa- sion would put a stop to applications of a similar descrip- tion being made at any future time. There was one point which it was highly probable would prove a barrier in the way of the engagement of the officers, even if the Board were agreeable to such a course being adopted, and that was the horror which some parents bad of a man holding such a position coming near their houses. It was very likely that some of the inhabitants would lock up their houses and go out if they saw an attendance officer at the top of the street. The sub-registrar would get handsomely paid for his work, and be might easily get other men to do the work. Mr. DEACON explained that the sole wish of the commit- tee in bringing the matter forward was to test the feeling of the Board. As far as the committee were concerned, they were perfectly willing to withdraw the recornmenda-

tion. The Comintern said he agreed pretty much with Mr. Taylor's remarks, as he thought the officers of the Board ought not to do any work but that for which they were engaged. Mr. SHAW was of opinion that the earning of extra pay in such a manner as suggested by the recommendation would "unsettle the officers." It was suggested that the recommendation be withdrawn, but Mr. Taylor said he should prefer that the question be put to the vote. He, however, ultimately agreed to the motion being withdrawn.

o r, rMANAGEMENTeom m endion This committee'sscSCHOOL atCOs were roved, on the motion of Mr. TAYLOR, seconded by the CHAIRMAN. They contained a report on the Government grants received by the schools during the year ending August 31st. Mr. TAYLOR said the committee had two reports before them, one applying to the Board and the other to voluntary schools. It was agreed that the retarns be adopted and printed. THE FINANCES.—THE YEAR'S ESTIMATE. The Finance Committee submitted their estimate of the income and expenditure of the Board for the year ending September 29th. 1881, viz. :—School Management Commit- tee. Simm's Cross School :—Eatimated expenditure, £1,225; school fees estimated, £400; Government grant, £554 95.; other sources, £2O. Warrington-road School :—Estimated expenditure, £760; school fees estimated, £l9O ; Government grant, £229 175.; other sources, £2. West Bank School : Estimated expenditure, £1,395; school fees estimated, £420; Government grant, £562 Sc.; other sources, Lit's. The dif- ference between the estimated expenditure and the receipts was £982 65. The estimated expenditure of the committees was :—District Education Committee, £352; sites and build- ing, £4O; Finance Committee, £1,741. This made the total sans respired £3,115 6s. Mr. SHAW, in moving the adoption of the estimates, said the Government grant for 1879, exclusive of the sum I received from the Science and Art Department, was £1,151 10s., against £1,347 14s. for 1880. The school fees for 1879 were £955 3s. 54., as compared with £1,106 12s. sd. for last year, or £l5O more. During the last year they had received £374 6s. Id. more than in 1879, and paid away more by £297 ss. Bd. • During last year the average attendance had been 179 more than in 1879. The cost of teaching per head of the children in average attendance for the year ending August 31st, 1880, was 4s. Old. After adding, the interest and repayments on loans in each school, be obtained the following results :-13s. 2d. per head in Simm's Cross school, Warrington-road. £l7s. 2d., and West Bank 12s. 7d. The difference between the two last named schools was very great. It was proposed that the £3,115 6s. should be re- duced by £Bl5, and that tke Board issue a precept on the overseers for £2,300, being the estimated amount of the deficiency in the school fund. He moved a motion to this effect, and that the precept be made payable on or before the 31st March. The CHAIRMAN seconded the resolution, and said he believed the amount would necessitate a rate of sd. in the £. It would no doubt be very gratifying to the ratepayers to I find that their schools were doing more work at a less coat than formerly. The motion was passed without dessent. THE BOARD'S CONTRACT FOR COKE. The CLERK read a reply from Mr. Roberts, enginer to the Local Board, as to the alleged non-sup Ply of coke during the frost. The communication stated that at the time referred to all parties were served alike in reference to the supply of coke; and if they had adopted any other course, they would have had to stop pumping water for the inhabitants. In conclusion, the enginer wished to remind the clerk that the present arrangements only related to the year ending the 31st December next, and that the carrying of it out was subject i to the proviso that there was coke n the yard when a supply was required. The CHAIRMAN: lam told that there is an actual written contract between us and the Local Board. Mr. TAYLOR urged the importance of sending a reply to the letter. The CHAIRMAN said he was not sure that Mr. Taylor was not right, considering the fact that Mr. Roberts quibbled in the manner seen in the letter, when he must have known there was a contract. llthe School Board silently acquiesced it simply meant that the Local Board would ao precisely the same thing on another occasion. I The CLERK read the correspondence which had taken place between himself and Mr. Roberts, from which it ap- peared that the Gas Committee had agreed to supply the Board with coke at 7s. per ton up to the 31st December, 1881. Mr. Muses( : It is rather good to say there is no contract after that. (Laughter.) Mr. TAYLOR: If we find in another fortnight that the flues at the schools are all blocked, and we have to spend £2O in opening them, the Local Board will be liable. The CHAIRMAN said it would amount to pretty much the same thing, as the cost would in either case come out of the pockets of the ratepayers. He reminded the Board that at the time of the discussion on the ques' ion of the fair there appeared to be a feeling on the part of the Lceal Board that the School Board had treated them slightly discourteously. As there was a little acrimoniousness, it would perhaps be as well to try and settle the matter amicably. Dr. O'KERFFE said he had no doubt the Chairman wished them to act in harmony with the Local Board and every other public body in the neighbourhood. The Gas Corn- ' mittee, he believed, acknowledged there was a contract to I let the Board have coke, but, if they had not supplied the pumping stations at the time referred to, the general public would have had to suffer the greatest inconvenience from a want of water. Mr. BROOK said that notwithstanding the observations of Dr. O'Keeffe, the only official document received from, them said the-e was no such contract. Dr. O'KEEFFE: Both Major Cross and Mr. Allen acknow- ledged that there was a contract. The CHAIRMAN : Then their servant should not have wi itten such a letter. Dr. O'KEEFFE : He wrote it on his own account. He was instructed to give an explanation, and he must have added the remark referred to himself. It was agreed that the Clerk should write to the Local Board stating that tile School Board could not accept the letter of Mr. Roberts, and calling their attention to the letters which had passed between them and Mr. Danby, in which a contract was clearly implied. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

CIIIIRCII OF ENGLANINTEMPERANCE SOCIETY, OUGHTRING- I TON BRANCIL—On Monday evening a public meeting was held under the auspices of tae above society in the Parochial Schools, Oughtrington, at which there was a mood atten- dance. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. B. Dew"hurst, who gave an address setting forth the :advantages of temperance as instanced by his own experience. Addresses were also given by the Rev. W. 11. L. Cogswell, M.A., of St. Oswalds, Chester, and the Rector (the Rev. J. Cullen, M.A.) Songs were given by Mrs. G. B. Dewhurst, and Mrs. G. C. Dew- hurst, and by several members of the church choir. Votes of thanks to tho chairman and speakers brought a most successful meeting to a close. LYMM CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.—The annual monthly meeting of the above society was held on Monday, in the schoolroom, Brookfield-road, at which there was a fair attendance. Mr. Dan Boyd (president), occupied the chair, and gave an address. An address was also given by the Rev. 3. Adamson, of Altrincham, which was most attentively listened to. Recitations and dialogues were given by the members. A Lancashire reading given by Mr. Jas. Mort provoked much laughter. Several songs were rendered by the choir in creditable style, under the leadership of Mr. J. G. Ardern.
Wenarmyrort CEMETERY. - The interments in the War- rington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday, were —Adults, 8; children, 8; total, 16.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. George Pilkington. A VIOLENT SON AT FARNWORTR.—Thornas Fletcher, master wheelwright, of School -brow,Farnworth, was brought up in custody charged with committing wilful damage to a door and window of his father's house.—Complainant said that the prisoner came there on Saturday, asked for his wife and children, and, because be would not give prisoner ad- mission, he broke in the windows and door, doing damage to the amount of ss. He should be glad if the Bench would remand the prisoner, so that he might undergo a medical examination, as complainant believed him to be suffering from mental derangement. Last summer his son was sent to Haydock Lodge Asylum for one month, owing to his ex- cessive drinking. Prisoner had again been indulging in liptor.—Prisoner, in a somewhat excited manner, said, in answer to the charge, that he went to the house for his wife and children, and, as his father would not admit him, he broke one of the uindows, which he considered be was quite justified in doing.—The Inspector of Police stated that on the previous Thursday the prisoner was in the neighbour- hood and caused a large crowd to collect, as a number of children were wheeling him about upon a hand cart.—Mr. Pilkington said the young man would be remanded until Wednesday, as he did not consider he was fit to beat liberty, and in the mean time he would be examined by a medical man as to his mental condition. TUE SIIIPWRIGIIT AND HIS LODGER.—Edward Leach, alias Thomas Leach, who had been apprehended on coming out of gaol after suffering one munth's imprisonment for stealing a coat, was charged with having, on the 7th ult., stolen two silver guards and other property, belonging to Jonathan Shepherd, shipwright, 28, Gladstone-street.—The prosecutor said that on the 7th ult, the prisoner came to his I house, and en his statement that he was an engineer from I Crewe, he was taken in as a lodger. He remained until thel 9th ult., when he departed, saying he was going to Carlisle, and he did not see him again. On the 12th ult. he missed a long silver watch guard, a common guard, a shoulder shawl, and two handkerchiefs, all of which were now produced by the police. At the time when Leach remained at the house the goods were all kept in the looking glass drawer in his bddroom.—John Duffy said that on the 16th ult, the prisoner came to the place where he (witness) was at work, and offered him a watch guard pawn ticket, for which he gave him ninepence. He gave the ticket to P.C. Clarkaon.—The prisoner was committed for trial at the Quarter Sessions. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Bibby (chairman) and Mr. • George Pilkington. DrtmexErtrrEss. —For being guilty of this offence in Fishers-road, Lugsdale, on the 12th inst., Patrick Murray, Mary Murray, Mary Melia, and John Melia were each fined ss. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment, on the evidence of P.C. Strickland.—James Pye was fined a similar amount and costs for a like offence on the 12th inst. P.C. Clarkson proved the case. UNLAWFUL REMOVAL OF GOODS.—Patrick O'Brien was charged by Mr. Thomas Carlile with having, on the 25th January, unlawfully removed certain goods.—Mr. T. Carlile said lie was agent for Mr. J. W. Carlile, and the defendant was tenant of a cottage belonging to that gentleman. O'Brien owed Bs. 6d. for rent, and witness called for it, but did not receive payment. He again visited the house about a week after, and found that the defendant had left and re- moved his goods. O'Brien had, however, still possession of the key.—A woman, named Mrs. Connor, stated that she , saw the goods being taken away on the 25th January, at an hour when it was quite dark.—The wife of defendant appeared, and said the cottage was in a delapidated condi- tion. Her husband had now been out of work some seven weeks, but she was quite willing to pay the arrears on the! following Saturday.—The Magistrates agreed to accept the defendant's wife's promise, or, her paying 6s. 6d. costs. ALLEGED ILLEGAL PAW*.TING. Margaret Hughes was charged with illegally pawning goods belonging to James Mcßride, between September, 1880, and January, of this year.—Mr. Beasley defended.—James Mcßride said he re- cently lodged with the defendant at Sutton's-lane. He found he had lost five shirts, two pairs of trousers, and a flannel shirt, and he asked defendant about the goods, on which she told him they were in pawn, and gave him the tickets produced. They bore the name of Mrs. Hughes, but he had never given her any authority to pledge the articles, which were worth 255. In answer to the question why she had pawned the goods, defendant said, " One will do many things when they are in distress." In cross-examination by Mr. Beasley, complainant denied having left defendant in debt for board and lodgings. He never asked her to pledge goods for him. —Mr. Joseph Jamieson proved the pledging of the things at his mother's shop in Anne-street.—Mr. Beasley said the mouth of defendant was closed, or otherwise he could soon put a very different complexion upon the matter. The com- plainant did not come into court with clean hands, for he stated that after he had lodged with the defendant a short time, his payments became irregular, and, at the time he left, a was owing for board and lodging. Defendant was also aware that some of the goods were pawned in Decem- ber, and yet he remained at the house.—Mrs. Hughes stated that she had a distinct authority to pawn the goods.—The Chairman said the magistrates did not consider there was sufficient evidence to convict, and the summons would be

dismissed. COAL Srrger.mo.—Margaret Ann Dawson, who had been I convicted several times previously, was charged, on remand, I with stealing 561bs. of coal, the property of Messrs. Richard Evans, from a wagon on the Marsh, upon the 16th instant. Thli prisoner was seen to take the coal from near one of the wagons by a clerk who was in an office near the place, and he canght her and gave information to the police.—She was sent to gaol one month, with hard labour. THE CASE OF A VIOLENT SON. Thomas Fletcher, master wheelwright, was again brought up, from Monday, charged with committing wilful damage to a door and win- dow, belonging to his father. The latter sated that he had seen Dr. Cooper that morning, and he said the prisoner would be rational enough if he would only keep from drink. The prisoner had promised him (witness) that he would abstain from it altogether. He hoped that, under these cir- cumstances, the Bench would kindly permit him to with- draw the charge.—The Chairman: Then you forgive him the damage he has done ?—Complainant: Yes, I will pay that myself.—Prisoner said that if the magistrates would look over the case he promised to abstain from all intoxi- cating drink in the future, and live a better life. The Chairman (to the prisoner): On that promise you will be discharged.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY
AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of, this Authority was held in the Board-room, at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present— Mr. John Ashton (in the chair), Rev. J. N. Tanner, Messrs. J. Smith, sen., J. Midwood, J. Knowles, J. Weir, J. Darby- shire, J. Challoner, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk).

FRODSHAM SEWERAGE. A letter was read from the Local Government Board which stated that notices of the enquiry which they had instructed one of their inspectors to hold in respect to the appeal against the apportionment to the township and lordship of Frodsham had been sent, and requesting that the notices be posted as required in the district. MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANIMAL REPORT. The MEDICAL OFFICER (Mr. J. G. Bride) reported that during the last quarter of the year 1880 the returns of the registrar recorded 150 births and 75, deaths in the three dis- tricts making a birth rate of 8.35. and a death rate of 4.17 per 1,000. Of the births, 79 were males, and 71 females; and of the deaths n were males, and 37 fetriales. During the corresponding quarter of 1879, the number of birth i was 144, the birth rate being 8.02 per 1,000; and the nunffier of deaths was 88, the death rate being 4.90 per 1,000. The number of births for the entire district in 1880 was 613, and the number of deaths 325, being a birth rate of 34.14,1 and a death rate of 18 lOtper 1,000. The greatest difficulty was experienced in obtaining information respecting infectious disease. The plan adopted in some towns of offering a small fee of half a crown to medical men in charge of such cases , for a report of each case as it came to their knowledge, he.l \respectfully suggested might with great advantage obtain in that district. There was a great need of a better water supply to Preston Brook and Dutton cottages, notwithstand- ing the improved state of things at Preston-o'-th'-Hill. Mr. Bride expressed a hope that the Authority would see their way to carry out the Frodsham sewerage scheme as early as possible, as well as to improve the water supply to the same ~ _

1.0.G.T. MORNING STAR LODGE, NO. 302, St. HELESTS.-A united lodge meeting was held under the auspices of the above lodge, on Thursday evening, at King's cocoa-rooms; Westfield House, convened for the purpose of electing a visiting deputy for the St. Helens lodges. A good number was present. Bro. R. W. Kirkus, Tr.S., of Liverpool, was invited to preside, and after he had made a few opening remarks, Bro. T. Pickersgill, W.C.T., Morning Star Lodge, explained the object of their meeting together that evening, and invited members present to state their views on the subject. In response, Bros. Lindon, and Haddy, W.C.T., both of Ebenezer Lodge, addressed the meeting, after which Bro. T. Pickersgill, W.C.T., Morning Star Lodge, was unanimously elected V.D. for St. Helens. At this stage of the proceedings, and at the unanimous re- quest of the members present, Bro. Kirkus read his paper on "Duty and work." The paper was a very able and pithy one, and speaking on philanthropy and philanthropists lof the past and prestnt, likened our work and duty to theirs. Strong drink was making terrible inroads on the peace of society,theirduty as Good Templars was plain on the gigantic Iwork of eradicating and eventually banishing from their midst, the drink fiend, and its direful work. Their course of I action was plain too, and the suggested spheres of labour open to each one, were so numerous and varied, that even the most timorous in their ranks could do something to help to emancipate the slaves of strong drink. In conclusion he urged the membership to renewed vigour and effort, in pro- moting the work cf temperance, as it was plainly their duty solo do. A vote of thanks was accorded to Bro. Kirkus for his deeply interesting and pithy paper. A very pleasant time was spent in a kind of experience meeting relative to the good emanatitg from the Good Templar cause, which was taken part in by Bros. Kirkus, Haddy, Bird, Douglas, Linden, and T. Pickersgill. A vote of thanks was given to Bro. Kirkus, for his presence that evening. £lO TO £SO.—TOBACCONISTS COMMENCING.-A Pamphlet, How to open a Shop from £lO, post free —Address, H. Myxns ro., Cigar and Tobacco Manufacturers, (P 101 Euston-road, London, and at Birmingham. Established n years. Wholesale

THE EXAMINER, .SATURDAY FEBRUARY 26, lBBl. RUNCORN POLICE COURT. •

MoNuay.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick (chairman), and Mr. Charles Hazlehurst. THE CASE OF ALLEGED NON-PAYMENT FOR SERVICES OF THE FIRE BRIGADE.—Mr. Ashton, re igistrate's clerk, stated that in the case of the summons d • ainst Mr. Stephen Ravenscroft, farmer, Kingsley, who wa, charged at the pre- vious sessions, by the Runcorn Boat, of Commissioners, with not having paid the sum of £24 59., being the amourt charged by the Fire Brigade for attending a fire at Kingsley, a settlement had been arrived at. A HINT TO YOUTHFUL COAL DEALERS.—A youth named Richard Done, was charged with allowing his donkey and cart to remain in Bridge-street for an unreasonable time, on the 16th inst.—P.C. Bossons gave evidence to the effect that defendant's donkey and cart were allowed to remain in the street without anyone in charge of them, for twenty minutes, and during that time about a dozen carts and some carriages, had to pass the point where they were. Defendant was fined ss. and costs, 10s. 6d. THE FURIOUS DRIVING NUISANCE IN BRIDGE-STREET.— A respectably drsssed lad named Isaac Johnson was sum- moned for furiously driving a horse and and cart in Bridge. street, on the 16th instant.—P.C. Hibbert stated that about a quarter to four o'clock in the afternoon he was on duty at the police station, and saw the defendant driving a horse and can past" at a sort of wild gallop." He followed him up Budge-street, and afterwards reported him.—Superintendent Williamson said he was in his office at the time, and saw the horse gallop past. The lad did not use all the effort he might have done to stop it, and he sent P.C. Hibbert after him. He (witness) also made enquiry into the matter, and he was informed that the galloping of the horse was caused by the defendant "jerking" it when near the Post Office. Of course their worships knew that it was a very dangerous practice for anyone to drive at a pace like that mentioned in a town like Runcorn, and especially so at that part of any thoroughfare where there was such a de- clivity as at the bottom of High-street. The Bench must be aware that in a case where a horse was rapidly driven at such a point, it would be nearly impossible for any foot passenger to get out of the way. He had no desire to press the case, but he wished the public to understand that such conduct could not be tolerated.—Mr. Thomas Acton, farmer, Norton, said the defendant was in his employ. He could not understand the horse running away, as it ryas such a slow one that be invariably avoided taking it out. It had a very "hard-mouth," and he could easily comprehend that it would be very difficult for a person of the age of defen- dant to stop it if it commenced galloping. Defendant, in reply to the Bench, said the horse was started off by a large' black dog at the time it was coming down High-street.,— ' The magistrates said they would adjourn the case fora week I in order that defendant might call as a witness a boy who was in the cart at the time. DRUNK on IN A Fa 2—Mary Ann Hellier was charged with having been drunk in High-street on the 19th inst.— Sergeant McMichael pro sed the case.—Defendant said she , was subject to fits, and the officer who took her in custody I found her in one. She was not drunk —The superinten- dent of police gave evidence which clearly proved the pri-1 Boner was very drunk when apprehended.—She was fined ss. and 9s. 4d. costs, or in default of payment seven days' imprisonment. ALLEGED GROSS ASSAULT ON A PUBLICAN.—JOI3III Williams, Henry Smith, and James Colclough, were charged with violently assaulting Mr. Thomas Hodgkinson, land- lord, and stealing his jacket, containing ss. Bd. in money.— The complainant said he kept the Mariners' Hotel, Percival's- , 'lane. On the previous Thursday night, prisoners were at his house together with a man named Larkin. They caused some disturbance, and he had to get the prisoner Colclough and Larkin out. In about ten minutes afterwards they re- entered, set upon him, got him down, and kicked him in the stomach. They kept crying out, "Give it him." They also struck him a number of times. He was wearing the jacket produced at the time, and it contained about ss. Bd. The prisoners took the jacket and the money. During the row, and before the garment was taken. prisoner Smith entered and struck him several times. Prisoner Williams was standing close to him when the assault took place, and was there when the jacket, which was worth 16s. 6d., was pulled off. Some persons came to his assistance, and prisoners left. About ten minutes after the assault, and also on the Friday morning, Williams came into the house and said "it was a shame" he (complainant) should have been assaulted in the manner be had.—John Pugh, boat dis- charger, living in Holloway, and Master Thomas Hodgkin- son also gave evidence as to the assault.—Master Albert Williams, son of Mr. Williams, grocer, Top Locks, said that on the night of the disturbance he heard a number of men talking near the shop, and one of them (whom he could not recognise) said, "Never mind, we have got the jacket."— Mary Millington, wife of Wm. Millington, living in a court off Duke-street, said she had known the prisoner Williams between two and three years. On Thursday night, between nine and ten o'clock, Williams came to her house with the jacket, and asked if he could leave it until morning. She allowed him to do so, and he went away. On the following morning she gave the jacket up to the police.—Sergeant McMichael stated that he apprehended the prisoner Williams after finding the jacket at the house of the last witness. On being charged, Williams said he found the jacket in the street.—lnspector Hollingworth stated that he apprehended the prisoner Smith on Saturday morning, and he said, "I did bit him' but I know nothing of the jacket." On Sunday morning he received Colclough into custody at Manchester Town Hall, but he did not make any acknowledgment of his I guilt.—Prisoners were committed to the Knutsford Quarter I Sessions for trial. I THURSDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman), and Mr. S. B. Chadwick. ROBBERY BY A NEEHEW.—Wm. Ernest Bradbury, aged 14, was charged with having, on the 19th inst, stolen 10s., the money of John Thomason, butcher, Bridge-street. Mrs. Thomason said her husband was uncle to the prisoner, who was an orphan, and had lived with them two years. On the previous Thursday' night, she had safe in her drawer in her I bedroom, two packets of copper, each of which contained ss. I On the following Sunday, she missed the money. Though the prisoner had been out of the way some days, he was seen in the yard of the house on Saturday. She gavel information to the police after missing the money, and they apprehended the prisoner. For some time past he had been in the habit of stopping out all night and keeping bad company. She had frequently missed things out of the house. She had been to Superintendent Williamson about the matter, and that gentleman had had the youth in the police office and warned him what would be the result of his evil courses, if he continued them. She had done what she could to reclaim the prisoner, but all her efforts bad proved a failure.—P.C. Bossons said he met the prisoner on the 22nd inst, and said to him, "1 suppose you know what I want you for ?" He said "yes." He asked him what he had done with the money, and he answered that he had been to Liverpool and spent it.—lnspector Hollisgworth said Mrs. Thomason had frequently complained of the lad.—Prisoner was ordered to be imprisoned 21 ,days', with hard labour, and afterwards to be sent to a refofmatory for five years. THE SOCIAL EVlL.—Louisa Spencer was charged with soliciting men for an immoral purpose, in High-street, on the 23rd inst. P.C. Hibbert proved the case, and as the prisoner had been convicted twice previously, she was fined 40s. and 68. 4d. costs, or, in default of payment, one month's imprison- ment.

Mr. DAVIES said the monopolies granted to railway com- panies were granted by Act of Parliament, and he took it that the powers of the railway commission were also granted by Act of Parliament; and, therefore, as far as the legality of the proceedings Of the Court of Commission were con- cerned they were just on the same basis as the powers of the rail way companies. He had been reading the minutes of a railway company, in which the chairman of the company said several coal proprietors on that line bad objected very much to the railway company carrying coal for long distances at even less rates than for shorter distances because it suited the company, who said they would do what they liked. The colliery proprietors said they were suffering in consequence, but the chairman actually con- tended that the company had a right to carry at any rate they liked. After that it was absolutely necessary to have a court of appeal such as the Railway Commissioners. Mr. DLECKLY remarked that if Mr. Moon could show that the Commission had done anything in the course of their existence to injure the railway companies he would have some ground of complaint, but if he was dis- satisfied because they interfered with the arbitrary powers of the railway companies that was the very thing for which it was established. He hoped the Chamber would keep the question before them so that if there was any bill brought into Parliament they could make themselves beard when tlae time came. He had no doubt Mr. Chamberlain would do some- thing, because the people of Birmingham and Staffordshire complained very bitterly of the inequality to which they were subjected. With regard to the resolutions on bank- ruptcy, it was decided to endeavour to consolidate them so that the meeting would not have any conflicting resolutions put before them. They did that and a series of resolutions was passed which the Chamber would see from the report had been submitted to the President of the Board of Trade. These, he thought, upon the whole, carried out in more de- tail than they had done, the principles which they had from tine to time represented in various ways to the Government and it appeared to him the best way of dealing with the bankruptcy bill was to inform the Government what prlo- - it was they thought ought to be applied, in what way debtors should be dealt with, and under what circumstances bankruptcy proceedings should be taken. He thought if Mr. Chamberlain followed out the suggestions which were made to him he would introduce a bill which would be of very great service indeed to the community. The subject was discussed at considerable length, and he thought, upon the whole, discussed with very much advantage. e f lowing resolutions were passed by the Chambers:—" That in the opinion of the Association the principle that the creditor of a bankrupt should have the power of directing the administration of the estate by one or more trustees, selected by themselves, is a sound one, and ought to be ad- hered to in any new legislation on the subject of bank- ruptcy." "That no debtor shall be entitled to his discharge, except on an order of the Court granting such discharge to be made on application, of which at least seven days' notice shall be given to every creditor who has proved his claims. MAKINBON AND WILCOCK, in returning their sincere thanks to their numerous patrons and the public generally for the very kind and liberal support they have hitherto received, hope, by strict attention to the interests of their clients, and the prompt and faithful discharge ot their duties, to continue to merit the same; the more so, as they are able to offer ad- vantages not generally enjoyed by those engaged in the same business, Mr. Makinson having had from early youth practical experience of the English Timber, Stone and Building Trades, and of Farming in all its branches, being at the present time a farmer himself on a large scale; and, in addition, having served his apprenticeship to the ENGINEERING and MILLWRIGHT busi- ness, besides having had, during the last TEN years, consider- able practice in Valuing and Selling Colliery, Quarry, and other Machinery and Working Plant, Growing and Fallen Timber, I Farming Stocks, Growing and Gathered Produce, Stocks-in- Trade, household Furniture Innkeepers' Effects, Houses, Buildings, Landed Estates and Property generally, and also in eases involving Damage and Trespass. Mr. WILCOCK, also, has had the advantage of being brought up to Farming, together with that of having served an appren- ticeship to an eminent Veterinary Surgeon, combined with the experience he has had since his connection with this firm, enables him to give judicious and valuable advice in all cases in which be may be consulted. In a:inclusion, M. and W. beg their friends and the public generally to note that they have a trustworthy and efficient staff of assistants in their employ, who have been carefully trained to watch over the interests of those who favour the firm with their patronage; whilst last, but not least, their system of advertising, and the tacilities they possess of ensuring an extensive circulation, enable them to offer the utmost pos- sible publicity to any sales entrusted to their management.
